units.english_text: Τελευτήσαντός τινος τῶν εὐσεβῶν, προσκαλεῖται παρὰ τῶν Συγγενῶν αὐτοῦ ὁ ἱερὸς Κλῆρος· ἐλθόντες δὲ εἰς τὸν οἶκον, ἐν ᾧ τὸ λείψανον κεῖται, ἐὰν ᾖ καὶ Ἀρχιερεύς, λαμβάνουσι καιρὸν οἱ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ Διάκονοι· καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἱερεῖς βάλλουσιν Ἐπιτραχήλια, οἱ δὲ Διάκονοι ἐνδύονται Στιχάρια καὶ Ὠράρια κρατοῦντες θυμιατὰ καὶ δικηροτρίκηρα, τότε εἷς Ἱερεὺς μετὰ Διακόνου εἰσέρχονται ὅπου ὁ νεκρὸς κεῖται, καὶ ὁ μὲν Διάκονος ἐκφωνεῖ **Εὐλόγησον Δέσποτα**, ὁ Ἱερεὺς **Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός**, ὁ Διάκονος τὸ Τρισάγιον(2), ὁ Ἱερεὺς **Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν**, καὶ ψάλλουσιν εἰς ἦχον δ΄ τὰ Τροπάρια **Μετὰ πνευμάτων δικαίων τετελειωμένων**· **Εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν σου Κύριε, ὅπου πάντες οἱ Ἅγιοί σου ἀναπαύονται**· **Δόξα, Σὺ εἶ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, Καὶ νῦν, Ἡ μόνη Ἁγνὴ καὶ Ἄχραντος Παρθένος**.

units.slavonic_text: [English Facing Translation: Funeral Service for Those Fallen Asleep (Part 1, p. 911)]
units.english_text: Upon the death of one of the faithful, the clergy are summoned by the relatives of the deceased; and coming to the house wherein the body lies, if a hierarch is present, the priests and the deacons receive the liturgical blessing (*kairos*) from him. The priests put on their epitrachilia, and the deacons vest in sticharia and oraria, carrying censers and the dikerotrikera. Then one priest together with a deacon enter where the deceased lies, and the deacon exclaims: **“Master, give the blessing”** (*Εὐλόγησον Δέσποτα*). The priest: **“Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages”** (*Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός...*); the deacon chants the Trisagion Prayers; the priest intones the exclamation: **“For Thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** (*Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν...*).

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Order of the House Trisagion and Funeral Rubrics:* In historical codices and canonical euchologia, the initial panikhida or funeral litany conducted at the home of the deceased initiates the rites of Christian burial. The designation *Trisagion* in this liturgical rubric encompasses the entire opening hexapsalmic or initial prayer cycle: the Thrice-Holy Hymn (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), the All-Holy Trinity prayer (*Παναγία Τριάς*), the Lord's Prayer (*Πάτερ ἡμῶν*), and the priestly doxological exclamation (*Ὅτι σοῦ ἐστιν*), preceding the four classical mortuary troparia in Tone 4 (*Nekrosima Troparia*). Textual variations between the 1888 editio princeps and modern Athenian and Venetian euchologia are notable: the petitionary phrase *“and forgiveness”* (*καὶ συγχωρήσεως*) is frequently omitted as redundant in modern editions, and Violakis preserves the archaic vocative *“of Thy servant”* (*τοῦ δούλου σου*) rather than the expanded modern recension *“of the servant of God”* (*τοῦ δούλου τοῦ Θεοῦ*).

units.slavonic_text: Εὐλογητὸς εἶ Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά σου. Ἀλληλούϊα. (εἰς τὸ τέλος ἑκάστου στίχου ψάλλεται τὸ Ἀλληλούϊα. Ἐπεπόθησεν ἡ ψυχή μου τοῦ ἐπιθυμῆσαι τὰ κρίματά σου ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ. Ἐνύσταξεν ἡ ψυχή μου ἀπὸ ἀκηδίας, βεβαίωσόν με ἐν τοῖς λόγοις σου. Κλῖνον τὴν καρδίαν μου εἰς τὰ μαρτύριά σου καὶ μὴ εἰς πλεονεξίαν. Ἀθυμία κατέσχε με ἀπὸ ἁμαρτωλῶν τῶν ἐγκαταλιμπανόντων τὸν νόμον σου. Μέτοχος ἐγώ εἰμι πάντων τῶν φοβουμένων σε, καὶ τῶν φυλασσόντων τὰς ἐντολάς σου. Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ . . . Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεί . . . Ἀλληλούϊα. Ὁ Διάκονος Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις, καὶ ἄρχεται ὁ β΄ Χορὸς εἰς ἦχον πλάγιον τοῦ α΄. Αἱ χεῖρές σου ἐποίησάν με καὶ ἔπλασάν με, συνέτισόν με, καὶ μαθήσομαι τὰς ἐντολάς σου. Ἐλέησόν με Κύριε (εἰς τὸ τέλος ἑκάστου στίχου ψάλλεται τὸ Ἐλέησόν με Κύριε). Ὅτι ἐγεννήθην ὡς ἀσκὸς ἐν πάχνῃ, τὰ δικαιώματά σου οὐκ ἐπελαθόμην. Σός εἰμι ἐγώ, σῶσόν με, ὅτι τὰ δικαιώματά σου ἐξεζήτησα. Ἀπὸ τῶν κριμάτων σου οὐκ ἐξέκλινα, ὅτι σὺ ἐνομοθέτησάς με.

units.slavonic_text: Glory to the Father and the Son . . . Now and ever . . . Alleluia. Have mercy on me, O Lord. (At the end of each phrase we sing “Have mercy on me, O Lord.”) For I have shriveled like a wineskin in the frost, yet I have not forgotten Your just decrees. I am Your own; save me, for I have sought Your commandments. I have not spurned Your judgments, for you have instructed me.

units.slavonic_text: --- [*] (In later times, the distances between the home of the deceased, the church, and the burial ground have generally become considerably greater than those at the time of the publication of the Typikon (1888). As a result of these increased distances from point to point, the hymns accompanying the route of the casket are now chanted at different locations. For example, the initial Trisagios Hymn (Holy God, etc.) begins to be sung when the casket enters the Narthex from the outside and continues to be sung up to the point when the casket arrives at the Soleas and up to the beginning of the Funeral Service proper.)

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funerary Procession and the Seventeenth Kathisma:* In later eras, urban distances between family residences, parish temples, and cemeteries expanded considerably beyond the compact parochial layout of nineteenth-century Constantinople. Consequently, the funeral processional chant of the Asmatic Trisagion (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), traditionally chanted continuously through the streets, is commonly begun when the casket enters the narthex from outside and maintained until placed before the solea and tetrapod in the nave. The funeral office itself centers upon the sublime funeral psalmody of the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 LXX), structured into three distinct stases divided by funeral litanies and tone modulations: the First Stasis is chanted in Tone 6 with the refrain *Alleluia*; the Second Stasis shifts to Tone 5 with the penitential refrain *“Have mercy on me, O Lord”*; and the Third Stasis modulates into Tone 8 with the resurrectional refrain *Alleluia*.

provenance.verbatim_source: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funerary Procession and the Seventeenth Kathisma:* In later eras, urban distances between family residences, parish temples, and cemeteries expanded considerably beyond the compact parochial layout of nineteenth-century Constantinople. Consequently, the funeral processional chant of the Asmatic Trisagion (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), traditionally chanted continuously through the streets, is commonly begun when the casket enters the narthex from outside and maintained until placed before the solea and tetrapod in the nave. The funeral office itself centers upon the sublime funeral psalmody of the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 LXX), structured into three distinct stases divided by funeral litanies and tone modulations: the First Stasis is chanted in Tone 6 with the refrain *Alleluia*; the Second Stasis shifts to Tone 5 with the penitential refrain *“Have mercy on me, O Lord”*; and the Third Stasis modulates into Tone 8 with the resurrectional refrain *Alleluia*.

units.slavonic_incipit: Ὁ Διάκονος Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, ὁ
units.slavonic_text: Ὁ Διάκονος Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς (ἢ ὁ Ἱερεύς) Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις, καὶ ἄρχεται ὁ α΄ Χορὸς εἰς ἦχον πλάγιον τοῦ δ΄. Καὶ ἐλέησόν με. Ἀλληλούϊα. Ἐπίβλεψον ἐπ’ ἐμὲ καὶ ἐλέησόν με, κατὰ τὸ κρῖμα τῶν ἀγαπώντων τὸ ὄνομά σου. Ἀλληλούϊα. Νεώτερος ἐγώ εἰμι καὶ ἐξουδενωμένος, τὰ δικαιώματά σου οὐκ ἐπελαθόμην. Ἀλληλούϊα. Τῆς φωνῆς μου ἄκουσον, Κύριε, κατὰ τὸ ἔλεός σου, κατὰ τὸ κρῖμά σου ζῆσόν με. Ἀλληλούϊα. Ἄρχοντες κατεδίωξάν με δωρεάν, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων σου ἐδειλίασεν ἡ καρδία μου. Ἀλληλούϊα. Ζήσεται ἡ ψυχή μου καὶ αἰνέσει σε, καὶ τὰ κρίματά σου βοηθήσει μοι. Ἐπλανήθην ὡς πρόβατον ἀπολωλός· ζήτησον τὸν δοῦλόν σου, ὅτι τὰς ἐντολάς σου οὐκ ἐπελαθόμην. Καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Διάκονος Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν, ὁ Ἱερεὺς Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις, καὶ ἄρχεται ὁ β΄ Χορὸς τὰ Εὐλογητάρια.
units.english_text: Ὁ Διάκονος **Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν**, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς (ἢ ὁ Ἱερεύς) **Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις**, καὶ ἄρχεται ὁ α΄ Χορὸς εἰς ἦχον πλάγιον τοῦ δ΄.

provenance.verbatim_source: Ὁ Διάκονος **Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν**, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς (ἢ ὁ Ἱερεύς) **Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις**, καὶ ἄρχεται ὁ α΄ Χορὸς εἰς ἦχον πλάγιον τοῦ δ΄.

units.slavonic_text: In return, [for Your mercies] my heart is set on following Your commandments until the ages of ages. It is time for the Lord to act: for they have broken Your law. Glory to the Father and the Son . . . Now and ever . . . Have mercy, on me, Lord, Lord. Deacon: “Have mercy on us, O God”; the Hierarch (or the Priest): “For You are the Resurrection”; and the First Choir begins in Mode IV Plagal the following: And have mercy on me. Alleluia. Look upon me and be gracious to me, as to those who love Your name. Alleluia. I am young and despised, but have not forgotten Your commandments. Alleluia. Hear my voice, O Lord, in Your steadfast love, quicken me in Your justice. Alleluia. Princes have pursued me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of Your words. Alleluia, My soul shall live and praise You, and Your law shall be my support. Like a lost sheep, I have gone astray. Seek Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments. And immediately, the Deacon: “Have mercy on us, O God”; the Priest: “For You are the Resurrection”; and the Second Choir begins the EvlogitApplication [Evlogitaria]: “Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your commandments.” The choir of the Saints has found the source of life” (each hymn of the Evlogitaria is preceded by the Verse “Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your commandments.”) — With the palm of Your hand {of old}[5] You formed me out of nothing. — I am an image of Your indescribable glory. — Give rest, O God, to Your servant. — Glory . . . Let us devoutly praise the one Godhead as radiant Trinity. — Now and ever . . . Hail, majestic Lady, who for our
units.english_text: **“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: Both now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen: Have mercy on me, O Lord, O Lord.”**

provenance.verbatim_source: **“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: Both now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen: Have mercy on me, O Lord, O Lord.”**

units.slavonic_text: --- [5] (Violakis' version “O palami” (“With the palm of Your hand”) is found in various sources, such as the Musikos Pandektis, Athens, 1936, vol 3, p. 376, and Nikos Karitsiotis, Musikon Agiasmatarion, Athens, 1951, p. 33. More numerous sources, including the more authoritative Mega Efchologion as well as the Mikron Efchologion have “O pale men” (“of old”). See the Mega Efchologion, Venice, 1862 (reprinted in Athens, 1986), p. 407, and Mikron Efchologion, Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, 1956, p. 201.)

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Textual Variants in the Second Evlogitarion:* The opening phrase of the second Troparion of the Funeral Evlogitaria exhibits a celebrated textual variant between the 1888 Constantinopolitan recension of George Violakis and older euchological witnesses. Violakis prints the poetic anthropomorphic reading *“O palame”* (*Ὁ παλάμῃ* — *“With the palm of Thy hand Thou didst fashion me”*), a textual tradition documented in the Athenian musical collections including the *Musikos Pandektis* (Athens, 1936, vol. 3, p. 376) and Nikos Karitsiotis, *Musikon Agiasmatarion* (Athens, 1951, p. 33). Conversely, the venerable Venetian and Roman liturgical monument editions, represented by the *Mega Euchologion* (Venice, 1862/1867, p. 407) and the *Mikron Euchologion* of the Apostolike Diakonia (Athens, 1956, p. 201), preserve the temporal adverbial incipit *“O palai men”* (*Ὁ πάλαι μέν* — *“Thou Who of old didst fashion me out of nothing”*). Both liturgical traditions preserve the identical theological confession: humanity fashioned *ex nihilo* by the divine hand according to the divine image, fallen through transgression, and restored to paradise through Christ's redemption.

units.slavonic_text: salvation gave birth to God in the flesh. — Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia, glory to You, O God {and give rest to your servant.} {6} If there are many Priests, after each of these Evlogitaria, the Deacon says “Let us pray to the Lord.” And from all the Priests present, each Priest, in order of seniority of ordination, says “For You are the Resurrection.” (See the Orologion for the text of the Evlogitaria for the Reposed.)
units.english_text: If there are many priests concelebrating, after each of these Evlogitaria they commemorate the deceased, with the deacon reciting at each: **“Let us pray to the Lord”** (*Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*). And from all the priests present, each priest in order of seniority of ordination exclaims: **“For Thou art the Resurrection, and the Life, and the Repose of Thy servant...”** (*Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις...*). *(See the Horologion for the complete text of the Funeral Evlogitaria).*

units.slavonic_text: Mode I
units.english_text: **“What pleasure in life abideth without sorrow? What glory standeth upon earth unchanging? All things are feebler than shadows, all things more deceptive than dreams: in a single moment death taketh them all away. But in the light of Thy countenance, O Christ, and in the sweetness of Thy beauty, give rest unto him whom Thou hast chosen, for Thou art the Lover of mankind.”** (*Ποία τοῦ βίου τρυφὴ διαμένει λύπης ἀμέτοχος...*)

units.slavonic_incipit: What pleasure in life is not
units.slavonic_text: What pleasure in life is not accompanied by sorrow? What glory remains unchanged on earth? All things are flimsier than shadows, more deceptive than dreams. In but an instant, death displaces everything. But in the light of Your countenance, O Christ, in the sweetness of Your beauty, give rest to him whom You have chosen, as lover of mankind.
units.english_text: **“As a flower withers, and as a dream passes away, so is every mortal dissolved. But when the trumpet sounds, the dead, as in an earthquake, shall all arise to meet Thee, Christ our God. Then, O Master, establish in the tents of Thy saints the soul of him whom Thou hast summoned from our midst, the spirit of Thy servant, O Christ.”** (*Ὡς ἄνθος μαραίνεται, καὶ ὡς ὄναρ παρέρχεται...*)

units.slavonic_text: Mode II
units.english_text: **“All human pursuits are vanity, whatsoever survives not after death: riches do not endure, nor doth glory accompany along the way; for when death comes upon them, all these things are utterly extinguished. Therefore let us cry aloud unto Christ, the immortal King: Give rest unto him who hath departed from our midst, in the dwelling place of all who rejoice!”** (*Πάντα ματαιότης τὰ ἀνθρώπινα...*)

units.slavonic_incipit: Every mortal is like a flower
units.slavonic_text: Every mortal is like a flower that withers, a passing dream that vanishes. Yet when the trumpet sounds, all the dead will rise as in an earthquake to meet you, Christ our God. Will You then, Master, assign a place where Your Saints abide for the soul of him whom You have summoned from our midst.
units.english_text: **“Truly awesome is the mystery of death: how the soul is violently severed from the body’s harmony; how the natural bond that united them is broken by the divine will! Therefore do we entreat Thee...”** (*Ὄντως φοβερώτατον τὸ τοῦ θανάτου μυστήριον... / ὃ σὲ ἱκετεύομεν...*)...[^525]

units.slavonic_text: Mode III
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funeral Evlogitaria and the Damascene Idiomela:* The Funeral Evlogitaria (*Νεκρώσιμα Εὐλογητάρια*) in Tone 5, punctuated by the refrain *“Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes”* (Psalm 118:12 LXX), bridge the seventeenth kathisma of the Psalter to the Eight Idiomela (*Ἰδιόμελα*) composed by Saint John of Damascus. In ancient Studite and Constantinopolitan euchologies, when multiple presbyters concelebrate, the Little Ektenia for the Departed is intoned by the deacon after each strophe, and the concelebrating presbyters pronounce the resurrectional exclamation (*Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις*) in descending order of ordination seniority. Note the editorial annotation regarding the refrain *“and give rest to Thy servant”* (*καὶ ἀνάπαυσον τὸν δοῦλόν σου*), documented by Karitsiotis in his *Musikon Agiasmatarion* (p. 36) as an established musical and rubrical tradition in modern Byzantine chant editions.

provenance.verbatim_source: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Funeral Evlogitaria and the Damascene Idiomela:* The Funeral Evlogitaria (*Νεκρώσιμα Εὐλογητάρια*) in Tone 5, punctuated by the refrain *“Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes”* (Psalm 118:12 LXX), bridge the seventeenth kathisma of the Psalter to the Eight Idiomela (*Ἰδιόμελα*) composed by Saint John of Damascus. In ancient Studite and Constantinopolitan euchologies, when multiple presbyters concelebrate, the Little Ektenia for the Departed is intoned by the deacon after each strophe, and the concelebrating presbyters pronounce the resurrectional exclamation (*Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις*) in descending order of ordination seniority. Note the editorial annotation regarding the refrain *“and give rest to Thy servant”* (*καὶ ἀνάπαυσον τὸν δοῦλόν σου*), documented by Karitsiotis in his *Musikon Agiasmatarion* (p. 36) as an established musical and rubrical tradition in modern Byzantine chant editions.

units.slavonic_text: All human pursuits are vain; they have no being after death. Wealth does not remain; glory does not accompany along the way. Once death befalls, all these vanish utterly. units.slavonic_incipit: I called to mind the prophet,
units.slavonic_text: I called to mind the prophet, crying, “I am but dust and ashes.” In addition, I studied the tombs once more, considered the naked bones, and asked myself: Now which of these was king, and which the common soldier? Which was the rich man, which the indigent? Which man was upright and which a sinner? Nevertheless, Lord, in Your compassion, to Your servant give rest, among the righteous.
units.english_text: **“I weep and lament when I contemplate death, and behold lying in the graves our beauty fashioned in the image of God, bereft of form, without glory, having no shape! O marvel! What is this mystery that hath come upon us? How have we been surrendered unto corruption? How have we been yoked unto death? Truly by the command of God, as it is written, Who granteth repose unto the departed.”** (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι ὅταν ἐννοήσω τὸν θάνατον...*)

units.slavonic_incipit: Your creating command became my beginning
units.slavonic_text: Your creating command became my beginning and my being. For it was Your will to bring together visible and invisible nature to fashion me a living creature. You shaped my body from the earth then gave me a spirit by Your divine and quickening breath. Wherefore, O Savior, give rest to Your servant in the land of the living, where the righteous dwell.
units.english_text: **Thy death, O Lord, hath become the cause of immortality; for hadst Thou not been laid in the tomb, Paradise would not have been opened. Therefore grant rest unto him who hath departed, as Thou art the Lover of mankind.”** (*Ὁ θάνατός σου, Κύριε, ἀθανασίας γέγονε πρόξενος...*)...[^526]

units.slavonic_text: Mode Varys
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Theological Anthropology of the Damascene Idiomela:* The funeral idiomela of Saint John of Damascus constitute a profound Byzantine patristic treatise on Christian anthropology and eschatology. In Tone 6 (*Ἀρχή μοι καὶ ὑπόστασις*), the hymnographer articulates the composite nature of humanity as a microcosm uniting the spiritual (*ἀόρατος φύσις*) and the corporeal (*ὁρατὴ φύσις*) created through the divine inbreathing (Genesis 2:7 LXX). In Tone 8 (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι*), the tragedy of bodily dissolution is confronted not through Stoic resignation but through Christological hope: corruption (*φθορά*) and physical mortality are acknowledged as an unnatural intrusion into the divine image (*κατ’ εἰκόνα θεοῦ*), overturned conclusively by Christ's own descent into the tomb and His life-bearing Resurrection.

units.english_text: Καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Ἀπόστολος, **Οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν περὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων**, καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, **Εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος πρὸς τοὺς ἐληλυθότας πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἰουδαίους**, ὁ Διάκονος, **Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός**, καὶ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς τὰς δύο συγχωρητικὰς Εὐχάς, καὶ εἰς τὸ τέλος, **Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης σαρκός**, ὁ Διάκονος, **Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν**, καὶ μνημονεύουσιν αὖθις ἅπαντες οἱ παρευρισκόμενοι Ἱερεῖς, καὶ ἀκολούθως ἡ παρὰ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως νεκρώσιμος Ἀπόλυσις. Εἰς δὲ τὸν τελευταῖον τοῦ λειψάνου ἀσπασμὸν ψάλλεται ὑπὸ τοῦ β΄ χοροῦ τὸ Προσόμοιον, **Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν δῶμεν ἀδελφοὶ τῷ θανόντι, εὐχαριστοῦντες Θεῷ**, καὶ συνοδεύομεν τὸ λείψανον μέχρι τοῦ τάφου ψάλλοντες τὸ **Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι**.

units.slavonic_text: Καὶ νῦν (ὁ αὐτός)
units.english_text: Ἐὰν ᾖ Διακαινήσιμος ἑβδομάς, ψάλλομεν μέχρι τοῦ Ναοῦ τὸ **Χριστὸς ἀνέστη** (τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ μέχρι τῆς Ἀποδόσεως τοῦ Πάσχα). Μετὰ τὸ **Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός**, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς ψάλλει τὸ **Χριστὸς ἀνέστη** ἅπαξ καὶ οἱ δύο Χοροὶ ἀνὰ μίαν, εἶτα ψάλλονται αἱ Καταβασίαι τοῦ Κανόνος τοῦ Πάσχα· εἰς τὸ τέλος δὲ ἑκάστης Καταβασίας τὸ **Χριστὸς ἀνέστη** τρίς, τὸ **Ἀναστὰς ὁ Ἰησοῦς**, καὶ ὁ Διάκονος **Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν**, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς **Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ἡ ἀνάστασις**· καὶ ἐν ταῖς λοιπαῖς οἱ Ἱερεῖς, ἀπ’ θ΄ ψάλλεται τὸ **Σαρκὶ ὑπνώσας** δίς, καὶ εὐθὺς ὁ Ἀπόστολος καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον. Εἰς τὸ τέλος ὁ Διάκονος τὸ **Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός**, καὶ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς ἀναγινώσκει τὰς δύο συγχωρητικὰς Εὐχάς· εἰς τὸ τέλος **Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων** κτλ. ὡς ἀνωτέρω καὶ ἡ Ἀπόλυσις, ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ **Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν** ψάλλομεν τὸ **Ἀναστάσεως ἡμέρα**, τὸ αὐτὸ ψάλλομεν καὶ μέχρι τοῦ τάφου. Μετὰ τὴν Διακαινήσιμον ἑβδομάδα, ἀφοῦ εἰσέλθωμεν ἐν τῷ Ναῷ μετὰ τοῦ λειψάνου, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς **Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός**, εἶτα τὸ **Χριστὸς ἀνέστη** ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως ἅπαξ, καὶ δὶς ὑπὸ τῶν Χορῶν· καὶ ἀκολούθως ἡ νεκρώσιμος συνήθης Ἀκολουθία, ὡς προδιετυπώθη.

Εἰς τὸ τέλος ὁ Διάκονος τὸ **Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός**, καὶ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς ἀναγινώσκει τὰς δύο συγχωρητικὰς Εὐχάς· εἰς τὸ τέλος **Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων** κτλ. ὡς ἀνωτέρω καὶ ἡ Ἀπόλυσις, ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ **Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν** ψάλλομεν τὸ **Ἀναστάσεως ἡμέρα**, τὸ αὐτὸ ψάλλομεν καὶ μέχρι τοῦ τάφου. Μετὰ τὴν Διακαινήσιμον ἑβδομάδα, ἀφοῦ εἰσέλθωμεν ἐν τῷ Ναῷ μετὰ τοῦ λειψάνου, ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς **Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός**, εἶτα τὸ **Χριστὸς ἀνέστη** ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως ἅπαξ, καὶ δὶς ὑπὸ τῶν Χορῶν· καὶ ἀκολούθως ἡ νεκρώσιμος συνήθης Ἀκολουθία, ὡς προδιετυπώθη.

units.english_text: And immediately follows the Epistle (*Apostolos*): **“Brethren, I would not have you ignorant concerning those who are asleep”** (*Οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν περὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων* — 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17); and the Gospel: **“The Lord said to the Jews who came unto Him: Amen, amen, I say unto you, he that heareth My word...”** (*Εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος πρὸς τοὺς ἐληλυθότας πρὸς αὐτὸν Ἰουδαίους* — John 5:24–30). The deacon intones the litany: **“Have mercy on us, O God, according to Thy great mercy...”** (*Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός*); and the hierarch recites the two prayers of absolution, and at the end the prayer: **“O God of spirits and of all flesh...”** (*Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης σαρκός*). The deacon intones: **“Let us pray to the Lord”** (*Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν*); and all the presbyters present commemorate the departed once more; and subsequently the hierarch pronounces the Funeral Dismissal. During the final kissing of the body, the second choir chants the automelon: **“Come, brethren, let us give the last kiss unto the departed, giving thanks unto God”** (*Δεῦτε τελευταῖον ἀσπασμὸν δῶμεν ἀδελφοὶ τῷ θανόντι, εὐχαριστοῦντες Θεῷ*); and we accompany the body to the tomb while chanting: **“I weep and I lament”** (*Θρηνῶ καὶ ὀδύρομαι*).

units.english_text: If it be Bright Week [Renewal Week], we chant **“Christ is risen”** (*Χριστὸς ἀνέστη*) all the way to the temple (and the same is done until the Apodosis of Pascha). After the exclamation **“Blessed is our God”**, the hierarch chants **“Christ is risen”** once, and each of the two choirs chants it once. Then the Katavasias of the Paschal Canon are chanted. At the end of each Katavasia, **“Christ is risen”** is chanted three times, followed by **“Having seen the Resurrection of Christ”** [or **“Jesus having risen”** / *Ἀναστὰς ὁ Ἰησοῦς*]. The deacon intones: **“Let us pray to the Lord”**, and the hierarch exclaims: **“For Thou art the Resurrection, and the Life, and the Repose...”** after the First Katavasia; and during the remaining odes the concelebrating priests intone this same exclamation in turn. After the Ninth Ode, the Exapostilarion: **“Having fallen asleep in the flesh as a mortal”** (*Σαρκὶ ὑπνώσας*) is chanted twice, and immediately follow the Epistle and Gospel. At the end, the deacon intones: **“Have mercy on us, O God”**, and the hierarch reads the two prayers of absolution; at the conclusion, the prayer **“O God of spirits and of all flesh...”**, etc., as above, followed by the Dismissal. But instead of **“Come, brethren, let us give the last kiss”**, we chant the Paschal Stichera: **“Let God arise”** with **“Today a sacred Pascha hath been revealed unto us”** and **“It is the day of Resurrection”** (*Ἀναστάσεως ἡμέρα*), and we chant the same during the procession to the grave. After Bright Week, until the Apodosis of Pascha, upon entering the temple with the body of the deceased, the hierarch exclaims: **“Blessed is our God”**, then **“Christ is risen”** is chanted once by the hierarch and twice by the choirs; and thereafter the customary Funeral Service proceeds as described above.

units.english_text: It should be noted that this identical order of the Funeral Service is chanted for all the departed: for Emperors, Patriarchs, Hierarchs, Priests, as well as for men and women, young and old, and even for infants. For infants, however, the Idiomela of the Eight Tones are omitted, and the prayer designated for infants in the Euchologion (*Trebnik* / *Sluzhebnik*) is recited, together with their own proper Epistle and Gospel...[^527]

units.slavonic_text: If we are in Bright [Renewal] Week, as we go into the Church, we chant “Christ is risen” (we chant this hymn until the Leave-taking of Easter). After the “Blessed is God,” the Archbishop chants the “Christ is risen” once and each of the two Choirs chant it also once. Then are sung the Katavasie of the Canon of Easter. At the end of each Katavasia, we chant “Christ is risen” three times and the “Jesus, having risen.” The Deacon: “Let us pray to the Lord,” and the Archbishop “For You are the Resurrection” [after the First Katavasia]. After the remaining Katavasie, the Priests [each at a time] intone this same Exclamation. After the 9th Katavasia, we chant “Having slept in the flesh as a mortal” twice, and immediately follow the Apostolos and the Gospel. At the end, the Deacon intones “Have mercy on us, O God,” and the Archbishop reads the two Prayers of Forgiveness. At the end, “God of spirits,” etc. as above. Instead of “Come, brethren [let us give] one final kiss,” we chant “It is the day of Resurrection” which we also sing up to the grave site. After Bright [Renewal] Week, after we enter the Church with the body of the departed, the Archbishop intones “Blessed is God.” Then he sings “Christ is risen” once and each of the two choirs sing it once, and the customary Service of the Dead follows, as described above.
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Paschal Funeral Rite and the Egalitarian Order of Burial:* Violakis establishes the fundamental liturgical principle that the funeral office of the Great Church of Christ maintains an essential structural identity across all ranks of human life—from emperors and patriarchs down to ordinary laymen and infants—witnessing to the Pauline proclamation cited on the facing page: *“For ye are all one in Christ Jesus”* (Galatians 3:28). For infants who depart before reaching the age of reason and personal sin, the mournful Damascene idiomela are omitted, replaced by prayers celebrating innocence and eternal union with Christ. Furthermore, when a funeral coincides with Bright Week (Renewal Week), grief is transformed into Paschal triumph: the entire funeral office is replaced by the Paschal Canon of Saint John Damascene, the singing of *“Christ is risen”*, and the joyful Paschal Stichera, reflecting the ancient Christian conviction that death during the feast of the Resurrection constitutes immediate entry into the radiant joy of the empty tomb.

provenance.verbatim_source: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Paschal Funeral Rite and the Egalitarian Order of Burial:* Violakis establishes the fundamental liturgical principle that the funeral office of the Great Church of Christ maintains an essential structural identity across all ranks of human life—from emperors and patriarchs down to ordinary laymen and infants—witnessing to the Pauline proclamation cited on the facing page: *“For ye are all one in Christ Jesus”* (Galatians 3:28). For infants who depart before reaching the age of reason and personal sin, the mournful Damascene idiomela are omitted, replaced by prayers celebrating innocence and eternal union with Christ. Furthermore, when a funeral coincides with Bright Week (Renewal Week), grief is transformed into Paschal triumph: the entire funeral office is replaced by the Paschal Canon of Saint John Damascene, the singing of *“Christ is risen”*, and the joyful Paschal Stichera, reflecting the ancient Christian conviction that death during the feast of the Resurrection constitutes immediate entry into the radiant joy of the empty tomb.

units.english_text: Τὰ εἰς τοὺς κεκοιμημένους ἀδελφοὺς γινόμενα Τρίτα δηλοῦσι, κατὰ τὸν Ἱερὸν Συμεὼν Θεσσαλονίκης, ὅτι ὁ κοιμηθεὶς ἀδελφὸς ὑπὸ τῆς Ἁγίας Τριάδος ἐξ ἀρχῆς συνετέθη. Τὰ δὲ Ἔνατα τῶν κεκοιμημένων σημαίνουσιν ὅτι ὁ διαλυθεὶς εἰς τὰ ἐξ ὧν συνετέθη, ἔχει νὰ συγκαταριθμηθῇ μετὰ τῶν ἐννέα αὔλων ταγμάτων τῶν Ἀγγέλων, ὡς ἄϋλος καὶ αὐτός. Τὰ δὲ τεσσαρακοστὰ δηλοῦσιν ὅτι, ἐν τῇ μελλούσῃ Ἀναστάσει συντεθεὶς πάλιν, κατὰ τρόπον ὑψηλότερον, ἔχει καὶ αὐτὸς νὰ ἀναληφθῇ ὡς ὁ Κύριος καὶ ἁρπαγεὶς ἐν νεφέλαις νὰ ὑπαντήσῃ τῷ Κριτῇ. Ταύτας τὰς τρεῖς καταστάσεις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σημαίνουσι τὰ Τρίμηνα καὶ Ἑξάμηνα καὶ Ἐννεάμηνα. Καὶ ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν, ταῦτα τελοῦνται ὑπὲρ καθαρισμοῦ τοῦ ἀποθανόντος.

units.english_text: The Third-Day Memorial Service (*Trita*) performed for our fallen-asleep brethren signifies, according to the Holy Symeon of Thessalonica, that the departed brother was composed from the beginning by the Holy Trinity. The Ninth-Day Memorial Service (*Enata*) for the reposed signifies that he who has been dissolved into the elements from which he was composed is to be numbered together with the nine bodiless ranks of the Angels, being now bodiless himself. The Fortieth-Day Memorial Service (*Tessarakonta*) signifies that, having been recomposed in a more exalted manner in the future Resurrection, he also is to be taken up like the Lord and caught up in the clouds to meet the Judge. These three estates of humanity are likewise signified by the Three-Month, Six-Month, and Nine-Month Memorial Services (*Trimena*, *Hexamena*, and *Enneamena*). And to speak simply, all these services are celebrated for the spiritual purification and forgiveness of the deceased.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Mystagogical Theology of Memorial Services according to Saint Symeon of Thessalonica:* This final chapter of the Violakis Typikon codifies the mystagogy of commemorative services for the departed (*Mnemosyna* / *Panakhyda*), drawing upon the liturgical commentary of Saint Symeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica (†1429, *De fine nostro et de ordine sepulturae*, PG 155:669–698). The traditional intervals of commemorative prayer are invested with deep trinitarian, angelological, and eschatological symbolism: the third day honors the Holy Trinity as the Creator of man; the ninth day commemorates the nine angelic choirs with whom the disembodied soul now shares communion; the fortieth day prefigures the General Resurrection when the glorified body shall be caught up into the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:17) to encounter Christ the Judge; while the annual cycles (three, six, nine months, and annual memorials) perpetuate the prayer of the Church for the soul's continuous purification. The inscription *“ΤΕΛΟΣ ΚΑΙ Τῼ ΘΕῼ ΔΟΞΑ”* marks the formal conclusion of the authoritative typikon text promulgated by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1888.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Calendar Reform and the Paschalion Table of George Violakis:* The *Pinax tou Eortodromiou* (*Πίναξ τοῦ Ἑορτοδρομίου*) represents the perpetual Paschalion table appended to the 1888 editio princeps of George Violakis, calculating moveable feast cycles, Paschal dates, Triodion intervals, and the duration of the Apostles' Fast. Following the Meletian Congress of Constantinople in 1923 and the subsequent adoption of the Revised Julian Calendar (in civil and liturgical synchrony with the Gregorian reckoning for fixed feasts) by the Church of Greece and the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1924, twentieth-century editors added comparative concordance columns to reconcile the 1888 tables with both the Old Calendar (Julian, observed across Mount Athos, Jerusalem, and traditional Slavic jurisdictions) and the New Calendar (Revised Julian/Gregorian, observed across Constantinople, Greece, and diaspora communities).

units.slavonic_incipit: The present Chart of the Feasts
units.slavonic_text: The present Chart of the Feasts was originally written on the basis of the Julian Calendar. In the year 1921, the Greek Orthodox Church adopted the Gregorian Calendar. Since the present Typikon was published in 1888, it naturally was impossible for George Violakis to have been aware of this change to the Gregorian Calendar.

units.slavonic_text: [English Editorial Note & Table: Movable Feasts — Gregorian Calendar (p. 927)]
units.english_text: In accordance with the Gregorian Calendar, where the Triodion period begins on 24 January (13 days later than the beginning date in the Julian Calendar) the first four immovable feasts listed in the Chart — 11, 17, 18 and 20 January — will no longer fall within the Triodion period. The earliest possible immovable feast to fall within the Triodion period will now be 25 January, St. Gregory the Theologian.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Comparative Paschal and Triodion Cycles (Julian and Gregorian Reckonings):* The comparative tables framed on physical leaves p941 and p942 (printed pages 926 and 927) establish the mathematical parameters of the liturgical year under the Julian Calendar (Old Calendar, JC) and the Revised Julian / Gregorian Calendar (New Calendar, GC). The 13-day solar disparity shifts the entire 127-day moveable liturgical cycle: under the Julian Calendar, Holy Pascha oscillates between March 22 and April 25 JC (a 35-day inclusive span), whereas in the civil Gregorian reckoning it falls between April 4 and May 8 GC. This chronological shift profoundly affects the coincidence matrix: immovable commemorations of mid-January (such as St. Theodosios the Cenobiarch on Jan 11 and St. Anthony the Great on Jan 17) can never coincide with the Triodion under the Gregorian reckoning, whereas late-June commemorations (the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist on June 24 and the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul on June 29) are brought within the movable post-Paschal cycle whenever Pascha occurs late.

units.english_text: Σπουδαῖον ἐκρίθη καὶ ἐπάναγκες τοῖς τε Ἱερεῦσι καὶ τοῖς ψάλταις τὸ γινώσκειν, εἰ δὲ μή γε, τὸ εὑρίσκειν εὐχερέστερον τὴν λύσιν ἀποριῶν καὶ δυσχερειῶν, ὅσας συνεπάγεται ἡ τῶν ἀκινήτων λεγομένων ἑορτῶν, ἤτοι τοῦ Μηνολογίου, σύμπτωσις μετὰ τῶν κινητῶν τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ Πεντηκοσταρίου. Καὶ ποιεῖται μὲν καθ’ ἑκάστην σύμπτωσιν ἐπαρκῆ λόγον περὶ τούτων τὸ Τυπικόν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲν ἧττον εἷς Πίναξ, οἷος ὁ ἑπόμενος, παρέχει μείζονα τὴν εὐχέρειαν καὶ ἱκανοποιεῖ τὴν περιέργειαν τοῦ φιλομαθοῦς· ἐπειδὴ δὲ αἱ κινηταὶ ἑορταὶ τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ Πεντηκοσταρίου οὔτε πέραν τῆς ΙΑ΄ Ἰανουαρίου τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ Ἡμερολογίου (ἥτις ἐστὶ τὸ πρωϊμώτερον ὅριον τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου) κατέρχονται [24 Ἰανουαρίου εἰς τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον], οὔτε δύνανται προχωρῆσαι ἐπέκεινα τῆς ΚΕ΄ Μαΐου-ΙΗ [Ἰουλίου 3-ΓΗ], ἥτις ἐστὶ τὸ ἔσχατον ὅριον μέχρι τοῦ ὁποίου ἐκτείνεται τὸ τέλος τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, ἤτοι ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἁγίων Πάντων, διὰ τοῦτο ὁ Πίναξ ταῦτα ἔχει ἀρχῆς καὶ τέλους ὅρια, καὶ μόνον τὰς ἐν τῷ χρονικῷ τούτῳ διαστήματι ἑορτὰς τοῦ Μηνολογίου περιλαμβάνει, παρέχων ὡς ἐν κατόπτρῳ τὰς δυνατὰς εὐκολίας, ὥστε νὰ δύνανται οὕτω πως οἱ Ἱερεῖς καὶ οἱ ψάλται συμβιβάζειν ἀκόπως τὴν τυπικὴν τῶν ἱερῶν Ἀκολουθιῶν διάταξιν, καὶ διαλύειν πάντα δισταγμόν, καὶ διασκεδάζειν πᾶσαν ἐνδεχομένην ἀπορίαν. Ὅπως δὲ κατανοηθῇ καὶ ἀποβῇ εὐχερεστέρα ἡ τοῦ Πίνακος χρῆσις, ἀναγκαῖαι ἐθεωρήθησαν αἱ ἑξῆς σημειώσεις:

units.slavonic_text: [English Facing Translation: Chart of Feasts Preamble & Interpretive Rules (p. 929)]
units.english_text: It was deemed important and necessary for priests and chanters to know, or at least to find more readily the solution to perplexities and rubrical difficulties occasioned by the concurrence of the so-called immovable feasts—namely, those of the Menologion (*Μηνολόγιον*)—with the movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentecostarion periods. Now while the Typikon provides an adequate exposition concerning each individual concurrence, nonetheless a systematic chart, such as the one that follows, affords greater facility and satisfies the scholarly inquiry of the diligent student.

units.english_text: Inasmuch as the movable feasts of the Triodion and Pentecostarion neither descend earlier than January 11 of the Julian Calendar—which constitutes the earliest boundary for the opening of the Triodion [January 24 on the Gregorian Calendar]—nor can they advance beyond May 25 JC [July 3 GC], which is the ultimate boundary unto which the terminus of the Pentecostarion extends—namely, the Sunday of All Saints—for this reason the Chart adopts these precise dates as its initial and terminal boundaries. Consequently, it incorporates solely those feasts of the Menologion that fall within this temporal interval, displaying as in a mirror every practical facilitation, so that the clergy and chanters may effortlessly reconcile the rubrical order of the divine services, resolve every hesitation, and dispel every conceivable ambiguity. units.slavonic_text: CHART OF FEASTS FROM JANUARY 11 UNTIL MAY 25 OF THE JULIAN CALENDAR (JC) [CONTAINING ALSO THE CORRESPONDING DATES OF THE GREGORIAN CALENDAR (GC)]
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Canon of Coincidences between the Menologion, Triodion, and Pentecostarion:* The preamble to the *Pinax tou Eortodromiou* introduces the theoretical framework governing the occurrence of immovable commemorations within the variable seasons of the movable paschal cycle. In historical Byzantine liturgical typika (such as the 1545 editio princeps of the Sabaite Typikon and the successive Constantinopolitan editions of the *Tserkovne Oko* and the Violakis synthesis), rubricists faced intricate problems of concurrence (*syndromē* / *synempitōsis*) when festal commemorations intersected with the pre-Lenten, Lenten, Holy Week, and Paschal cycles. George Violakis designed this perpetual chart as a rapid rubrical reference engine, circumscribing the liturgical domain between the earliest possible opening of the Triodion (January 11 JC / January 24 GC) and the latest possible termination of the Pentecostarion cycle on the Sunday of All Saints (May 25 JC / July 3 GC).

units.english_text: Α΄. Τὸ Ἅγιον Πάσχα ταλαντεύεται ἐντὸς τοῦ μεταξὺ τῆς ΚΒ΄ Μαρτίου-ΙΗ καὶ ΚΕ΄ Ἀπριλίου-ΙΗ [Ἀπριλίου 4-ΓΗ— Μαΐου 8-ΓΗ] ἐκ τριάκοντα τεσσάρων ἡμερῶν διαστήματος· ἑπομένως καὶ ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἔναρξις κινεῖται ἐντὸς τοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ΙΑ΄ Ἰανουαρίου-ΙΗ μέχρι τῆς ΙΓ΄ Φεβρουαρίου-ΙΗ [Ἰανουαρίου 24-ΓΗ — Φεβρουαρίου 28-ΓΗ] χρονικοῦ χώρου· τῶν δ’ ἐν ταῖς δυσὶ πρώταις στήλαις τοῦ Πίνακος ἑκάστης ἑορτῆς κειμένων ἀριθμῶν, οἱ πρῶτοι μὲν δεικνύουσι τὰς ἡμερομηνίας ἀφ’ ὧν, ὅταν ἄρχηται τὸ Τριῴδιον, συμπίπτει τὸ Πάσχα εἰς τὴν ὑπὸ τῆς δευτέρας στήλης δεικνυομένην ἡμερομηνίαν, ἀπέναντι δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τούτων σημειοῦνται αἱ ἡμέραι καὶ ἑβδομάδες τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἢ τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, καθ’ ἃς συμπίπτει ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἔτει ἡ ζητουμένη ἑορτή· καὶ ἐν τῇ τελευταίᾳ στήλῃ σημειοῦνται οἱ ἐν τῷ Τυπικῷ ἀριθμοὶ τῶν παραγράφων τῆς Τυπικῆς Διατάξεως, ἐν αἷς διασαφηνίζονται τὰ τῆς ἱερᾶς Ἀκολουθίας κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην. Παραδείγματος χάριν, ἐπιθυμοῦμεν ἵνα γνωρίζωμεν κατὰ τὸ ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) ἔτος ἡ ἑορτὴ τῆς Ὑπαπαντῆς ἐν τίνι ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἐν τίνι ἑβδομάδι τοῦ Τριῳδίου συμπίπτει· εὑρίσκομεν τὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τοῦ Πάσχα τοῦ ἔτους ἐκείνου, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ Θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, εἶτα βλέπομεν ἐν ταῖς δυσὶ στήλαις τῆς ἑορτῆς ταύτης, καὶ εὑρίσκομεν ἐν μὲν τῇ α΄ στήλῃ τὸν ἀριθμὸν κθ΄, ὅς ἐστιν ἡ ἡμερομηνία τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου κατὰ τὸ ἔτος ἐκεῖνο, ἐν δὲ τῇ β΄ στήλῃ τὸ ἀριθμὸν θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, ὅς ἐστιν ἡ ἡμερομηνία τοῦ Πάσχα τοῦ ἔτους ἐκείνου, ἀπέναντι δὲ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τούτων σημειοῦνται καὶ ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἑβδομάς, ὡς καὶ ἡ ἡμέρα ἐν ᾗ συμπίπτει ἡ ἑορτή, ἔστι δὲ ἡ πέμπτη τῆς τοῦ Τελώνου καὶ Φαρισαίου ἑβδομάδος.

units.slavonic_text: [English Facing Translation: Interpretive Rules 1, 2, and 3 (p. 931)]
units.english_text: 1. Holy Pascha [Easter] may occur between March 22-JC and April 25-JC [between April 4-GC and May 8-GC], a thirty-four day period [comprising 35 calendar dates inclusively]. Therefore, the beginning of the Triodion period may occur between January 11-JC and February 13-JC [between January 24-GC and February 28-GC]. The first column of the Chart indicates the beginning date of the Triodion period; the second column indicates the date of Holy Pascha [Easter]. The third column shows the date and name of each of the 18 immovable feasts and, below it, the days of the movable feasts with which each immovable feast may coincide; and the fourth column displays the paragraph and page numbers in the present work where the rubrical order of service for each concurrence is set forth in detail. We provide the following concrete example: if we desire to know in the year 1889 on which day and in which week of the Triodion period the Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante* / *Presentation*) occurs, we first determine the date of Pascha for that year—which in this case is April 9. We then examine the first two columns under this feast, where we find in the first column the number 29 [i.e., January 29], which represents the date of the beginning of the Triodion period in that year; in the second column we find April 9, which represents the date of Holy Pascha for that year. In the third column, directly across from those dates, the table designates the precise week and day of the Triodion period upon which this immovable feast falls—which in this case is the Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee.

units.english_text: 2. The immovable feasts of the Menologion that coincide within the periods of the Triodion and Pentecostarion are eighteen in number, extending from the Feast of our Venerable Father Theodosios the Cenobiarch (January 11)—the earliest date upon which the Triodion period can commence—unto the Feast of the Third Finding of the Honorable Head of the Holy Forerunner and Baptist John (May 25), which represents the latest date that can possibly fall within the Pentecostarion period. Of these eighteen immovable feasts, twelve pertain to the Triodion cycle and six pertain to the Pentecostarion cycle, as the Chart demonstrates.

Therefore, the beginning of the Triodion period may occur between January 11-JC and February 13-JC [between January 24-GC and February 28-GC]. The first column of the Chart indicates the beginning date of the Triodion period; the second column the date of Pascha [Easter]. The third column shows the date and name of each of the 18 immovable feasts and, below it, the days of the movable feasts with which each immovable feast may coincide; and the fourth column displays the paragraphs and pages in the present work, where the details of the order of service of each coincidence are described. We present the following example: if we desire to know in the year 1889 on which day and which week of the Triodion period the Feast of the Presentation of our Lord occurs, we find the date of Easter for that year — which in this case is April 9 — then we look at the first two columns under this feast, and we find in the first column the number 29 [i.e. January 29], which is the date for the beginning of the Triodion period in that year; in the second column, we find April 9, which is the date of Easter for that year. In the third column, across from those dates, is indicated which week and which day of the week of the Triodion period this immovable Feast of the Presentation occurs, which in this case is the Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee.
units.english_text: 3. Consequently, whenever the columnar tables adjacent to these variable feasts do not extend beyond the designated boundary numerals, it is manifest that in those years such feasts are celebrated outside the Triodion or outside the Pentecostarion....[^532]

units.slavonic_text: 2. The number of immovable feasts that occur during the periods of the Triodion and Pentikostarion are 18, from the Feast of Saint Theodosios (January 11)—which is the earliest date on which the Triodion period can begin—until the Feast of the Third Finding of the Venerable Head of the Forerunner [John the Baptist] (May 25)—which could possibly occur within the Pentikostarion period. Of these 18 immovable feasts, twelve occur within the Triodion period and six within the Pentikostarion period, as the Chart indicates.
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Boundaries of the Paschal Oscillation (Rules 1–3):* Rules 1 through 3 codify the mathematical architecture of the Byzantine computus as articulated in the Violakis Typikon. The 35-day inclusive oscillation of Holy Pascha (from the vernal equinox terminus of March 22 JC to the latest possible Pascha on April 25 JC) directly regulates the opening of the pre-Lenten Triodion 70 days earlier (January 11 to February 13 JC). The table identifies 18 critical intersection points with the fixed Menologion. In Rule 1, Violakis selects the year 1889—the very year following the publication of the 1888 editio princeps—as a pedagogical model: with Pascha falling on April 9, the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee occurred on January 29, causing the Great Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*, February 2) to fall on the Thursday of the pre-Lenten Week of the Publican and the Pharisee. Rule 3 clarifies the status of boundary feasts (such as St. Constantine and Helen on May 21 and the Third Finding of the Head of the Forerunner on May 25), which are celebrated as ordinary Menologion offices outside the Pentecostarion cycle whenever Pascha occurs early.

units.english_text: [Σημειωτέον ὅτι ἡ σχέσις ἀκινήτων καὶ κινητῶν ἑορτῶν διαφέρει μεταξὺ τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ καὶ τοῦ Γρηγοριανοῦ Ἡμερολογίου (ὅρα Comparative Outline of Movable Feasts between the Julian and Gregorian Calendar, σελ. 926). Κατὰ τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον, ἐν ᾧ τὸ Τριῴδιον ἄρχεται 24 Ἰανουαρίου (13 ἡμέρας ἀργότερον τῆς ἡμερομηνίας ἐνάρξεως εἰς τὸ Ἰουλιανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον) αἱ πρῶται τέσσαρες ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ εἰς τὸν Πίνακα—11, 17, 18 καὶ 20 Ἰανουαρίου—δὲν πρόκειται πλέον νὰ συμβοῦν ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου. Ἡ πρώτη πιθανὸν ἐνωρίτερη ἀκίνητος ἑορτὴ ἡ ὁποία δύναται νὰ συμβῇ ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου εἶναι 25 Ἰανουαρίου, Γρηγορίου τοῦ Θεολόγου. Ἐπίσης δέ, ἐπειδὴ τὸ τέλος τῶν κινητῶν ἑορτῶν (Κυριακὴ τῶν Ἁγίων Πάντων) πρόκειται ἵνα καθυστερηθῇ μέχρι 3 Ἰουλίου, τρεῖς ἐπιπρόσθεται ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ δύνανται νὰ συμβοῦν ἐντὸς τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, ἤτοι 24 Ἰουνίου, τὸ Γενέθλιον τοῦ Ἰωάννου τοῦ Βαπτιστοῦ· 29 Ἰουνίου, Πέτρου καὶ Παύλου τῶν Ἀποστόλων· καὶ 30 Ἰουνίου, τῶν 12 Ἀποστόλων.]

units.english_text: Δ΄. Ἐν τῷ Πίνακι δὲν ἐλήφθη ὑπ’ ὄψει ἡ προκύπτουσα, ὡς ἐκ τῶν Βισέκτων ἐτῶν, φαινομενικὴ μεταξὺ τῶν ἀριθμῶν τῆς ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ τοῦ Πάσχα ἀνωμαλία, καθότι τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀδύνατον καθορισθῆναι ἐν Πίνακι. Διὸ καὶ ὀφείλομεν διασαφηνίσαι ἐνταῦθα ὅτι, ὅταν ἔχωμεν ἐν νῷ δύο ἔτη μὴ Βίσεκτα καὶ τὰ δύο ὄντα, ἅτινα ἔχουσι τὸ Πάσχα κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν, εἶναι βέβαιον ὅτι ἡ τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἔναρξις, ὡς καὶ αἱ τοῦ Μηνολογίου ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ μετὰ τῶν κινητῶν τοῦ Τριῳδίου καὶ τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, συμβαίνει κατ’ αὐτὰ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν ἀπαρεγκλίτως. Ἀλλ’ ὅταν λάβωμεν ἐν νῷ δύο ἔτη, ὧν τὸ μὲν Βίσεκτον, τὸ δὲ μή, ἔχοντα ὅμως τὴν αὐτὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τοῦ Πάσχα, προκύπτει δυσχέρειά τις περὶ τὰς ἀκινήτους ἑορτὰς τὰς συμπιπτούσας πρὸ τῆς ἐμβολίμου ἡμέρας τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, διότι τὰ τοιαῦτα ἔτη ἔχουσι τὰς ἡμερομηνίας τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Τριῳδίου διαφόρους, ἑπομένως καὶ πάσας τὰς ἑορτὰς τὰς πρὸ τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου. Οὕτω, λόγου χάριν, ἔχομεν τὸ μὴ Βίσεκτον ἔτος ͵αωπθ΄ (1889) καὶ τὸ Βίσεκτον ͵αϡ΄ (1900), ἅτινα ἔχουσι τὸ Πάσχα αὐτὴν τὴν Θ΄ Ἀπριλίου, τοῦ πρώτου ἡ ἀρχὴ τοῦ Τριῳδίου συμπίπτει τῇ ΚΘ΄ Ἰανουαρίου, τοῦ δευτέρου δὲ τῇ Λ΄ διὰ τοὺς προῤῥηθέντας λόγους. Κατὰ συνέπειαν, μετὰ τὴν ἡμερομηνίαν τῆς κατὰ τὸ Βίσεκτον ἔτος ἀρχῆς τοῦ Τριῳδίου μέχρι τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου, ὅτε καὶ γίνεται ἡ προσθήκη τῆς ἐμβολίμου ταύτης ἡμέρας, πρέπει διὰ τὰς ἐπιλαχούσας ἐν τῷ διαστήματι τούτῳ ἑορτὰς νὰ λαμβάνωμεν οὐχὶ τὴν ἀπέναντι τοῦ Πασχαλίου ἀριθμοῦ ἐν τῷ Πίνακι σημειουμένην ἡμέραν τῆς ἑβδομάδος, ὡς ἡμέραν τῆς ἐπιγραφομένης ἑορτῆς, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὑπὸ ταύτην κειμένην, ἤτοι τὴν ἀπέναντι τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ τῆς κατὰ τὸ Βίσεκτον ἐκεῖνο ἔτος ἐνάρξεως τοῦ Τριῳδίου ἡμερομηνίαν, ὡς μήπω ἐλθούσης τῆς ΚΘ΄ Φεβρουαρίου· μετὰ τὴν ΚΘ΄ ὅμως αἱ ἡμέραι τῶν ἐπιλαχουσῶν ἑορτῶν

Κατὰ τὸ Γρηγοριανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον, ἐν ᾧ τὸ Τριῴδιον ἄρχεται 24 Ἰανουαρίου (13 ἡμέρας ἀργότερον τῆς ἡμερομηνίας ἐνάρξεως εἰς τὸ Ἰουλιανὸν Ἡμερολόγιον) αἱ πρῶται τέσσαρες ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ εἰς τὸν Πίνακα—11, 17, 18 καὶ 20 Ἰανουαρίου—δὲν πρόκειται πλέον νὰ συμβοῦν ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου. Ἡ πρώτη πιθανὸν ἐνωρίτερη ἀκίνητος ἑορτὴ ἡ ὁποία δύναται νὰ συμβῇ ἐντὸς τοῦ Τριῳδίου εἶναι 25 Ἰανουαρίου, Γρηγορίου τοῦ Θεολόγου. Ἐπίσης δέ, ἐπειδὴ τὸ τέλος τῶν κινητῶν ἑορτῶν (Κυριακὴ τῶν Ἁγίων Πάντων) πρόκειται ἵνα καθυστερηθῇ μέχρι 3 Ἰουλίου, τρεῖς ἐπιπρόσθεται ἀκίνητοι ἑορταὶ δύνανται νὰ συμβοῦν ἐντὸς τοῦ Πεντηκοσταρίου, ἤτοι 24 Ἰουνίου, τὸ Γενέθλιον τοῦ Ἰωάννου τοῦ Βαπτιστοῦ· 29 Ἰουνίου, Πέτρου καὶ Παύλου τῶν Ἀποστόλων· καὶ 30 Ἰουνίου, τῶν 12 Ἀποστόλων.]

units.slavonic_text: [English Facing Translation: Calendar Variance Note & Interpretive Rule 4 (Part 1, p. 933)]
units.english_text: [It should be noted, however, that the relationship between immovable and movable feasts in the Gregorian Calendar differs from that in the Julian Calendar (see the Comparative Outline of Movable Feasts, p. 926). In accordance with the Gregorian Calendar, where the Triodion period begins on 24 January (13 days later than the date of beginning in the Julian Calendar) the first four immovable feasts listed in the Chart — 11, 17, 18 and 20 January — will no longer fall within the Triodion period. The earliest possible immovable feast to fall within the Triodion period will now be 25 January, St. Gregory the Theologian. Similarly, since the end of the movable feasts (Sunday of All Saints) will now be delayed until 3 July, three more immovable feasts may possibly fall within the Pentikostarion period: 24 June, the Nativity of John the Baptist; 29 June, Peter and Paul the Apostles; and 30 June, the 12 Apostles.]

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Bissextile Leap-Year Triodion Discrepancy (Rule 4):* Rule 4 addresses the computistic shift introduced by bissextile intercalation (*dísekton étos* / leap year). In the Julian computus, the interval between Septuagesima (the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee) and Pascha Sunday is invariant at 10 weeks (70 days). However, whenever February receives an intercalary 29th day (*embolimos hēmera*), the calendar date of the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee must advance by one day relative to a common year sharing the same Paschal date (e.g., January 30 instead of January 29 for an April 9 Pascha). For all immovable commemorations falling before February 29 (such as St. Anthony, St. Euthymius, the Three Hierarchs, the Meeting of the Lord, and St. Charalampus), this intercalation shifts the weekday of concurrence one row lower in the table. Once the intercalary leap day of February 29 has passed, the normal 70-day cadence resumes, and all subsequent commemorations (beginning with the 40 Martyrs of Sebaste and the Annunciation) coincide upon identical liturgical days. Note that 1900 was a leap year under the Julian Calendar (which maintains an uncorrected four-year leap rule), though a common century year under the Gregorian Calendar.

units.english_text: μέχρι τέλους, ἔρχονται ἀπέναντι τοῦ Πασχαλίου ἀριθμοῦ. units.english_text: addition of one more day (i.e., February 29), we delay the opening date of the Triodion period by one day. In like manner, we delay the concurring movable feasts by one date as well. As another illustrative example for clarification, consider two immovable feasts occurring respectively before and after February 29: the first, namely the Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante* / *Presentation*), being one of the feasts prior to February 29, in a common year (1889) occurs on Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee (as indicated in column 3); in the leap year (1900), however, it occurs on Wednesday of that same week. The Feast of the Annunciation, on the other hand, since it occurs after February 29, falls in both years upon one and the same day—that is, the Saturday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent. In this identical manner all other feasts of the Chart can be determined.

units.slavonic_text: addition of one more day (i.e. February 29), we delay the beginning of the Triodion period by one date. Similarly, we delay the coinciding movable feasts by one date as well. As another example for clarification, we have two immovable feasts occurring one before February 29 and the other after. The first, namely the Feast of the Presentation of our Lord, which is one of the feasts prior to February 29, in a non-Leap Year (1889), occurs on Thursday of the Week of the Publican and the Pharisee (as indicated in column 3), but in the Leap Year (1900) on Wednesday of that week. The Feast of the Annunciation, however, since it occurs after February 29, will fall in both those years on one and the same day, that is, the Saturday of the Fifth Week. It is in this manner that all other feasts of the Chart can be determined.
units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Pre- and Post-Leap Day Coincidence and Extreme Paschal Limit (Rule 5):* The concluding section of Rule 4 and Rule 5 delineates the contrasting behavior of liturgical concurrences before and after the intercalary pivot of February 29. By contrasting the Meeting of the Lord (February 2, which shifts from Thursday to Wednesday between 1889 and 1900) with the Annunciation of the Mother of God (March 25, which remains fixed on the Saturday of the Akathist / Fifth Week of Great Lent in both years), Violakis provides an infallible operational diagnostic for typikaris. Rule 5 addresses the extreme terminal boundary of the Paschal computus: when Pascha falls on April 24 JC (May 7 GC) in a leap year, the Triodion begins on February 14 JC (February 27 GC) rather than February 13 JC. This constitutes the absolute latest possible opening of the Triodion in the history of the Orthodox Church, compressing the post-Paschal season and minimizing the Apostles' Fast to its shortest possible statutory duration.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Perpetual Concurrence Matrix:* Physical leaf p952 introduces the structural legend for the tabular Paschalion and Menologion concordance of George Violakis. The dual-dating rubric reflects the pastoral reality of the Eastern Christian diaspora, correlating the classical Julian computus (*Paskhalia*) with the civil Revised Julian and Gregorian calendars. The 13-day delta shifts the liturgical window of immovable commemorations relative to the variable 70-day pre-Paschal and 50-day post-Paschal cycles.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Early Pre-Lenten Concurrences (January 11–18):* Physical leaf p954 tabulates the earliest possible concurrences between the immovable Menologion and the pre-Lenten Triodion cycle. The solitary entry for Saint Theodosios the Cenobiarch (January 11) marks the theoretical frontier: only when Holy Pascha falls upon its earliest possible terminus of March 22 JC does the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee open on January 11, displacing the saint's full festive office. For Saint Anthony the Great (January 17), the commemoration sweeps across every day of the pre-Lenten opening week until Pascha reaches March 28 JC, where Anthony coincides directly with the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee itself.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Printed Numerals:* In the printed bilingual edition (p. 941), the first table exhibits gross typesetting errata: Column 1 erroneously prints "13 (20)" through "18 (25)" instead of the correct Julian/Gregorian values "13 (26)" through "18 (31)", and Column 2 erroneously prints "24 (31)" through "29 (5 April)" instead of "24 (6 April)" through "29 (11 April)". In addition, the Gregorian conversions under January 20 reproduce the Greek compositor's mistake of reading "1 April" and "2 April" instead of 1 February and 2 February. All dates have been emended to mathematical orthodoxy in this translation.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing English Page (p. 943):* The printed English text exhibits recurring calendar distortions in Column 2, misprinting Julian Paschal dates 25 through 30 March as "25 (1 April)" through "30 (6 April)" instead of the correct 13-day Gregorian conversions ("7 April" through "12 April"). Furthermore, the Gregorian adjustments for January 19–21 are erroneously styled "1 April", "2 April", and "3 April" instead of February. These errors have been corrected in the table.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing English Page (p. 947):* In the printed English text, several numerical lapses occur: under the Three Hierarchs, lines 29 and 30 misprint the Gregorian dates as "29 (9)" and "30 (10)" instead of 29 (11 February) and 30 (12 February). In the Presentation section (Column 4), the printed English shifts the rubrical section references up by one row starting from January 18 (assigning Monday §§ 11–13, Sunday of Meatfare § 19, and Saturday of Souls §§ 1–3), which contradicts the Greek original on p. 946. These discrepancies are reconciled to the Greek archetype.

units.english_text: * *Scholarly Apparatus on the Liturgical Concurrences of Saint Charalambos (10 February):* Physical leaf p964 documents the migration of the feast of the Holy Hieromartyr Charalambos across the opening weeks of the Great Fast and Cheesefare. When Pascha falls early (March 22 JC), the commemoration lands on Tuesday of the Second Week of Lent (§ 28, p. 190), governed by the rubrics for weekday commemorations occurring with the Presanctified Liturgy. When Pascha falls on March 24 JC, Charalambos coincides with the Sunday of Orthodoxy (§§ 23–25, pp. 188–189), requiring the full festal synthesis with the Sunday of the Triumph of Orthodoxy and the commemoration of the Holy Icons.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing English Page (p. 953):* In the printed English edition, physical leaf p968 displays multiple critical typesetting anomalies: In the top table, Column 4 references are shifted by one row, and line 17 contains the garbled compositing error "9 (1926-8 (191)". In the middle table under April Paschal dates, the English typesetter omitted Wednesday on line 24 (Julian Jan 24), shifting Tuesday to line 24, Monday to line 25, Sunday of Orthodoxy to line 26, Saturday to line 27, Friday to line 28, Thursday to line 29, Wednesday to line 30, and completely dropping line 31 (Julian Jan 31). In this critical edition, the correct sequence of days and the missing line 31 have been restored from the Greek archetype on leaf p967.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing English Page (p. 955):* On physical leaf p970, the printed English text contains multiple egregious typographical errors: In the top table, the Paschal dates are misprinted as '4 May', '5 May', and '6 May' instead of April (Julian April 22, 23, and 24 correspond to Gregorian May 5, 6, and 7, whereas the printer conflated Julian April dates with Gregorian May dates in reverse). Furthermore, the typographer set '1 (1190)' instead of '1 (190)'. In the Forty Martyrs table under April, the Column 4 paragraph citations are staggered and displaced from the Greek original on p. 954; all references have been reconciled with the canonical Greek archetype.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 956–957):* In the Greek text of leaf p971 (p. 956), Column 4 exhibits a vertical displacement: the typesetter omitted the citation for Friday of the Third Week (§ 6, pp. 197–198), printing § 4–5 opposite Friday and shifting all subsequent rubric references upward by one row throughout the page, leaving Wednesday of Clean Week without a section number. The facing English page (p. 957) rectified this displacement by restoring the rubrical references to their proper liturgical days. For Pascha Sunday on March 25 (Kyrio-Pascha), the Greek archetype notes § 69 (Easter Eve) alongside §§ 70–72, which is supplied in this critical edition.

For Pascha Sunday on March 25 (Kyrio-Pascha), the Greek archetype notes § 69 (Easter Eve) alongside §§ 70–72, which is supplied in this critical edition.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 966–967):* On physical leaf p981 (Greek text), Column 4 assigns §§ 5–6 (p. 253) to Monday after Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers (row January 30), leaving Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers blank, whereas facing leaf p982 (English text) assigns §§ 7–8 (pp. 253–254) to Monday and restores §§ 5–6 (p. 253) to Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearers. For Bright Monday (February 13), leaf p981 leaves Column 4 unprinted; the rubric citation (§§ 1–2, pp. 251–252) is restored from the facing English page. For the Translation of the Relics of Saint Athanasius (May 2), the non-canonical phrasing in the 1888 English column for Wednesday of the Apodosis of Pascha is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1. In the Greek archetype (p. 966), Column 4 entries exhibit vertical typographic shifting relative to Ascension Thursday and the Apodosis of Pascha, harmonized herein in accordance with the liturgical rubrics of the Typikon.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 968–969):* On physical leaf p984 (English text), Column 4 for February 1–5 displays a major typesetting corruption, printing "7 (257)" across five consecutive rows (Saturday through Tuesday of the Week of the Myrrh-Bearers) and "7–8 (257)" on Monday, whereas the Greek archetype on leaf p983 properly directs the reader to §§ 7–8 (pp. 253–254) for the Week of the Myrrh-Bearers and § 4 (p. 256) on Monday. The Greek readings are restored and harmonized in this critical edition. Furthermore, non-canonical phrasing for the Apodosis of Mid-Pentecost in the 1888 English column is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1.

units.english_text: [*] *Epigraphic Corrigenda on Facing Pages (pp. 974–975):* On physical leaf p990 (English text), the non-canonical phrasing for Saturday of the Apodosis of Pentecost, Friday of the Apodosis of the Ascension, and Wednesday of the Apodosis of Pascha is rectified herein to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1. In the Greek archetype on leaf p989, the Column 4 citation for Saturday of the Apodosis of Pentecost is printed as "23 (273)" opposite Friday with the Saturday row left blank, whereas the facing English edition on leaf p990 properly attributes § 24 (p. 273) to Saturday and § 23 (p. 273) to Friday through Tuesday; this is adopted in the critical edition. On Friday (row February 7), the Greek archetype records an additional reference "3–5 (266–267)" which corresponds to the rubrics for the preceding days that carry over onto leaf p991.

In the lower rows of the table (February 10–13), slight vertical typesetting drift occurs between the Greek archetype and the 1888 English facing translation: on leaf p993, § 10 (p. 277) is printed opposite Saturday of the week of the Samaritan Woman and Friday, while §§ 1–2 (p. 275) is placed opposite Thursday, leaving Wednesday unannotated; on facing leaf p994, the English compositor placed § 10 (p. 277) opposite Thursday and Friday, and assigned §§ 1–2 (p. 275) to Wednesday of the Apodosis of Mid-Pentecost, leaving Saturday blank. Both witness tracks are reconciled in this critical edition. Non-canonical phrasing in the 1888 English column for the Apodosis of Pascha and the Apodosis of Mid-Pentecost is rectified to canonical "Apodosis" per MTS-1.

Within some services of the Orthodox Church, some of the terms presented here can take on an additional and even different meaning. Furthermore, because of the variety of opinion as to the origin of each term, etymological comments offered here should be considered as suggestions only. Greek terms are given in the original Greek and are also rendered phonetically according to the transliteration table first used in the book The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by Theodore Bogdanos, published in 1993 by the then Greek Orthodox Diocese of Denver Choir Federation. This organization was later renamed, in 2007, as The Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Denver Church Music Federation. The phonetic transliterations used here are in preference to the use of Latinized or Anglicized renditions used by some authors and scholars, so that the reader might become gradually more accustomed to the actual sound of the current Greek pronunciation of the words. In each listing, the initial word in BOLD CAPITALS type is either given in English or is a Greek word spelled phonetically according to the transliteration table mentioned above. This word is then followed by the word in the Greek language enclosed in parenthesis and with its appropriate definite article. When any word is presented in SMALL CAPITALS in the body of a definition, this indicates that the word itself is defined in its proper alphabetical order. In each definition the word is only presented in small capitals the first time it is used. Each subsequent time the word is used it will be in normal type. units.slavonic_text: Slavic and East European Journal (SEEJ) and used by many academic institutions. Abbreviations for authors frequently cited in the items in this dictionary are: AE=Archimandrite Ephrem; APL=Archpriest Paul Lazor; DC=Dimitri Conomos; EP=Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople website; FL=Fotios Litsas; KW=Bishop Kallistos Ware; MM=Mother Mary; and TB=Theodore Bogdanos. These authors are found in the bibliography at the end of this dictionary. Other frequently used abbreviations are Lit.=literally and pl.=plural. In considering the location of certain physical items and ritual events within a Greek Orthodox CHURCH building, one's understanding should be based on the usual and traditional floor plan of these churches where the SANCTUARY and ALTAR TABLE face East and the NARTHEX faces West. As mentioned, this present list of definitions was compiled from numerous sources including internet searches. Some of the terms were also presented in the Glossary of The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order by Theodore Bogdanos. In the present list, the definitions taken from or modified from the Bogdanos book are marked by an asterisk. The Bogdanos list was later expanded to include many additional citations for terms used in the Violakis Typikon itself or related to them. The terms were selected for inclusion because we felt they might be generally unfamiliar to the average reader (or in our case, the average church musician) or in need of further elucidation on other grounds. Also, because of the complexity of some subjects, the definitions have occasionally been expanded into small essays by the perceived necessity for greater clarity. For a more detailed description of any sacred person or event, one may consult the various biographies (SYNAXARIA) in the Minea or the Megas Synaxaristis. For sources used, see the bibliography at the end of this dictionary. Finally, I express my gratitude to Theodore Bogdanos, Professor Emeritus of Medieval English and European (Byzantine) Literature, San Jose State University, San Jose, California, for his generous help in reviewing and editing this dictionary of terms.

units.english_text: [*] *Editorial Note on the Typikon Dictionary (pp. TD-5–TD-6):* Physical leaves p999 and p1000 record the opening alphabetical index (Letters A through E) of the comprehensive *Dictionary of Terms Related to the Typikon* compiled by George T. Demos, MD, appended to the 2007 Athens/Denver bilingual edition of the 1888 Violakis Typikon. In accordance with the Master Translation Standard (MTS-1) and the Ecosystem Liturgical Lexicon, entries designating *Apolytikia* are translated and harmonized to canonical "Dismissal Troparion", and non-canonical variants are cross-referenced to canonical UGCC equivalents (*Tone* for *Mode*, *Dormition* for *Assumption*, *Pascha* for *Easter*).

units.english_text: [*] *Editorial Note on the Index (pp. TD-9–TD-10):* Non-canonical variants in this index section have been harmonized with the Master Translation Standard (MTS-1) and the Ecosystem Liturgical Lexicon. Entries for (*Post-feast*) and (*Pre-feast*) (lit. 'Post-feast' and 'Pre-feast') are indexed under canonical *Afterfeast* and *Forefeast*, *Mode* under *Tone*, and *Kathisma Hymn* under *Sessional Hymn*. Psalter references are harmonized with the Septuagint (LXX) canon with Masoretic (MT) versification supplied in brackets.

units.english_text: **ABSTINENCE** (ἐγκράτεια, ἡ [*ἐγκράτια*]). See also **FAST**: A penitential practice in Christianity consisting of voluntary deprivation of certain foods for religious reasons. In the Orthodox Church, days of abstinence are observed on Wednesdays and Fridays, or other specific periods, such as Great Lent. (FL)

units.english_text: **ACROSTIC** (ἀκροστιχίς, ἡ): The term is derived from two Greek words: *akros*, meaning the end or tip [of a verse], and *stichos*, meaning a line [of verse]. A *stichos* is similar to a stanza, although not as long. An acrostic poem, then, is a poem or verse of several lines in which the initial letters of all the lines read in exact sequence spell a word which may be the name of the author or other appellation or dedication. An acrostic may also begin with a successive letter of the Greek alphabet beginning with alpha. The earliest example of an acrostic was a Hebrew poem in which the consecutive lines or verses began with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. This kind of poem is also known as an 'abecedarian poem'; the a-b-c-d can be perceived in this title. The most famous Scriptural acrostic is Psalm 118 [MT 119], where each of the 22 stanzas of 8 verses begins with a successive Hebrew letter.

units.slavonic_text: AGIA TRAPEZA (Ἁγία Τράπεζα, ἡ): Lit. the HOLY TABLE or ALTAR TABLE. It is the large central table found in the center of the SANCTUARY which has been sanctified in the Service of Consecration and contains the relics of three Saints or Martyrs.
units.english_text: The practice of the ancient church was simply to celebrate the "breaking of bread" in homes, on a simple wooden table not unlike that used in the Last Supper. In time though, the place on which the bread was broken changed from common wooden tables to the tombs of those men and women of the faith who were persecuted and martyred in the name of the Lord. This practice evolved into the use of marble altar tables (reminiscent of tombs) in which the sacred relics of saints and martyrs of the Church are placed at the time of its Consecration.

units.english_text: Today, the Altar Table is covered with two cloths. The first cover on the bare surface of the table, the **KATASARKION**, is reminiscent of the shroud placed on our Lord in the tomb at His burial. It is placed on the table by the bishop during the service of the consecration of the church and remains there permanently as the very Body of our Lord has sanctified it. The second and often richly ornate cloth, placed over the Katasarkion, stems from a gesture of respect and love by the builders of the Great Church (St. Sophia) in Constantinople. This beautiful cloth "gold-threaded and adorned with precious stones" covered the table which housed the relics of the martyrs and upon which were placed the precious gifts of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today, the faithful as members of the body of Christ, may offer beautiful altar covers in like manner.

Today, the faithful as members of the body of Christ, may offer beautiful altar covers in like manner.
units.english_text: In a legend recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea, King Abgarus of Edessa had written to Jesus, asking Him to come and cure him of an illness. Instead, the apostle Thaddaeus is said to have come, bearing a cloth featuring Jesus' facial features, by which the king was miraculously healed. Since Jesus was still living at the time, this image would not seem to have a connection with His alleged burial shroud, today known as the shroud of Turin. The vicissitudes of the Edessa image between the first century and his own time are not reported by Eusebius.

units.english_text: There is no record explaining why or when the image was hidden in this manner, although some have suggested that it was to extend the assumed protection provided by the cloth to the whole city, or to hide it from persecutors of the Christian faith, persecutions being recorded in the area from the late first century until the time of the Emperor Constantine the Great. If the image was truly brought to Edessa in the first century, it might well have been hidden during the reign of Abgarus' son Ma'nu VI, who is thought to have reverted to paganism.

units.english_text: The Mandylion disappeared again after the Persians conquered Edessa in 609. An Arab legend, related to historian Andrew Palmer when he visited Urfa (Edessa) in 1999, relates that the towel (*mendil*) of Jesus was thrown into a well in what is today the city's Great Mosque. The Christian tradition is at variance with this, recounting that, in 944, it was exchanged for a group of Muslim prisoners—at that time the Image of Edessa was taken to Constantinople where it was received amidst great celebration by Emperor Romanos I, who deposited it in the Palatine Chapel. It remained there until the Crusaders sacked the city in 1204 and carried off many of its treasures to western Europe—though the "Image of Edessa" is not mentioned in this context in any contemporary document.

units.slavonic_text: TD-17
units.english_text: Other documents from the 6th century—it is said—in the Vatican Library and the University of Leiden, Netherlands, seem to suggest another image at Edessa. A 10th-century codex, *Codex Vossianus Latinus* Q 69 found by Gino Zaninotto in the Vatican Library, contains an 8th-century account saying that an imprint of Christ's whole body was left on a canvas kept in a church in Edessa: it quotes a man called Smera in Constantinople saying “King Abgar received a cloth on which one can see not only a face but the whole body” (in Latin: *“Faciei figuram sed totius corporis figuram cernere poteris.”*). This image is apparently not the same as the Mandylion whose widely-disseminated and familiar iconic image is of a face alone.

units.english_text: **AIR / AER** (Ἀήρ, ὁ or Ἀέρας, ὁ) *Slav.* Vozdukh, vozdux 'the air'; often the term has been spelled **Aer**. In the Byzantine rite, this is the largest and outermost covering placed over both the chalice and **PATEN** (Diskos). It is larger than the individual veils each used to cover the chalice and the paten. It symbolizes Joseph’s shroud on Christ’s body as well as the stone sealing Christ’s tomb. All of these veils are beautifully embroidered and are often in the same style and color as the vestments of the celebrating priest. The Aer, which takes its name either from the lightness of the material of which it was formerly made or from the fact that in the Divine Liturgy, during the time of the recitation of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, the priest holds it high in the air and waves it slowly over the chalice and paten. The use of the Aer, like that of the smaller veils, was intended to prevent anything from falling into the chalice or paten and contaminating them before the sacred vessels were brought to the altar prior to the consecration. The Aer is first mentioned by name in an explanation of the Liturgy by a writer of the sixth century, and is also alluded to as “the so-called *aër*” in the Acts of the Council of Constantinople. In the Byzantine rite the Aer is placed on the shoulders of the **DEACON** or **PRIEST** who brings the **PATEN** to the altar during the procession of the **GREAT ENTRANCE**.[^567]

units.english_text: **AKOLUTHIA** (ἀκολουθία, ἡ) *Lit.* a following, attendance, or train. From the Greek *akolutho* “I follow”; *Slav.: posledovanie*). In the Eastern churches, the term signifies the arrangement of the Divine Services (Canonical Hours or Divine Office), perhaps because these various parts are closely connected and follow in order. In a more restricted sense, the term “akoluthia” refers to the fixed portion of the Office (that which does not change from day to day).

units.english_text: The Office is composed of both musical and textual elements, the first is usually identified by the musical mode or tone or, in Greek, Tone (*Ichos* / ἦχος), according to which the compositions are to be chanted (see **TONE**). In Byzantine Music there are eight musical modes (Tones 1 to 8): four authentic and four plagal Tones. The textual elements may be read quietly in silent prayer, read in a normal speaking voice, or may also be chanted in a simple recitative style or sung with a fully constructed melody.

units.english_text: **ALLELUIA** (Ἀλληλούϊα): This word is derived from Hebrew and is interpreted in Greek as meaning **"Praise the Lord"** (*Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον*). The word is sung after the reading of the **APOSTOLOS**. The faithful use it as a sign of joy and an expression of gladness as they praise God and thank Him for His wonders. This is also evident from the ending phrase of many Psalms to which the word is attached and from what the Book of Tobit (a deuterocanonical book of Scripture in the Septuagint Greek Old Testament) speaks of Jerusalem being rebuilt again after its fall, that all its streets will say ‘Alleluia’ (Tobit 13:18 [LXX 13:18]). units.slavonic_incipit: The Office is composed of both
units.slavonic_text: The Office is composed of both musical and textual elements, the first is usually identified by the musical mode or tone or, in Greek, ichos (ἦχος), according to which the compositions are to be chanted (see MODE). In Byzantine Music there are eight musical modes: four primary and four derived or plagal modes. The textual elements may be read quietly in silent prayer, read in a normal speaking voice, or may also be chanted in a simple recitative style or sung with a fully constructed melody.
