units.english_text: who sing to Thee: Alleluia!', but also in many places in the daily day and night services. The word is especially frequent in the rites for funerals and the mournful days of the fasts, when ‘Alleluia’ is sung in Vespers in place of the usual Prokimenon and in Matins instead of **"The Lord is God"** (*Θεὸς Κύριος*). Of this ‘Alleluia’, the instruction of the Typikon says: “But if it is ‘Alleluia’, that is if there is a fast, if we do not sing **'The Lord is God,'** we make the Great Prostrations. Otherwise etc.” Note that the Latin Church follows an opposite custom to the Eastern Church which expressly forbids the use of Alleluia on fast days and at mournful rites, and limits it to joyful days only, especially the day of Easter, when they sing it very often, as **"Christ is risen"** is frequently sung on Pascha. (The foregoing discussion of the use of Alleluia is found in the *Horologion*, before the Prayer of St. Ephrem the Syrian.)

units.english_text: **ALTAR** (Ἱερὸς Βωμός, Ἱερὸν Βῆμα): Used by the Church interchangeably for the entire **SANCTUARY** as well as for the Holy Table (Ἁγία Τράπεζα) itself. For the sake of clarity in this book the term is used to signify exclusively the Holy Table, on which the consecration of the Holy Gifts takes place. It has also been known by the terms **HOLY ALTAR, HOLY SANCTUARY, IERON VIMA, SANCTUARY** or simply **VIMA**.

units.english_text: **ALTAR TABLE** (Ἁγία Τράπεζα, ἡ): The consecrated table upon which the Divine Liturgy is celebrated. The Altar Table contains relics of the Saints which are placed within it at the time of the Church’s Consecration.[^569]

units.english_text: **AMOMOS** (Ἄμωμος, ὁ): See also **PSALM 118 [MT 119]**. A common abbreviation for the entire 17th **KATHISMA** of the Greek Old Testament Psalter (Ψαλτήριον, τό). This Kathisma contains only Psalm 118 [MT 119]. The abbreviation is so named because of a form of the key word in Greek in the first verse of the Psalm: **"Blessed are the undefiled in the way"** (*Μακάριοι οἱ ἄμωμοι ἐν ὁδῷ*). This Psalm, like the others, has 3 parts called Stases or Sections (Στάσεις).

This Kathisma contains only Psalm 118. The abbreviation is so named because of a form of the key word in Greek in the first verse of the Psalm (Μακάριοι οἱ ἄμωμοι ἐν ὁδῷ.) units.english_text: As Christians began to build churches, a special place was designated from which the homily could be preached and the Gospel could be read. This place was called the amvon, today’s pulpit. It was a place erected in the middle of the church to which the deacon or priest would ascend via a stairway. Later in the church’s development the pulpit was attached to a column on the north side of the **NAVE**. As seen today, the pulpit is usually constructed on the soleas, to the north side of the **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (Royal Doors) of the **HOLY SANCTUARY** (the central opening in the iconostasis).

units.english_text: **ANAGINOSKOMENA** (ἀναγινωσκόμενα, τά): *Lit.* 'texts which are read.' In the Eastern Church today, these readings are presented as pericopes (excerpts) that are read throughout the year in the various services of the Church. Even though *Anaginoskomena* is the Eastern term used for what the Catholic Church calls the deuterocanonical books and what Protestant traditions call apocrypha or pseudepigrapha, the *Anaginoskomena* are not grouped together as one separate category as they are in the 1611 King James Version (KJV) of the Bible or Brenton’s LXX with Apocrypha. They are instead integrated throughout the Greek Septuagint (LXX).

units.slavonic_text: TD-23
units.english_text: In the Eastern Christian tradition, there is no single uniform list of what the term *Anaginoskomena* includes. One can examine various Bibles for these variations. 2 Esdras in the KJV is called 3 Esdras in the Slavonic Bible and listed as an appendix, but is not in the Septuagint, and therefore not in the Greek Bible. The Slavonic Bible does not include 4 Maccabees, but it is found as an appendix in the Greek Bible. This is the only book the Eastern Church universally considers as apocryphal.

units.slavonic_text: what St Athanasios refers to as “other books besides these not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness. But the former, my brethren, are included in the Canon, the latter being [merely] read; nor is there in any place a mention of apocryphal writings.”

units.slavonic_incipit: In the Orthodox tradition, there is
units.slavonic_text: In the Orthodox tradition, there is no fully accepted list of what the term Anaginoskomena includes. One can just look at various Bibles for these variations. 2 Esdras in the KJV is called 3 Esdras in the Slavonic Bible and listed as an appendix, but is not in the Septuagint, and therefore not in the Greek Bible. The Slavonic Bible does not include 4 Maccabees but it is found as an appendix in the Greek Bible. This is the only book the Orthodox Church universally considers as apocryphal.
units.english_text: In the LXX, **PSALM 151** is labeled not as 151 but as 'outside the number' (*ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ*) and it is found as an appendix to the 150 Psalms of David. There are, following the Psalms in various ancient liturgical psalter books and biblical manuscripts such as *Codex Alexandrinus*, what are known as the Odes, which are liturgical canticles quoting or alluding to other parts of Scripture. The most commonly used is Ode 14 (a morning hymn based on Luke 2:14 and various portions of the Psalter) and is known as the Great Doxology. This doxology is used at the end of **MATINS (ORTHROS)** before the Divine Liturgy begins, every Sunday and at Great Compline during the Great Fast (Lent).

units.slavonic_text: TD-24
units.english_text: The Prayer of Azarias with the Song of the Three Holy Children, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon, are all found as part of the Book of the Prophet Daniel in the LXX. In addition, the Prayer of Azarias is Ode 7 and the Song of the Three Holy Children with additional verses is Ode 8 of the nine biblical Odes, which is also listed in the 14 Odes in Rahlfs’ LXX, but arranged as Odes 9 and 10 in *Codex Alexandrinus* and Swete’s LXX. The Prayer and Song, preceded by the canonical part of Daniel 3, are chanted during Holy Saturday Vespers.

units.slavonic_text: TD-25
units.english_text: Some analogia are fashioned so that they may be folded for easy portability. Some are intricately carved of fine wood and others are a simple frame intended to be completely covered with richly embroidered cloths (antipendia). The analogion used by the chanters is a special type which has two or three slanted sides and which may rotate to allow the chanters to more easily access the numerous liturgical books that may be used in the services. (FL)

units.english_text: **ANAPHORA** (ἀναφορά, ἡ) the 'Offering' or 'Offertory' (Eucharistic Prayer): The Anaphora is the most sacred part of the Divine Liturgy in which the offerings of bread and wine are consecrated as the Body and Blood of Christ. In the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, the rite begins with this prayer text: **"Let us stand well! Let us stand with fear!"** (*Στῶμεν καλῶς· στῶμεν μετὰ φόβου...*) up to and including the hymn text **"Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Sabaoth..."** (*Ἅγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, Κύριος Σαβαώθ...*) which is taken from Isaiah 6:1–3. This hymn text in the Latin rite is called the *Sanctus*.

units.slavonic_text: ANAMNISIS (ἀνάμνησις, ἡ): Lit. Remembrance or commemoration. It is that portion of the ANAPHORA in which the celebrant Priest remembers or recalls the words Christ uses in the institution of the Lord’s Supper.
units.english_text: In the Great Entrance Offertory of the Byzantine rite, the priest, accompanied by the deacon and the acolytes and censer-bearers, goes to the **PROTHESIS** (the Table of Preparation where the **PROSKOMIDI** is performed). Nearing the end of the singing of the Cherubic Hymn, the clergy solemnly bring the blessed but as yet unconsecrated bread and wine out of the **SANCTUARY** through the northern door of the **ICONOSTASIS**

units.slavonic_text: ANAPHORA (ἀναφορά, ἡ) the ‘Offering’ or ‘Offertory’: The Anaphora is the most sacred part of the Divine liturgy in which the offerings of bread and wine are consecrated as the body and blood of Christ. In the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, the rite begins with this prayer text: “Let us stand reverently! Let us stand in awe! (Στῶμεν καλῶς· στῶμεν μετὰ φόβου...) up to and including the hymn text “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Angelic Hosts...” ("Αγιος, ἅγιος, ἅγιος, Κύριος Σαβαώθ...) which is taken from Isaiah 6:1-55. This text in the Latin rite is called the Sanctus.

units.english_text: and proceed to the center of the church or at least directly in front of the **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (Royal Doors), where, turning to the people and holding the sacred gifts they pray successively for the ecclesiastical and secular authorities. In the Byzantine rite today, prayers are said for the hierarchs, the synod, and various other church dignitaries. The clergy then proceed solemnly to the altar bearing the Eucharistic gifts through the **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (Royal Doors). This part of the Liturgy is called the Great Entrance. After the paten (diskos) and chalice have been placed on the altar, the priest completes the Offertory with the prayer of the Anaphora: **“Receive also the supplication of us sinners and let it reach Thy Holy Altar; enable us to bring before Thee gifts and spiritual sacrifices for our sins and for the sins of the people that have been committed in ignorance. Make us worthy of finding favor with Thee so that our sacrifice may be well received by Thee, and the good Spirit of Thy grace may rest upon us, upon these Gifts set forth, and upon all Thy people.”** («Πρόσδεξαι καὶ ἡμῶν τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν τὴν δέησιν, καὶ προσάγαγε τῷ ἁγίῳ Σου Θυσιαστηρίῳ καὶ ἱκάνωσον ἡμᾶς προσενεγκεῖν σοι Δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας πνευματικὰς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἁμαρτημάτων, καὶ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ ἀγνοημάτων· καὶ καταξίωσον ἡμᾶς εὑρεῖν χάριν ἐνώπιόν Σου, τοῦ γενέσθαι σοι εὐπρόσδεκτον τὴν θυσίαν ἡμῶν καὶ ἐπισκηνῶσαι τὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτός Σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ προκείμενα Δῶρα ταῦτα καὶ ἐπὶ πάντα τὸν λαόν Σου.»)

units.slavonic_text: and proceed to the center of the church or at least directly in front of the BEAUTIFUL GATE, where, turning to the people and holding the sacred gifts they pray successively for the ecclesiastical and secular authorities. In the Greek Orthodox Church today, prayers are said for the national leaders, the Holy Synod, and various other church dignitaries. The clergy then proceed solemnly to the altar bearing the eucharistic elements through the BEAUTIFUL GATE. This part of the Liturgy is called the Great Entrance. After the paten and chalice have been placed on the altar, the priest completes the Offertory with the prayer of the Anaphora: “Receive also the supplication of us sinners and let it reach Your Holy Altar; enable us to bring before You gifts and spiritual sacrifices for our sins and for the sins of the people that have been commited in ignorance. Make us worthy of finding favor with You so that our sacrifice may be well received by You, and the beneficient spirit of Your grace may rest on us, on these Gifts, and on all Your people.” («Πρόσδεξαι καὶ ἡμῶν τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν τὴν δέησιν, καὶ προσάγαγε τῷ ἁγίῳ Σου Θυσιαστηρίῳ καὶ ἱκάνωσον ἡμᾶς προσενεγκεῖν σοι Δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας πνευματικὰς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμετέρων ἁμαρτημάτων, καὶ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ ἀγνοημάτων· καὶ καταξίωσον ἡμᾶς εὑρεῖν χάριν ἐνώπιόν Σου, τοῦ γενέσθαι σοι εὐπρόσδεκτον τὴν θυσίαν ἡμῶν καὶ ἐπισκηνῶσαι τὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτός Σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ προκείμενα Δῶρα ταῦτα καὶ ἐπὶ πάντα τὸν λαόν Σου.»)

units.english_text: Tones of the Oktoechos and sung in alternate succession from Sunday to Sunday throughout the church year as part of the Cycle of the Eight Tones (see **TONE**). Although this cycle commences on the Sunday of Pascha, the Anastasima Dismissal Troparia (lit. 'Anastasima Apolytikia') begin to be sung on the Third Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearing Women) with **"When You descended"** (*Ὅτε κατῆλθες* / *Ote Katilthes*) in Tone 2. In the Divine Liturgy on Sundays, the Resurrection Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Anastasimon Apolytikion') is usually sung immediately before and after the Small Entrance.

units.english_text: **ANATOLIKON** (*Ἀνατολικόν, τό*; *pl.* **ANATOLIKA** / *Ἀνατολικά, τά*): A hymn or the group of hymns of the Praises (*Ainoi* / Αἶνοι) sung in Sunday Matins (Orthros) and addressed to the Lord. The name derives from two possible sources: 1. From the scriptural verse **"Dawn is His Name"** (*«Ἀνατολὴ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ»*, Zechariah 6:12 LXX); or 2. From the name of their possible author, Anatolios.

units.slavonic_incipit: Byzantine Modes and sung in alternate
units.slavonic_text: Byzantine Modes and sung in alternate succession from Sunday to Sunday throughout the church year as part of the Cycle of Modes (see MODE). Although this cycle commences on Easter Sunday, the Anastasima Apolytikia begin to be sung on the Third Sunday of Easter (Sunday of the Myrrh Bearers) with Ὅτε κατῆλθες (Ote Katilthes) in Mode II. In the Divine Liturgy on Sundays, the Anastasimon Apolytikion is usually sung immediately before and after the Small Entrance.
units.english_text: **ANAVATHMOS** (*ἀναβαθμός, ὁ*; *pl.* **ANAVATHMI** / *ἀναβαθμοί, οἱ*) *Slav.* *Stepénny Antifóny* [Gradual Antiphons]: A short hymn or series of hymns based on the Psalms of Ascent (Gr. *Anavathmi*) numbered LXX 119–133 [MT 120–134], which are sung at Matins on Sundays and feasts having an appointed Gospel. On Sundays they are divided into three Antiphons, except for Tone 8, which has four Antiphons. They are sung immediately before the Prokimenon. On feasts, only the first Antiphon of Tone 4 is sung. In some traditions the final hymn from the Second Antiphon in Tone 4 is used rather than repeating the third Antiphon. (adapted from AE).[^573]

units.english_text: **ANTIMINSION** (*Ἀντιμήνσιον, τό*) *Slav.* *Antimins*: The Antiminsion of today is a consecrated rectangular cloth of linen or silk into which are sewn holy relics of a martyr or saint, embodying the ancient liturgical tradition of celebrating the Eucharist over the tombs of the martyrs who died rather than renounce Christ, and whose blood, united with the Blood of Christ, formed the foundation of the Church. The antiminsion bears iconographic representations of the Entombment of Christ, the four Evangelists, instruments of the Passion, and scriptural verses relating to the Holy Eucharist. The antiminsion is folded and wrapped within an outer protective silk cloth called the **ILITON** (*Εἱλητόν*); often red in color, it symbolizes both the swaddling clothes of Christ at His Nativity and the winding-sheet or burial shroud (*sindon*) in which His sacred Body was wrapped at His Crucifixion and Burial.

units.slavonic_text: ANTIMINSION (᾿Αντιμήνσιον, τό) Slav. Antimins: The Antiminsion of today is a rectangular piece of cloth, of linen or silk, into which is sewn the incorruptible relic of a Saint or Martyr, making real the early liturgical connection with the Martyrs who died rather than renounce Christ, and whose blood, after the Blood of Christ, formed the very foundation of the Church. The antiminsion has representations of the entombment of Christ, the four Evangelists, and scriptural passages related to the Eucharist. The antiminsion is usually wrapped in another protective cloth, usually of silk, called the ILITON; often red in color, it symbolizes the swaddling-clothes with which Christ was wrapped after His birth or the winding-sheet or shroud in which His body was wrapped after His Crucifixion.
units.english_text: The word Antiminsion is a hybrid Greek-Latin compound (*ἀντί* and *mensa*), meaning 'in place of the table.' While the **ALTAR TABLE** must always be consecrated with **RELICS** deposited within its sepulcher, it was not always feasible for the bishop to travel to every community for an altar consecration. For this reason, bishops consecrated these cloths or portable wooden tablets and distributed them to communities to serve in lieu of a fully consecrated stone altar table. This also provided portable altars for military chaplains, missionaries, and traveling clergy serving in remote regions.[^574]

units.slavonic_incipit: The word Antiminsion is a combination
units.slavonic_text: The word Antiminsion is a combination of Greek and Latin meaning ‘in place of the table’. While the HOLY TABLES were always to have been consecrated with RELICS placed inside of them, it was not always possible for the Bishop to visit each community to do so. For this reason, Bishops could consecrate these cloths or boards and send them to communities to be used in place of a consecrated Holy Table. This also allowed for portable Holy Tables for travelers. Military Chaplains and Missionaries may also use an Antiminsion instead of the table when serving in remote areas.

units.english_text: secrated. This solemn consecration may occur as part of the Consecration of a church, or in a distinct liturgical service. In this rite, the bishop anoints a small pocket sewn into the Antiminsion into which he deposits the holy relics of the saints and Holy Chrism (Myron). The bishop then seals the relics in place with fragrant wax-mastic. He may also imprint his episcopal seal upon the cloth. He then inscribes the Antiminsion with the dedication of the church for which it is consecrated, dating and signing the document. Inscribed upon every Antiminsion are the sacred words: **“By the grace of the All-Holy, Life-giving Spirit, this Antiminsion, the Holy Table, is consecrated for the Offering on it of the Body and Blood of our Lord in the Divine Liturgy.”**

units.english_text: **APICHIMA** (*ἀπήχημα, τό*; also *προήχημα*, *ἐνήχημα*): A musicological term in Byzantine chant for an intonation formula functioning as a melodic mnemonic. It is a melodic formula sung solo by the Archcantor or Protopsaltis without an accompanying ison. Its liturgical function is to guide the chanters as an *aide-mémoire* to establish the melodic scale and modal characteristics of the Tone about to be chanted. The apichima is intoned immediately prior to commencing the hymn, giving the starting pitch for the choir.

units.english_text: **APOCRYPHA**: In modern biblical usage, the term Apocrypha designates ancient Jewish sacred writings that are not part of the Rabbinic Hebrew canon but are recognized as canonical Scripture within Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism. Among these books are Tobit, Judith, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), and the Wisdom of Solomon. Protestant traditions follow the narrower Hebrew Masoretic canon in classifying these works as noncanonical. In Catholic theology the term *deuterocanonical* is applied to these sacred books. Pseudepigrapha, by contrast, are noncanonical or spurious texts falsely attributed to biblical authors.

units.slavonic_text: APOCRYPHA: In modern usage the Apocrypha refers to ancient Jewish books that are not part of the Hebrew Bible but are considered canonical in Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism. Among the various books included are Tobit, Judith, Baruch, and the Maccabees as well as Ecclesiasticus and the Wisdom of Solomon. Protestant churches follow Jewish tradition in judging these works apocryphal or noncanonical. The term deuterocanonical is used to refer to works accepted in one canon but not all. Pseudepigrapha are spurious works for which biblical authorship is claimed.
units.english_text: **APODOSIS** (*ἀπόδοσις, ἡ*) *Slav.* *Otdaniye* (*Отданіе*): (lit. 'giving back' or 'leave-taking'). See also **FEASTS**. The final day of the period of **METHEORTA** (Afterfeast), on which the liturgical observance of a feast comes to an end. The order of service on the day of the Apodosis is fundamentally identical to that of the feast day itself. The Apodosis of a major feast usually occurs eight days after the actual feast day (on its octave). The Apodosis of Pascha occurs on the fortieth day, on the eve of the Ascension. (TB and FL).

According to some sources, it has been named the “Dismissal Hymn” because it is chanted also at the end of Vespers, just before the “Dismissal Prayer” (ἀπόλυσις). It is the characteristic hymn of the day or of the feast, and is often referred to by some as ‘the TROPARION of the Day’. It is used in all the offices and in the Liturgy.
units.english_text: The Dismissal Troparion is also sung at the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy, at Matins, and at the Small Hours. The Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Apolytikion') changes according to the liturgical calendar to commemorate the feast of the day. For example, the Dismissal Troparion of the Nativity of Christ is: **“Thy Nativity, O Christ our God, hath shone upon the world the light of knowledge...”** (*«Ἡ Γέννησίς Σου, Χριστὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν...»*). The Dismissal Troparion for the Annunciation is: **“Today is the fountainhead of our salvation and the manifestation of the eternal mystery: the Son of God becometh the Son of the Virgin, and Gabriel announceth the good tidings of grace. Therefore, let us also cry aloud with him unto the Mother of God: Rejoice, full of grace, the Lord is with thee!”** (*«Σήμερον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν τὸ κεφάλαιον...»*).

units.slavonic_text: Also, it is a dismissal prayer or hymn said or sung at the end of the Liturgy and at other times during Matins and Vespers. units.english_text: **APOSTOLOS** (*Ἀπόστολος, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Apostol* (*Апостолъ*): The liturgical lectionary containing the New Testament pericopes drawn from the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of the Holy Apostles (Paul, Peter, John, James, and Jude), arranged for reading throughout the Ecclesiastical Year. It is commonly designated as the Epistle Book. The appointed pericope is read as the first scriptural lection at the Divine Liturgy prior to the Holy Gospel. The Apostolos also contains the **PROKIMENA** and **ALLELUIAS** with their verses sung before and after the Epistle lection.

units.slavonic_text: APOSTOLOS (᾿Απόστολος, ὁ) Slav. Apostol: An Orthodox service book containing portions of New Testament scriptures either from the Acts of the Apostles or from the Letters of St. Paul and arranged for use during the Orthodox Ecclesiastical Year. The book may also be referred to as the Epistle Lectionary. The prescribed lections are read as the first scripture reading in the Divine Liturgy and before the Gospel reading. The book usually includes the PROKIMENA and ALLELUIAS sung before and after the prescribed lection.
units.english_text: **ARCHIERATIKON** (*Ἀρχιερατικόν, τό*) *Slav.* *Chinovnik* (*Чиновникъ*); *Roman Pontifical*: In Greek, the 'Book of the Hierarch.' It is the pontifical liturgical book used by the **BISHOP** during a Hierarchical Divine Liturgy and other episcopal rites. It corresponds functionally to the presbyteral **IERATIKON** (*Sluzhebnik*), but contains the ceremonial rubrics and pontifical prayers reserved exclusively to bishops. In addition to the orders for the All-Night Vigil and the Divine Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom, St. Basil the Great, and the Presanctified Gifts, the Archieratikon contains the pontifical ordinals for major orders (deacon, presbyter, bishop) and minor orders (reader, subdeacon), along with the orders for the consecration of holy antiminsia and the dedication of churches.[^576]

units.english_text: the conciliar acts of the ecumenical synods. The dignity was also adopted widely in the Christian West, persisting in regular usage until the ninth century. Originally the archimandrite was simply the superior or abbot of his own monastery; gradually, however, he acquired supervisory jurisdiction over multiple monastic communities, and by the eleventh century archimandrites of great centers such as Mount Athos and Mount Olympus in Bithynia functioned as monastic abbots-general. In modern Greek practice two classes of archimandrites exist: monastic archimandrites governing their monasteries, and honorary or chancery archimandrites—celibate presbyters holding administrative posts in patriarchal or diocesan chanceries. Archimandrites are elevated by the authority of a Patriarch, Metropolitan, or Bishop, and in certain monasteries by monastic election. An archimandrite possesses the liturgical right to wear a pectoral cross and the **EPIGONATION** (*palitsa*) during the Divine Liturgy, and to prefix the sign of the cross to his signature after the manner of hierarchs. Monastic archimandrites also bear the pastoral staff (*rabdos* / *posokh*) and wear the monastic mantle embellished with four embroidered *tabulae* representing the Old and New Law (“the tables of the law”). Their vesture includes the black veil (*epanokalimavkion*) worn over the cylindrical kamilavkion and draping down the back. Archimandrites hold precedence over all other presbyters; among themselves precedence is determined by the date of elevation, though an archimandrite blessed by a patriarch outranks those elevated by lower hierarchs. A solemn liturgical ordinal governs their installation. The dignity exists across the Greek, Ukrainian, Melkite, Italo-Greek, Russian, and Bulgarian Churches, but is not attested among the non-Chalcedonian traditions (Copts, West Syrians, Ethiopians, Armenians). units.english_text: **ARTOKLASIA** (*Ἀρτοκλασία, ἡ*) *Slav.* *Blagoslovenie khlebov* (*Благословеніе хлѣбовъ*): The liturgical rite of the Blessing of Loaves (lit. 'breaking of bread,' from Gr. *klasis*, breaking, and *artos*, leavened bread) celebrated before the Dismissal Troparion (lit. 'Apolytikion') at Great Vespers during an All-Night **VIGIL** or Litiya. In parish practice it is often celebrated on major feasts at **VESPERS** or **MATINS**, or at the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy. The ceremony commemorates Christ’s miraculous multiplication of the five loaves to feed the five thousand men who had assembled to hear Him preach (Matthew 14:13–21; Mark 6:30–44; Luke 9:11–17; John 6:1–14). The five loaves of wheat bread, accompanied by vessels of wheat, wine, and olive oil, are blessed by the priest with the prayer of Artoklasia, recalling that the Lord Himself is the true “Bread of Life” descended from Heaven.[^578]

units.slavonic_text: ARTOKLASIA (᾿Αρτοκλασία, ἡ) Slav. Blagoslovenie xlebov: The ceremony of the Blessing of Loaves, or Breaking (Gr. klasis) of Bread (Gr. artos) that takes place before the APOLYTIKION at Vespers when there is an All-night VIGIL. In today’s Greek Orthodox churches, it is celebrated on important feasts even when there is no Vigil, at VESPERS or MATINS or usually after the LITURGY. The ceremony commemorates Christ’s miraculous blessing of the five loaves to feed about five thousand people without provisions who had come to hear Him preach near a sea shore (Mathew 16:13-21; Mark 6:30-44; Luke 9:11-16; and John: 6:1-14.) The ceremony also symbolizes the Lord Himself as the “bread of life” that has descended on mankind from Heaven. The ceremony for such occasions can be found in the bilingual edition of the Divine Liturgy published by the Archdiocese of Thyateira in the United Kingdom. (modified from AE)

units.slavonic_text: BALDACHIN: Sometimes written as baldachino or baldaquin, this is a permanent dome-like canopy made of fabric, wood, stone or metal. In some churches, such a structure may be erected over the altar supported by columns. It is often seen also as a canopy over the bishop’s throne.

The term also provides the official honorific title addressed to an Eastern Patriarch or Major Archbishop (“Your Beatitude”). (From FL).

units.english_text: **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (*Ὡραῖα Πύλη, ἡ* / *Royal Doors*): The double doors in the center of the **ICONOSTASIS**, designated in the *Typikon* as the Beautiful Gate or Royal Doors, through which only ordained clergy may pass while vested for divine service. In Eastern liturgical theology, the Beautiful Gate symbolizes the gates of Paradise opened by the Resurrection and the virginal womb of the Most Holy Theotokos through which Christ entered the world. Behind the doors hangs the liturgical veil or curtain (*katapetasma*), which is drawn closed at prescribed moments, especially during the communion of the clergy. The side doors on either side of the Iconostasis are termed the Angel Doors because icons of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are depicted upon them; they are also called the Deacon's Doors because the deacons enter and exit through them during litanies and censings. When lay servers are blessed to enter the sanctuary, they use the Angel Doors.[^579]

units.slavonic_text: *BEAUTIFUL GATE (῾Ωραῖα Πύλη, ἡ): The gate in the center of the ICONOSTASIS is referred to in the Typikon as the Beautiful Gate through which only members of the clergy may pass. In the liturgical theology of the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Beautiful Gate symbolizes the womb of the Virgin Mary. There may also be present a curtain that is drawn closed at certain times during the services, especially during the preparation of communion during the Divine Liturgy. The doors at either end of the Iconostasis are called Angel Doors because the icons of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel are usually depicted on them; alternatively, they may also be called deacon’s doors because the deacons frequently enter and leave the sanctuary through them. Laymen, when permitted to enter the sanctuary, will use one of the Angel Doors.

units.english_text: **BISHOP** (*Ἐπίσκοπος, ὁ*): *Lit.* 'Overseer.' The Bishop or **HIERARCH** is the chief shepherd, high priest, and spiritual leader of a local eparchy or diocese. He holds hierarchical precedence over archimandrites, priests, and deacons. A bishop possesses the exclusive sacramental power to ordain candidates to the holy priesthood and major orders. He also administers the temporal and spiritual affairs of his diocese. In the apostolic period of the New Testament, the titles of bishop (*episkopos*) and elder (*presbyteros*) were used interchangeably for pastoral leaders of the local churches. However, by the late first and early second century (as witnessed in the epistles of St. Ignatius of Antioch), the Church reserved the title of bishop exclusively for the single chief shepherd consecrated to succeed the Apostles in their office of pastoral oversight (cf. Acts 1:15–26; 14:23; 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). (Adapted from Rev. John W. Morris, Ph.D., *Glossary of Orthodox Terminology*).

units.slavonic_text: BISHOP (᾿Επίσκοπος, ὁ) Lit. Overseer. Today's bishop or HIERARCH is the spiritual leader of a local community of Christians. He ranks above archimandrites, priests and deacons. Only a bishop has the sacramental authority to ordain one to the priesthood. He also administers his diocese. In the New Testament there is no clear distinction between the offices of bishop and elder (presbyter), both of which function as leaders of the community. However, by the mid- to late first century, the Church began to reserve the title of bishop for men of spiritual qualification who were consecrated to follow the Apostles in their office of oversight (see article, “The Four ‘Orders’ in Church Government,” at 1 Tim.; Acts 1:15 26; 14:23; 1 Tim. 3:1-7). (Rev. John W. Morris, Ph.D., Glossary of Orthodox Terminology)

units.english_text: **CANON** (*κανών, ὁ*; *pl.* *κανόνες, οἱ*; See also **KANON**, **KANONES**) *Slav.* *Kanon*: A principal structural component in the Matins (Orthros) service, although it also occurs at Compline, Midnight Office, and in various trebniki (services of supplication or *parakleseis*). A Canon is a lengthy poetic hymnographic composition structured into nine Odes, with each Ode consisting of multiple troparia, the exact number and appointment of which are regulated by the *Typikon*. Each Ode takes its overarching theme from, and is modeled upon, one of the nine Biblical Canticles (for example, Ode 1 is linked to the Canticle of Moses in Exodus 15:1–19, which serves as its biblical prototype). In parish churches, unlike monasteries, the full verses of the Biblical Canticles (apart from the Magnificat) are customarily omitted, and brief liturgical refrains (such as **"Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee"** or **"Most Holy Theotokos, save us"**) are chanted in place of the scriptural verses. In daily liturgical practice, most Canons contain only eight Odes, because Ode 2 is appointed solely on Tuesdays during Great Lent, although the poetic acrostics of the canons frequently indicate that nine odes were originally composed. Normally three canons, and on Sundays four canons, are prescribed, appointed in such a manner that each Ode, including the Heirmos, comprises 14 troparia. (Excerpted from PL and AE).[^581]

units.english_text: **CANONARCH** (*κανονάρχης, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Kanonarkh*: The Canonarch is a tonsured liturgical chanter or reader assigned to ensure that the choir chants the prescribed liturgical texts in the appointed Tone and with the proper melody. He performs this function by reciting, in a solemn recitative cadence, each phrase of a slow sticheron or hymn immediately before the chanter or choir chants it with its full melody and meter. The Canonarch holds precedence higher than an ordinary Reader and lower than a Subdeacon or Deacon. The Canonarch is tonsured by the Bishop through the cheirothesia for minor orders. In early Byzantine practice, this tonsure was linked with that of the subdiaconate or reader. The Slavonic *Typikon* prescribes that a monastic canonarch fulfills his liturgical office with his head covered (that is, wearing the monastic klobuk).

units.slavonic_text: CANON (κανών, ὁ· κανόνες, οἱ) See also KANON, KANONES: A principal part in the Orthros (MATINS) service although it may appear elsewhere. A Canon is a lengthy poetic form composed of nine odes, with each ode being made up of many hymns, the number and source of which are regulated by the TYPIKON. Each ode takes its theme from and is therefore linked to a Biblical canticle (e.g., Ode 1 is linked to Exodus 15:1-19, the Canticle of Moses) which serves as its source. In churches, except those located in monasteries, apart from the Magnificat, the Biblical Canticles are usually omitted, simple refrains taking the place of the biblical verses. In practice, most Canons contain only eight Odes, since Ode 2 is only used on Tuesdays in Lent, though the acrostics often suggest that there were originally nine odes. Normally three, and on Sundays four Canons are prescribed, in such a way as to make each Ode, including the Irmos, consist of 14 Troparia. (Excerpted from PL and from AE)
units.english_text: **CANTICLE** (*ᾠδή, ἡ*; ODE OR SONG) *Slav.* *Pesn'*: The English term is derived from the Latin *canticulum* (a diminutive of *canticum*, song, from *cantare*, to sing). It is employed in Western biblical terminology as the equivalent of the Vulgate *canticum*. The Authorized King James Version generally translates both Hebrew and Greek terms simply as "song."

units.slavonic_text: CANONARCH (κανονάρχης, ὁ): The Canonarch is one of the chanters or readers whose task is to see that the other singers sing the correct texts in the correct mode and with the correct melody by reciting in a recitative style each phrase of a slow (andante or slower) hymn before the chanter finally sings it with its proper melody and rhythm. The Canonarch is higher in rank than a Reader and lower in rank than the Deacon. The Canonarch is tonsured by the Bishop. This tonsure seems to have covered both the Subdeacon and the Canonarch similar to a single tonsure having covered the office of taper-bearer, chanter and reader. The Slavonic Typikon also mentions that a monastic canonarch performs his duties with a covered head (i.e. wearing a klobuk).

units.slavonic_incipit: Originally, all of the above odes
units.slavonic_text: Originally, all of the above odes (1-9) were chanted in their entirety every day, with a short refrain inserted between each verse. Eventually, short hymns (TROPARIA) were composed to replace these refrains, a process traditionally inaugurated by Saint Andrew of Crete. Normally, the Second Ode is omitted because of its severe judgment of man. The most notable exception to this is that of the Great Penitential Canon of St. Andrew of Crete which is chanted during Great Lent. Gradually over the centuries, the verses of the Biblical Canticles were omitted (except for the Magnificat), and only the composed troparia were read, linked to the original canticles by an irmos. During Great Lent, however, the original Biblical Canticles are still read. (Adapted from The Festal Menaion by MM and KW and the New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia at http://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03301a.htm)
units.english_text: In daily practice, the Second Ode is omitted from the Canon because of its severe, penitential denunciations of human sin. The primary exception to this universal rule is the Great Penitential Canon of Saint Andrew of Crete, which contains all nine Odes and is chanted during Great Lent.

provenance.verbatim_source: In daily practice, the Second Ode is omitted from the Canon because of its severe, penitential denunciations of human sin. units.slavonic_text: CASSOCK (ράσον, τὸ· χιτών, ὁ· ἱμάτιον, τό): Cassocks exist in two forms, the ‘inner cassock’ and the ‘outer cassock.’ The Inner (or under) cassock is a floor-length garment that has long sleeves fitted like shirtsleeves. The ‘outer (over) cassock’ is also a floor-length garment, but more loosely fitting, with large sleeves. The wearing of inner-cassocks and outer-cassocks is common to bishops, priests, deacons, monks and nuns. Permission to wear a cassock is often given to seminarians, monastic novices, sub-deacons and readers in some parishes.
units.english_text: Over the centuries, the direct chanting of the full scriptural verses of the Biblical Canticles was gradually discontinued (except for the Magnificat), and only the composed troparia of the canon were chanted, tied to the themes and rhythm of the biblical canticle by the opening **HEIRMOS** (lit. 'irmos'). During Great Lent, however, the ancient practice is preserved and the full Biblical Canticles are still chanted.

units.english_text: **CASSOCK** (*ράσον, τό* · *χιτών, ὁ* · *ἱμάτιον, τό*) *Slav.* *Podryasnik* / *Ryasa*: The cassock is the basic clerical and monastic garment of the Eastern Church, existing in two primary forms: the inner cassock (*anteri* / *podryasnik*) and the outer cassock (*raso* / *ryasa*). The inner cassock is an ankle-length tunic with closely fitted sleeves. The outer cassock is a loose, flowing robe with wide, open sleeves. Both inner and outer cassocks are worn by bishops, priests, deacons, monastics, and tonsured clergy. In modern parish practice, blessing to wear the cassock is also granted to seminarians, novices, subdeacons, and altar servers.

provenance.verbatim_source: **CASSOCK** (*ράσον, τό* · *χιτών, ὁ* · *ἱμάτιον, τό*) *Slav.* *Podryasnik* / *Ryasa*: The cassock is the basic clerical and monastic garment of the Eastern Church, existing in two primary forms: the inner cassock (*anteri* / *podryasnik*) and the outer cassock (*raso* / *ryasa*). The inner cassock is an ankle-length tunic with closely fitted sleeves. The outer cassock is a loose, flowing robe with wide, open sleeves. Both inner and outer cassocks are worn by bishops, priests, deacons, monastics, and tonsured clergy. In modern parish practice, blessing to wear the cassock is also granted to seminarians, novices, subdeacons, and altar servers.

units.english_text: **CENSER** (*θυμιατόν, τό* or *θυμιατήριον, τό*) *Slav.* *Kadilo* (*Кадило*): The liturgical vessel used for burning incense. In the Eastern Church the censer is suspended by four chains (three representing the Holy Trinity and one representing the Unity of the Godhead), often adorned with twelve bells symbolizing the proclamation of the twelve Apostles. Censers are used constantly throughout all liturgical services, especially at Vespers, Matins, and the Divine Liturgy. When a deacon serves, he performs the rubrical censings; otherwise, the celebrating priest censes. Tonsured altar servers may prepare and carry the censer, but only ordained clergy may swing it during public liturgical prayers. Censing symbolizes the sweet fragrance of the Holy Spirit, the sanctification of the faithful and the temple, and the ascending prayers of the Christian community rising up to heaven (cf. Revelation 8:3–4). The standard psalm verse chanted during censing at Vespers is: **“Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.”** (*«Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου, ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου· ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου, θυσία ἑσπερινή.»*, Psalm 140:2 LXX). Eastern Christians also utilize a small hand censer (**KATZION** / *κατζίον*), which has no suspending chains or bells and is swung in the form of a cross before sacred icons or deceased persons.

units.slavonic_text: CENSER (θυμιατόν, τό, or θυμιατήριον, τό): In the Eastern Orthodox Church a censer is similar in design to the Roman Catholic thurible, but with more than one chain and often with the addition of small bells. Censers are used constantly in Orthodox services, especially at every VESPERS, MATINS, and Divine Liturgy. If a deacon is present, he typically does much of the censing, otherwise the duty is that of the Priest. Tonsured servers or acolytes are permitted to prepare and carry the censer, but may not swing it during prayers. Censing is the practice of swinging a censer suspended from chains towards something or someone, typically an icon or person, so that the smoke from the burning incense travels in that direction. Burning incense generally represents the prayers of the people rising towards Heaven. One commonly sung Psalm during the censing is “Let my prayer rise like incense before You, my hands like the evening sacrifice.” («Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου, ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου· ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου, θυσία ἑσπερινή.») Some Orthodox Christians use a small hand censer (KATZION) on their home altars. The katzion, which may also be used in church, has no suspending chains or bells and is usually waved in a cross-wise fashion before the person or item being censed.

units.slavonic_text: Today, for censing in the home one may use granulated incense and small, concave charcoal briquettes. One lights the corner of the briquette with a flame, then places it in the censer and extinguishes the flame. After the glowing sparks traverse the entire briquette, it is ready to have incense placed on it.

units.english_text: **CHASMODIA** (*χασμῳδία, ἡ*): Liturgical cacophony or discordant singing resulting from disorder, rhythmic confusion, and lack of musical clarity during church services. units.english_text: **CHROMATIC SCALE** (*χρωματικόν*): In Byzantine chant theory, a modal scale employing chromatic intervals (augmented seconds and half steps) outside the diatonic scale. In modern Western musical terms, these tones correspond to the altered pitches (sharps and flats) of a keyboard. For example, while the diatonic Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal) uses the natural diatonic scale (C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C), the chromatic form of Tone 6 (Mode II Plagal) utilizes intervals with augmented steps (such as C–D♭–E–F–G–A♭–B–C).

units.slavonic_text: TD-42
units.english_text: **CHURCH** (*ἐκκλησία, ἡ* or *ἱερὸς ναός, ὁ*) *Slav.* *Tserkov'* / *Khram*: In Greek liturgical usage, the term *ecclesia* primarily denotes the Christian assembly or church building, while *hieros naos* (Holy Temple) emphasizes its consecrated liturgical function as the dwelling place of God. Christian architecture has historically developed in dialogue with theological doctrine, spiritual symbolism, and the cultural environment of each era. The earliest Christians assembled for the Eucharist in private homes (*domus ecclesiae*); during periods of imperial persecution, they gathered covertly in catacombs, caves, and secluded dwellings. Following the Edict of Milan issued by Constantine the Great in 313, Christians began erecting monumental public basilicas.

units.english_text: Among these sacred monuments, the most renowned and influential is the Great Church of the Holy Wisdom of God (**Hagia Sophia**) in Constantinople. units.slavonic_text: CHURCH (ἐκκλησία, ἡ or ἱερὸς ναός, ὁ): In Greek the first term is most often used to describe the structure of the building while the latter term “Holy Temple” implies also function. Orthodox Christians worship and continue to worship Christ in structures that are more often than not determined by the social, political and economic climate of their area and/or the theological understandings of the era. The earliest Christians gathered together and worshipped in private homes until persecutions began. From this point they sought refuge in caves, catacombs and other such areas where they could worship Christ in safety. Shortly after Constantine the Great issued the ‘edict of toleration’, Christians began to build churches.
units.english_text: In Eastern Christian tradition, churches are typically designed according to a cruciform plan crowned by a central dome, symbolizing heaven descending to earth and the cosmic sovereignty of Christ the Pantokrator. The interior is divided into three distinct liturgical areas: the **NARTHEX** (entrance vestibule), the **NAVE** (*naos*, where the faithful stand for worship), and the **SANCTUARY** (*bema* or Holy Table area, separated by the **ICONOSTASIS**). This tripartite division mirrors the ancient Tabernacle and Temple of Jerusalem (the Outer Court, the Holy Place, and the Holy of Holies). The architectural lines lead the eyes upward toward the dome, enriched by a hierarchical iconographic program reflecting the heavenly hierarchy and the redeemed cosmos. The structures frequently bear a golden Cross at their highest point, often illuminated through-[^586]

units.slavonic_incipit: One of these magnificent structures that
units.slavonic_text: One of these magnificent structures that remains largely intact today is the Church of Agia Sophia or “Holy Wisdom” in what was once the capital city of the Byzantine Empire, Constantinople. The building of this Church was commissioned by Constantine himself; however, after a fire destroyed much of the church and upon the exile of Saint John Chrysostom by Empress Eudoxia, the church was rebuilt by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian. Upon its completion and consecration on December 27, 537 this grandest of churches, was and remains the model for churches throughout Eastern Christendom.

units.slavonic_incipit: The intent of the Orthodox house
units.slavonic_text: The intent of the Orthodox house of worship is to create an awareness of God’s presence. No distinction is made between spiritual and sensory perception. Not only the spirit but also the senses experience the splendor and beauty of God’s creation. This total perception can be overwhelming. An old Russian chronicle relates that Prince Vladimir of Kiev could not decide which faith to adopt for himself and his people until his envoys reported from Constantinople that they had witnessed services there such that “We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth,” they declared, “for on earth there is no such splendor or such beauty, and we are at a loss to describe it. We know only that God dwells there among men.”
units.english_text: **CHYMA** (*χῦμα*): *Lit.* 'in a poured, flowing stream.' A liturgical rubric specifying that a text is to be read in a simple, continuous speaking tone or steady recitative rather than chanted with elaborate melismatic melodies. On occasion, the term also denotes a continuous, flowing recitative chant, such as the priest's chanted petitions. The *Typikon* explicitly distinguishes between these modes of execution, employing the directives **“it is said chyma”** (*λέγεται χῦμα*, simple reading) and **“it is chanted chyma”** (*ψάλλεται χῦμα*, straight recitative chanting).

units.slavonic_text: CHYMA (χῦμα): Lit. In a poured, flowing manner. Most commonly, the term is interpreted as “to be read.” On occasion, the term signifies chanting in a flowing, recitative style, like the priest’s chanted petitions. The distinction between reading and chanting is made clearer in the Typikon when we often have, in the first instance, ‘it is said chyma’ (λέγεται χῦμα) or, in the second instance, ‘it is chanted chyma’ (ψάλλεται χῦμα).
units.english_text: **CODEX** (*κῶδιξ, ὁ*; *pl.* **CODICES** / *κώδικες, οἱ*): Originally designating a bound collection of wooden tablets coated with wax for writing, the term *codex* came to denote a manuscript book composed of bound sheets of papyrus or parchment. The widespread adoption of the codex format was fundamentally spurred by early Christianity. While pagan and classical texts long continued to be written on scrolls (*volumina*), Christians embraced the parchment codex in the first and second centuries for liturgical and scriptural use, because a codex permitted writing on both sides of the folio (recto and verso), facilitated rapid cross-referencing between Old and New Testament passages, and was far more portable. By the fourth century, the codex had completely superseded the scroll for lengthy ecclesiastical documents and biblical manuscripts. In Christian iconography, Old Testament prophets are traditionally depicted holding scrolls, whereas the holy Evangelists hold bound codices.[^587]

units.slavonic_text: CODEX, pl. CODICES (κῶδιξ, ὁ, κώδικες, οἱ): This was the word for a book made of thin wooden strips coated with wax upon which one could write. The usual modern sense of codex, “book formed of bound leaves of paper or parchment,” is due to Christianity. By the first century B.C. there existed notebooks made of leaves of parchment, used for rough copy, first drafts, and notes. By the first century A.D. such manuals were used for commercial copies of classical literature. The Christians adopted this parchment manual format for the Scriptures used in their liturgy because a codex is easier to handle than a scroll and because one can write on both sides of a parchment but on only one side of a papyrus scroll. By the early second century all Scripture was reproduced in codex form. In traditional Christian iconography, therefore, the Hebrew prophets are represented holding scrolls and the Evangelists holding codices. The codex later replaced the scroll for writing lengthy church documents.

units.slavonic_text: the act and service of eternally remembering the life and death of any person. During feasts we also commemorate a sacred event or personality.
units.english_text: In Eastern liturgical practice, Compline exists in two distinct forms: **Great Compline** (*Μέγα Ἀπόδειπνον* / *Velikoye Povecheriye*) and **Small Compline** (*Μικρὸν Ἀπόδειπνον* / *Maloye Povecheriye*). Small Compline is celebrated on ordinary days throughout the liturgical year and includes an appointed Canon to the Most Holy Theotokos in the Tone of the week (from the *Oktoechos*). Commemorations of saints from the *Menaion* that cannot be celebrated on their appointed calendar day may be transferred and prayed at Compline, reading their proper canon alongside the canon of the Theotokos and singing their appointed aposticha stichera from Vespers. In addition, special canons are appointed for Compline during Forefeasts, Afterfeasts, and the Pentecostarion period. Compline concludes with the solemn Mutual Asking of Forgiveness between the celebrant and the congregation. In monastic tradition, notably on the Holy Mountain of Athos, the community venerates the holy relics and icons of the church at the conclusion of Compline and receives the blessing of the abbot or officiating priest.[^588]

units.slavonic_incipit: Compline is a service which is
units.slavonic_text: Compline is a service which is part of the daily cycle of services. It is the final church service of the day and takes place after supper prior to going to sleep. In the Greek Orthodox Church of today, the service exists in two forms: Great Compline and Small Compline. This Compline service or office whether the Great or Small form will include a Canon to the Theotokos in the Mode of the Week (found in the OKTOICHOS). Services to saints in the MINEON that for some reason cannot be celebrated on their appointed day may be done on the nearest convenient day at Compline. In such cases, the Canon for the Saint would be read in addition to the Canon to the Theotokos followed by the Hymns (STICHIRA) to the saint from VESPERS. There are also particular days such as FOREFEASTS, AFTERFEASTS, and days during the PENTIKOSTARION period that have special Canons for Compline composed for them. The service always ends with the mutual asking of forgiveness. In some Orthodox traditions, Evening Prayers (i.e. those said before sleeping) will be read near the end of Compline. In the monasteries of the Holy Mountain of Athos today, an ancient practice is observed in which all those of the community who are present at the end of Compline venerate the Relics and Icons in the church, and receive the blessing of the priest. For the exact order of prayer of the Great Compline Service in English, see http://www.goarch.org/chapel/liturgical_texts/greatcompline.

units.slavonic_text: CREED (Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως, τό): From the Latin credo, “I believe.” The Creed, known in Greek as the Symbol of Faith (Σύμβολον τῆς Πίστεως) meaning the “bringing together” of the worshippers to confess their Christian faith.
units.english_text: In the early Church, diverse baptismal confessions of faith existed across various apostolic sees. These confessions were rooted in the baptismal liturgy, wherein catechumens were required to solemnly profess their personal faith prior to descending into the baptismal font. The earliest apostolic confession was the concise profession that Jesus is the Christ and the Lord. Through this public confession, the catechumen was baptized into Christ, dying and rising with Him into the new life of the Kingdom of God in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (cf. Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4).

units.slavonic_text: The Nicene Creed is also called the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed since it was formally drawn up at the First Ecumenical Council in Nicaea (325) and further ratified at the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople (381).
units.english_text: As the Church expanded, local churches developed more detailed baptismal creeds to articulate the apostolic faith against emergent heresies. In the fourth century, the Arian crisis convulsed the Christian world regarding the eternal divinity of the Son of God (the divine Logos). The heresiarch Arius maintained that the Son was a created being, saying “there was a time when He was not.” Orthodox fathers, led by Saint Athanasius the Great, confessed that the Son is eternal, uncreated, and consubstantial (*homoousios*) with the Father.

units.slavonic_incipit: In the early Church there were
units.slavonic_text: In the early Church there were many different forms of the Christian confession of faith—many different “creeds.” These creeds were always used originally in service of Baptism. Before being baptized, a person had to state what he believed. The earliest Christian creed was quite likely a simple confession of faith that Jesus is the Christ, i.e., the Messiah, and that the Christ is Lord. By publicly confessing this belief, the person could be baptized into Christ, dying and rising with Him into the New Life of the Kingdom of God in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
units.english_text: This doctrinal conflict was resolved by the 318 Holy Fathers convened by Emperor Constantine at the First Ecumenical Council in Nicaea in 325, who promulgated the authoritative Symbol of Faith.[^589]

units.slavonic_text: menical Council, stated the following: “I believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages; Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten, not created, of one essence with the Father, through Whom all things were made; Who for us and for our salvation came down from the heavens and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man. Crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, He suffered and was buried; Rising on the third day according to the Scriptures, And ascending into the heavens, He is seated at the right hand of the Father; And coming again in glory to judge the living and the dead, His Kingdom shall have no end; And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of life, Who proceeds from the Father, Who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, Who spoke through the prophets;”

units.english_text: Orthodox Christian entering the communion of the Orthodox Church. In the same way, the Creed became part of the life of Orthodox Christians and an essential element of the Divine Liturgy of the Orthodox Church, at which each person formally and officially accepts and renews his baptism and membership in the Church. Thus, the Symbol of Faith is the only part of the Liturgy (repeated in another form just before Holy Communion) which is formulated in the first person singular. Most other hymns and prayers of the Liturgy are plural, beginning with “we”. The creedal confession begins with “I,” because faith is at first personal, and only then corporate and communal.[^591]

units.slavonic_text: In the church today, the deacon ministers to the bishop and priest in the divine services and assists in the celebration of the sacraments of the Church. A deacon may not, however, celebrate the sacraments by himself.
units.english_text: In addition, the deacon may perform other duties pertaining to Church life according to pastoral circumstance, with the blessing and at the direction of his bishop or priest: for example, the distribution of alms to the needy, or the distribution of the Holy Eucharist to the faithful from a second chalice at the Divine Liturgy. The deacon, however, may never consecrate the Holy Gifts.

units.slavonic_incipit: While, originally deacons of the Church
units.slavonic_text: While, originally deacons of the Church only assisted the bishops in good deeds and works of charity, in more recent centuries the diaconate had become an almost exclusive liturgical function where the deacons only assisted at the celebration of the church services. Today, deacons will often head educational programs and youth groups, perform hospital visitation, missionary work, and conduct social welfare programs.
units.english_text: Just as with bishops and presbyters, administrative distinctions of precedence exist among deacons. A senior deacon of a cathedral or principal church may be awarded the dignity of **PROTODEACON** (*πρωτοδιάκονος*, after the prototype of the Holy Protomartyr and Archdeacon Stephen), obtaining precedence when serving with other deacons. The chief deacon who attends specifically upon a bishop is designated an **ARCHDEACON** (*ἀρχιδιάκονος*). A deacon who has received monastic tonsure is called a **hierodeacon** (*ἱεροδιάκονος*).

units.english_text: **DEUTEROCANON** (*ἀναγινωσκώμενα, τά* / *Anaginoskomena*, "books read"): The ecclesiastical designation for the deuterocanonical books of the Sacred Scriptures. These comprise the holy books recognized by the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches as inspired, canonical components of the Christian Old Testament, which are absent from the rabbinic Hebrew Masoretic canon. The term *deuterocanonical* derives from the Greek meaning “pertaining to the second canon.” Although the etymology might suggest a secondary status, reflecting the historical deliberations before their universal conciliar ratification, the term in Catholic and Orthodox theology does not imply inferior authority or non-canonicity, despite occasional conflation by outside commentators with the Apocrypha.

units.slavonic_text: DEUTEROCANON (ἀναγινωσκώμενα, τά): The Roman Catholic term for the deuterocanonical books of the Bible. These are books considered by the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches to be canonical parts of the Christian Old Testament but are not present in the Hebrew Bible. The word deuterocanonical comes from the Greek meaning “belonging to the second canon.” The etymology of the word is misleading, but it does suggest the hesitation with which these books were accepted into the canon by some theological scholars. Note that the term does not mean non-canonical; despite this it has sometimes been used as a euphemism for the Apocrypha.
units.english_text: **DIAKONIKON** (*διακονικόν, τό*; Slav. *Diakonik*): The Diakonikon is the sacred vestry and liturgical repository situated on the south side within the **SANCTUARY**, where sacred vessels, vestments, and liturgical appointments are stored. The holy icon traditionally enshrined here depicts either the Resurrection (**"The Resurrection"** / *῾Η ᾿Ανάστασις*) or the Extreme Humility of Christ (**"The Extreme Humility"** / *ἄκρα ταπείνωσις*). It is likewise in the Diakonikon that icons brought by the faithful for blessing remain deposited for forty days.[^593]

units.slavonic_text: Protestant Christians usually do not classify any texts as deuterocanonical; they either omit them from the Bible, or include them in a section designated Apocrypha. The similarity between these different terms contributes to the confusion between the Roman Catholic and Orthodox deuterocanon and the texts considered noncanonical by other groups of Christians.
units.english_text: The **SANCTUARY** of the Church is the Holy of Holies, wherein man, through the grace of God, unites with the angelic hosts in offering unceasing thanksgiving and glory to our Heavenly Father. Notwithstanding its mystical transcendence, the Sanctuary functions with precise liturgical efficiency. Like the **NARTHEX** and the **NAVE**, the Sanctuary is architecturally disposed to serve the ritual actions of the clergy who officiate at the Divine Services.

units.english_text: Looking through the central **BEAUTIFUL GATE** (*Ὡραία Πύλη* / Royal Doors) into the Sanctuary, one observes a recessed marble table or niche on either side of the eastern wall. The table situated on the north (liturgical left) is the **PROTHESIS** (Table of Oblation / *Proskomide*), while that on the south (liturgical right) is the **DIAKONIKON**. The distinctive functions of these two sanctuary chambers are defined by the sacred vessels resting upon them and the sacred iconography adorning their respective walls.

units.english_text: The **PROTHESIS** is the sacred table upon which the Eucharistic Gifts of bread and wine are prepared during the Proskomide office, performed during the morning Matins (*Ὄρθρος* / Orthros) prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. In addition, the holy vessels and implements—the Holy Chalice, the Holy Paten (*Diskos*), the liturgical veils and Aer, the Asterisk, the Spear, and the Communion Spoon—are vested and preserved upon it. Upon the wall behind the Prothesis is customarily depicted the icon of the Nativity of Christ, commemorating that Christ is the sacrificial Lamb offered “on behalf of all and for all.”

units.english_text: In the early centuries of the Church, these subsidiary tables were not located within the sanctuary proper. Instead, the Eucharistic Gifts were prepared and the liturgical treasures preserved in an adjacent, independent structure designated the **SKEVOPHYLAKION** (*σκευοφυλάκιον*, vessel-guardhouse). From this external treasury the Holy Gospel and the Eucharistic Offerings were solemnly carried into the temple at the appointed liturgical moments by the clergy—a ceremonial movement preserved today in the processions of the Small Entrance with the Gospel and the Great Entrance with the Gifts. Over time, as liturgical architecture evolved, the separate *skevophylakion* fell into disuse, replaced by the integrated Prothesis and Diakonikon niches within the sanctuary itself.

units.slavonic_text: If one were to peer through the central BEAUTIFUL GATE into the Sanctuary, one would find a small marble shelf or table on either side of the back wall. This area on the left is known as the PROTHESIS while that on the right is known as the DIAKONIKON. The unique purpose of these areas in the Sanctuary can best be understood by the differing items that rest upon them and the differing icons that are found immediately behind them.
units.english_text: **DIATAXIS** (*διάταξις, ἡ*): Lit. arrangement, order, or rubrical disposition. In historical and contemporary liturgical usage, a Diataxis comprises precise rubrical directions for the celebrants, deacons, and chanters conducting the ceremonial rites of the Church. These rubrics (*rubrica*) were traditionally inscribed in red ink (cinnabar) to distinguish them from the black ink used for the recited prayers and liturgical texts. units.slavonic_incipit: The PROTHESIS is the place where
units.slavonic_text: The PROTHESIS is the place where the Eucharistic Gifts are prepared during the Morning MATINS Service (ORTHROS), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Additionally, it is the place where the Eucharistic items, i.e. the Holy Chalice, the Holy PATEN, the communion cloths, the spoon that dispenses the gifts etc., are stored. On the back wall of the PROTHESIS is traditionally found the icon of the Nativity, reminding us that Christ is the sacrificial lamb that is offered “in behalf of all and for all.” Early in the Church’s history, these shelves or tables were not found in the Sanctuary. Instead the Holy Gifts were prepared and the liturgical items of the Church were kept in a separate building called the SKEVOPHYLAKION. It was from this place that the Gospel and the Offerings were brought into the Church at the appropriate time in the service by the clergy (our processions today with the Gospel during the Small Entrance and the Offering during the Great Entrance are reminiscent of this practice). The SKEVOPHYLAKION or place for guarding the vessels,” with time, fell into disuse being replaced by the Prothesis and the Diakonikon, now located in the Sanctuary.

units.english_text: > “One of the most important extant Patriarchal Diataxes is attributed to a leading figure of the chancery in the second half of the 14th century: the Protonotary (*Πρωτονοτάριος*), Kyr Deacon Dimitrios Gemistos (ca. 1397), later designated the **MEGA SAKELLARIOS** (*Μέγας Σακελλάριος*) of the Great and Most Holy Church of God. An important scribal annotation recorded in the upper margin of folio 3r in manuscript Athos Vatopedi 135 (AD 1390), the principal codex of the Diataxis, provides a precise date for its composition: August 1386. If indeed Dimitrios Gemistos composed this Diataxis, this does not mean Gemistos created something entirely novel out of nothing. A comparative analysis of his Diataxis with other liturgical witnesses reveals that he compiled it by synthesizing both local and external traditions: the cathedral traditions of the patriarchal rite in Constantinople and the Athonite monastic Diataxis for the Divine Liturgy formulated by Philotheos Kokkinos (ca. 1300–1377/78), twice Patriarch of Constantinople (1353–1354, 1364–1376).

units.slavonic_text: “One of the most important extant Patriarchal Diataxes is attributed to a leading figure of the chancery in the second half of the 14th century. The Protonotary (Πρωτονοτάριος), Kyr. Deacon Gemistos (ca. 1397), [later called the MEGA SAKELLARIOS] of the Great and most-holy Church of God. An important note found in the upper margin of f. 3r in Athos Vatopedi 135 (AD 1390), the principle manuscript of the Diataxis, gives a precise date for its composition, August 1386. If indeed Dimitrios Gemistos wrote this Diataxis, this does not mean Gemistos created something entirely new out of nothing. A comparison of his Diataxis with other sources reveals that he composed it utilizing both local and foreign traditions: the traditions of the patriarchal rite in Constantinople and the Athonite Diataxis for the Divine Liturgy by Philotheos Kokkinos (ca. 1300-1377/78), twice patriarch of Constantinople (1353-54, 1364-1376). The present dissertation presents for the first time ever, a critical edition of Gemistos’ Diataxis as well as an investigation into its liturgical context and an exploration of the historical circumstances surrounding its creation.

Gemistos’ choice of the Philothean Diataxis speaks volumes about the powerful influence of Athonite, hesychast monasticism on the Constantinopolitan

units.slavonic_incipit: patriarchal throne. Looking beyond the historical
units.slavonic_text: patriarchal throne. Looking beyond the historical situation in which Gemistos’ Diataxis was created, one can already see developing the rough outline of the transformation the Byzantine Church will undergo, one that will allow it to survive through the long centuries of Turkish domination. This is a transformation that will have at its core a strong central patriarchate with a powerful bureaucracy using all the ancient imperial and religious symbols to convey its power.
units.english_text: > In order to discern these currents at work, the distinct strata of sources embedded within Gemistos’ Diataxis must be differentiated and identified. Subsequently, the manner in which he deployed his sources requires critical examination. Only at this juncture can we begin to comprehend why he selected the sources he employed. In other words, to ascertain precisely what Gemistos himself authored, what he adapted, and what he interpolated into his Diataxis, those sections displaying literary dependence must be compared systematically with their demonstrable exemplars (the Philothean Diataxis and the official Euchologion for ordination rites). An explanation must be formulated to account for their textual concordance as well as their variations. The findings of this analytical deconstruction illuminate the historical origins of the Diataxis.

units.slavonic_incipit: In order to see these currents
units.slavonic_text: In order to see these currents at work, the different layers of sources in Gemistos’ Diataxis need to be peeled apart and identified. Then, how he used his sources needs to be examined. Only at this point can we begin to understand why he used the sources he used. In other words, in order to understand what exactly Gemistos himself wrote, what he adapted, and what he inserted into his Diataxis, these sections in Gemistos’ Diataxis which show literary dependence must be further compared with their obvious sources (the Philothean Diataxis, the Euchologion for the ordination rites). An explanation must be found, or at least attempted, to account for their agreement, but also for their differences. The results of this fascinating deconstructing process cast light on the origins of the Diataxis.

units.slavonic_incipit: The first step in the process
units.slavonic_text: The first step in the process of thoroughly analyzing Gemistos’ Diataxis is to untangle the text of the Philothean Diataxis from it and place Gemistos in comparison with this direct ancestor in the Byzantine liturgical Diataxis tradition. Nowhere is Gemistos’ dependency on the Philothean Diataxis more apparent than in the prothesis rite: nearly seventy-five percent of the prothesis rite in Gemistos’ text is taken directly from the Philothean Diataxis either word-for-word or with only superficial modifications. Throughout the rest of his Diataxis, Gemistos used Philotheos’ Diataxis much less, and most of this other material is either original or from another, unknown source. Plainly, one of Gemistos’ reasons for composing his patriarchal Diataxis was to combine the Philothean Diataxis, and especially the prothesis rite from Philotheos’ Diataxis, with the patriarchal rite and Constantinopolitan traditions. units.english_text: > The initial phase in analyzing Gemistos’ Diataxis requires disentangling the Philothean Diataxis from his text and establishing Gemistos’ relationship to this direct precursor in the Byzantine Diataxis tradition. Throughout the remainder of his Diataxis, Gemistos utilizes Philotheos’ text far more sparingly, drawing primarily upon original compositions or unidentified sources. Evidently, one of Gemistos’ principal objectives in compiling his Patriarchal Diataxis was to synthesize the Philothean Diataxis—most notably its monastic Prothesis rite—with the patriarchal cathedral ceremonial and Constantinopolitan traditions. units.slavonic_text: was so controversial that his commemoration was forbidden by his immediate successor, Patriarch Makarios. What is more, Philotheos’ Diataxis represents the tradition of Athonite monasticism. Its incorporation within the patriarchal/cathedral liturgical tradition marks its ascendancy, and with it the ascendancy of the monastic tradition, within the larger Byzantine liturgical tradition. But perhaps it is equally a sign that the patriarchal chancery accepted not only Philotheos’ Diataxis as a new liturgical rule, but also marks a rehabilitation of Philotheos by the patriarchate.
units.english_text: > A distinct portrait of Dimitrios Gemistos emerges from the critical examination of his Diataxis and the differentiation of its sources. He was preeminently a Byzantine churchman, conservative in disposition and staunchly loyal to the Constantinopolitan patriarchate. Gemistos was likewise a career administrator, commencing his thirty-year tenure in the patriarchal chancery as a notary under Philotheos in the 1360s. By the close of his career he attained the high dignity of Mega Sakellarios (*Μέγας Σακελλάριος*), demonstrating distinguished administrative competence. As an experienced official, he possessed complete mastery of patriarchal chancery terminology and an intimate understanding of the bureaucratic hierarchy and traditions of the Great Church. The precision of his knowledge is corroborated by comparative analysis of surviving chancery records. Having served in the patriarchal administration for two decades prior to drafting his Diataxis, his administrative expertise was comprehensive. Gemistos’ institutional loyalty extended personally to the occupants of the patriarchal throne; his incorporation of the non-Constantinopolitan Philothean Diataxis was motivated not by an impulse toward innovation, but by institutional conservatism and reverence for Philotheos Kokkinos.

units.slavonic_incipit: A discernible image of Dimitrios Gemistos
units.slavonic_text: A discernible image of Dimitrios Gemistos emerges when the text of his Diataxis is studied and its various sources disentangled and investigated. He was first and foremost a Byzantine Churchman, conservative in nature and fiercely loyal to the Constantinopolitan patriarchate. Gemistos was also a career bureaucrat and began his thirty year career in the patriarchal chancery as a notary under Philotheos sometime in the 1360’s. By the end of his life he had become the Mega Sakellarios, thus proving himself to have been capable and successful. Characteristic of any successful bureaucrat, he was fully conversant with the official terminology of the patriarchate. Equally characteristic is Gemistos’ detailed understanding of the inner workings of the patriarchal bureaucracy, which had its own hierarchy and traditions. The accuracy of his understanding is readily corroborated by a comparison of other extant chancery documents. His mastery of the chancery is not the least bit surprising when we consider that Gemistos worked and flourished in the chancery for twenty years before he wrote his Diataxis. Gemistos’ loyalty to the patriarchate equally extended to individuals who sat on the patriarchal throne. For, as we have seen, even though Gemistos introduced a non-Constantinopolitan source, the Philothean Diataxis, into the Constantinopolitan rite, this was motivated not by a desire to innovate, but by conservatism and loyalty: it was done to settle liturgical questions but also because of his high regard for Philotheos Kokkinos.

units.slavonic_incipit: Constantinopolitan Patriarchate. For example, he shows
units.slavonic_text: Constantinopolitan Patriarchate. For example, he shows himself more than fluent in the technical vocabulary needed to describe the liturgical rites at the Hagia Sophia. In addition, Gemistos regularly offers in marginal notes alternate formulas which further demonstrate a vast knowledge of liturgical traditions. At times, these asides concern the patriarchal rite and Constantinopolitan traditions, but at other times he notes alternate rubrics for when the patriarch would not be celebrating the liturgy, or if the liturgy would not be celebrated in the “Great Church.”
units.english_text: > An examination of Gemistos’ other primary source embedded within the Diataxis, the Euchologion (*Εὐχολόγιον*), further demonstrates his fidelity to Constantinopolitan tradition. When Gemistos’ Euchology texts are compared with anterior and contemporary witnesses, it is evident that he remained faithful to received Constantinopolitan Euchology, while adapting his material to the specific liturgical requirements of Hagia Sophia and the patriarchal office. Gemistos’ revisions reflect a conservative effort to clarify and systematize liturgical order rather than introduce novelty. In one remarkable marginal note, he observes that even when customary rites appear superfluous or redundant, it remains far safer that received customs be observed and preserved than threatened with abrogation. Here Gemistos defends the ancient practice of subdeacons intoning the proclamation **"All who are faithful!"** (*Ὅσοι πιστοί*) twice during the Anaphora—a ceremonial action whose original historical rationale had become obscured by his era.

units.slavonic_incipit: An examination of Gemistos’ other major
units.slavonic_text: An examination of Gemistos’ other major source embedded within the Diataxis, the Euchologion, further confirms his fidelity to Constantinopolitan traditions. When the Euchology texts in Gemistos are compared with sources both anterior and contemporary to him, what emerges is that Gemistos indeed remained faithful to the Constantinopolitan Euchology tradition, but, at the same time, he tailored his Euchology sources to the specific liturgical needs of the Hagia Sophia and the elaborate patriarchal rite. Gemistos’ changes, however, demonstrate not an intent to innovate, but rather a conservative inclination that sought to clarify and codify more precisely the liturgical order. At one point he even insists in a curious marginal note that when prevailing customs “seem superfluous” and even “redundant,” it still is far “safer that the prevailing customs be said and maintained,” than the implied threat of their abrogation. Gemistos here is defending the ancient custom of having the subdeacons cry out, “Whoever is faithful (hosoi pistoi)!” twice during the anaphora, an act whose meaning had obviously been lost by Gemistos’ time.
