units.slavonic_incipit: Gemistos’ Diataxis exists in nineteen known
units.slavonic_text: Gemistos’ Diataxis exists in nineteen known manuscripts. The manuscripts date from Athos Vatopedi 135, copied in November 1390 shortly after the composition of the Diataxis in August 1386, to Athos Panteleimon 677 (AD 1890). Contained in these manuscripts are four basic recensions of the Diataxis: the longer and original “patriarchal” form of the Diataxis; an abbreviated archival form; a later, “archieratical” redaction; and another abbreviated form that concentrates solely on the rites of the Divine Liturgy. The original patriarchal recension describes the PROTHESIS rites, the vesting of the patriarch, the preliminary rite for metropolitan ordination, the ordination of readers and subdeacons, and then the Divine Liturgy of John Chrysostom. Interspersed within the Liturgy are the rites of metropolitan ordination, priests, and deacons. For all of these rites, the original text contains all the necessary Euchology and diakonika texts. Equally characteristic of the original text of the Diataxis is the presence of detailed instructions for the members of the patriarchal chancery and specific references to the architecture of the Hagia Sophia. The editor of the archival recension has removed all the Euchology and diakonika texts seemingly to conserve paper and space. The patriarchal and archieratical forms of the Diataxis are closely related in form and content. The distinguishing characteristics of the archieratical form are that the celebrant of the Divine Liturgy has been changed from patriarch to archiereus, and that most references to the architecture of the Hagia Sophia have been removed. It would seem that these changes were done so that the Diataxis could be used by other bishops in their own dioceses. The shorter, patriarchal recension of the Diataxis is more radical. Present are references to the patriarch, the Hagia Sophia, and various members of the patriarchal chancery; gone, however, are the rubrics for the prothesis rite along with all the euchology texts. Also present are some elements of the liturgical formulary not yet common to the strictly Constantinopolitan

units.english_text: > Textual evaluation of Gemistos’ manuscript tradition demonstrates that subsequent recensions arose in response to specific elements of the archetype. The original title explicitly announces that the Diataxis sets forth the order of the Patriarchal Divine Liturgy celebrated in the Great Church (Hagia Sophia) and “both how and when the order of ordinations takes place.” Consequently, authentic rubrics for the patriarchal liturgy and ordination offices constitute indispensable components of Gemistos’ original work. Because these core elements are missing in the Archieratical and Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recensions, both must be classified as secondary redactions.

units.slavonic_incipit: At first glance, the textual issues
units.slavonic_text: At first glance, the textual issues surrounding the Diataxis of Dimitrios Gemistos seem difficult to resolve. But a curious feature of the textual history of Gemistos’ Diataxis is that subsequent recensions were created in reaction to one or more characteristic element of the original Diataxis. A basic taxonomy of the manuscripts comes quickly into focus through a careful analysis of the various recensions. The very title of the Diataxis states that the Diataxis sets forth the details of the patriarchal Divine Liturgy celebrated in the Great Church (i.e., the Hagia Sophia) and “both how and when the order of ordinations take place.” Therefore, the content of the original text of the Diataxis must contain rubrics specifically for the patriarchal liturgy and the various ordination rites. This content presumed in the title, however, is missing in two recensions, the Archieratical and the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic.” Accordingly these two recensions can be described as later and not representative of the original text of the Diataxis. The editor of the Archieratical recension refashioned the Original Patriarchal recension of the Diataxis by changing the main celebrant from patriarch to archiereus and omitting any references to the concelebrating hierarchs, architectural features of the Hagia Sophia, and the members of the patriarchal chancery. By doing this, the redactor of this recension created a Diataxis appropriate to any hierarch and not just the patriarch of Constantinople during the Byzantine Empire. The redactor of the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recension was no less active. This editor removed the Euchology texts and the diakonika of CHR as well as the texts for the ordination rites, leaving only the rubrics for the celebration of the patriarchal liturgy and mere indications and incipits where these texts once stood.

units.slavonic_incipit: The guiding editorial principle of the
units.slavonic_text: The guiding editorial principle of the present edition has been to establish as near as possible the text that Gemistos originally wrote and not to create a hypothetical text that never existed. Additionally, no component part of the Diataxis should be seen as anything other than the original text of Gemistos’ Diataxis. In other words, this edition of the Diataxis is not a critical edition of the ordination rites
units.english_text: > The editor of the Archieratical recension adapted the Patriarchal archetype by substituting *archiereus* for *patriarch* and omitting concelebrating hierarchs, Hagia Sophia architectural rubrics, and chancery officials, thereby producing a manual serviceable for any diocesan hierarch. Similarly, the compiler of the Abbreviated Patriarchal “Eucharistic” recension deleted the Euchology prayers and diaconal petitions of Saint John Chrysostom as well as ordination rites, leaving only liturgical rubrics with incipits marking where prayers originally stood.

units.slavonic_incipit: of the Byzantine Church, or of
units.slavonic_text: of the Byzantine Church, or of the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, or of the Philothean Diataxis, but simply a critical edition of the 14th century patriarchal liturgical Diataxis of Dimitrios Gemistos. All attempts have been made to have a clear and straightforward critical apparatus following the normal methods for editing texts. I prepared the critical apparatus with an eye less towards philologists and more towards liturgiologists who are interested not only in the reconstruction of the original text but also its subsequent development. Consequently, the critical apparatus is fuller, and includes more variant readings than might be typical for a critical edition. The register of sources allows the reader of the text to distinguish what exactly Gemistos wrote, what he took from his sources, and what the general nature of the sources was. The first level of the critical apparatus contains the variant readings that serve to reconstruct the original text of the Diataxis. The second level of apparatus contains the variant readings from the archieratical recension of Gemistos' Diataxis when these readings do not bear witness to the original text. The third level of apparatus is exclusively reserved for those instances where Habert deviated from the text of his exemplar, Paris Greek 1362. This level also includes the various titles he gave to different sections of the Diataxis. I have attempted to include all of Habert's variations — all orthographical, all prayer variants etc., in order to give an accurate report of the nature of his text. Reflecting on Gemistos' work, students of the Byzantine liturgy might view Gemistos as an innovator. After all, he introduced the Athonite monastic Diataxis of Philotheos Kokkinos into the patriarchal cathedral rite of Constantinople, thus assuring the victory of the monastic rite over the cathedral rite. In so doing, Gemistos unwittingly cemented a process that had been going on for centuries. Yet this view of Gemistos is only partially accurate and gained only in hindsight. Gemistos was only one actor in a drama, which had been going on for almost a thousand years and involved countless people. units.slavonic_text: *(Printed Page TD-57)*
units.english_text: > The first level of the critical apparatus contains the variant readings that serve to reconstruct the original text of the Diataxis. The second level of apparatus contains the variant readings from the archieratical recension of Gemistos’ Diataxis when these readings do not bear witness to the original text. The third level of apparatus is exclusively reserved for those instances where Habert deviated from the text of his exemplar, Paris Greek 1362. This level also includes the various titles he gave to different sections of the Diataxis. I have attempted to include all of Habert’s variations—all orthographical, all prayer variants, etc., in order to give an accurate report of the nature of his text.

units.slavonic_text: *(Printed Page TD-57)*
units.english_text: > Reflecting on Gemistos’ work, students of Byzantine liturgy might view Gemistos as an innovator. After all, he introduced the Athonite monastic Diataxis of Philotheos Kokkinos into the patriarchal cathedral rite of Constantinople, thus securing the victory of the monastic rite over the cathedral rite. In so doing, Gemistos unwittingly cemented a process that had been developing for centuries. Yet this view of Gemistos is only partially accurate and gained only in hindsight. Gemistos was only one actor in a drama that had been unfolding for almost a thousand years and involved countless individuals. In fact, the victory of the monastic rite is not a story of a few individuals, but of many. If he did reflect on what he was doing, Gemistos[^601]

units.english_text: > probably saw himself as someone merely codifying existing traditions and liturgical practices. His view on this would be perfectly akin to another contemporary Byzantine liturgist, Archbishop Symeon of Thessalonika († 1429), who likewise reformed the liturgy. But Alexander Lingas, who has evaluated the content of Symeon’s reforms, concludes that far from being “revolutionary,” the reforms “represented the harmonization and systematization of existing precedents for the inclusion of texts and music from outside the Byzantine cathedral tradition.”[2] Only when the liturgical rites are viewed as static or unchangeable can these developments—or any developments—be considered as mere innovation and not simply the natural continuous evolution of the rites which is the substance of liturgical history.”

units.slavonic_text: times referred to as Guido scales. Diatonic music is written primarily using the notes from a diatonic scale; similarly, diatonic chords and diatonic intervals use notes from such a scale. The antonym is chromatic. (From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia.)
units.english_text: The natural scale consists of five whole tones and two semitones as produced upon the white keys of a keyboard instrument. A corresponding scale exists in each key. Music is termed “diatonic” if it is restricted to the notes of this scale, to the exclusion of chromatic tones. For example, in the key of C major, the melodic progression c–d–e and the chord d–a–c represent diatonic harmony. “Diatonicism” denotes music whose tonality is predominantly diatonic, that is, nonchromatic (see Powers, Harold S. and Jeffery, Peter in the bibliography).

units.slavonic_incipit: Diatonic scales are a fundamental building
units.slavonic_text: Diatonic scales are a fundamental building block of the European musical tradition. The term is sometimes used to refer to all the medieval ecclesiastical modes, but is generally used only in reference to the major and minor scales. The natural scale is a scale consisting of five whole tones and two semitones as it is produced on the white keys of a keyboard instrument. There is, of course, a corresponding scale in each key. Music is called “diatonic” if it is confined to the notes of this scale, to the exclusion of chromatic tones. For instance, in the key of C major, the melodic progression c-d-e and the chord d-a-c represent diatonic harmony. “Diatonicism” means music whose tonality is predominantly diatonic, i.e., nonchromatic. See Powers, Harold S. and Jeffery, Peter in the bibliography.

units.slavonic_text: ἔχει, καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν.») This is the point in the Divine Liturgy which has been designated “at the Diptycha” when, on some occasions, the MEGALYNARION AT THE DIPTYCHA is sung (see example on p. 148 of Bogdanos’ The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order. An alternate definition is that of a two-leaved hinged tablet of metal, ivory, or wood, the inner surface of which was covered with wax upon which characters would be scratched with a stylus. Between the two tablets others were sometimes inserted, thus giving rise to the names, triptych, polyptych, etc. In the early Church the names of the members, living or dead, were inscribed on diptychs. Saint Cyprian mentions them in the 3rd century and they were in use until the 12th century in the West, and the 14th in the East. The “diptychs of the living” contained the names of the patriarchs, the bishops, illustrious persons, lay and ecclesiastical, and benefactors. From them came the first ecclesiastical calendars and martyrologies. The “diptychs of the dead” contained the names of those who, when living, were qualified for inscription on the “diptychs of the living.” Thus originated the later necrologies. Exclusion from these lists invoked a grave ecclesiastical penalty. The contents of the diptychs were read aloud from the ambo or altar, and traces of the fixed usage of the Roman Church in the 5th century may still be found in the Canon of the Mass.

units.english_text: **DOMESTIKOS** (*Δομέστικος, ὁ*, pl. *Δομέστικοι, οἱ* / Domestikoi): In contemporary practice, as in antiquity, two ranks of Domestikoi minister in the Patriarchal Church of Saint George at the Phanar. The junior rank is that of Second Domestikos, which constitutes the initial grade within the order of cantors. The next rank in ascending order is First Domestikos, which is followed by the two principal choir leaders: the **Lambadarios** (*Λαμπαδάριος*, lead chanter directing the left choir at the analogion near the left end of the soleas) and the **Protopsaltis** (*Πρωτοψάλτης*, archcantor directing the right choir at the analogion near the right end of the soleas). The office of Second Domestikos is customarily assigned to younger singers noted for superior vocal agility and stamina.

units.slavonic_text: DOGMATIKON (Δογματικόν, τό) pl. DOGMATIKA (Δογματικά, τά): These are THEOTOKIA that conclude the STICHIRA at “Lord, I cry out” at Great Vespers on Saturdays. Their title comes from the fact that they are usually succinct presentations of the dogma of the Incarnation, with particular emphasis on the virginity and motherhood of Mary.
units.english_text: **DORMITION** (*Κοίμησις, ἡ*; lit. "falling asleep"): Used figuratively for death, specifically designating the repose of a sacred personage, preeminently the **Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos** (August 15). Both the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches profess that, following her sacred death, the Virgin Mary was assumed bodily into heaven. By the apostolic constitution *Munificentissimus Deus* of Pope Pius XII in 1950, the dogma of the bodily Assumption of the Virgin Mary was defined for the Catholic Church. In the Eastern tradition, preserved throughout patristic hymnography and the liturgical Typikon, the feast celebrates the bodily translation of the Mother of God to heaven after her death, with the Western Church customarily employing the title *Assumption* rather than[^605]

units.slavonic_text: DOMESTIKOS (Δομέστικος, ὁ) pl. DOMESTIKI (Δομέστικοι, οἱ): Today, as in the past, there are two ranks of Domestiki serving in the Patriarchal Church of St. George. The lowest rank is that of the Second Domestikos which is the first step in the order of the Domestiki. The next rank in ascending order is that of the First Domestikos which is followed by the two higher orders of the LAMBADARIOS or lead chanter serving at the ANALOGION near the left end of the SOLEAS and the PROTOPSALTIS or head chanter serving at the ANALOGION near the right end of the soleas. The Second Domestikos position is usually taken by younger men known for their high vocal quality and their endurance.

units.english_text: **DOXA** (*Δόξα*) **KAI NYN** (*Καὶ νῦν*): Standard liturgical abbreviations indicating the chanting of the minor doxology preceding appointed prayers and hymns in all ecclesiastical liturgical books (Sluzhebnyky and Horologia). The first formula abbreviates: **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"** («Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι»); the second formula abbreviates: **"Now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). See also **DOXASTIKON** below.

units.english_text: **DOXASTIKON** (*Δοξαστικόν, τό*, pl. *Δοξαστικά, τά*; Slav. *Slavnik*): A stichiron hymn sung after the verse **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"** (*Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι*) at the conclusion of a series of stichira at Vespers or Matins. It expounds in an extended, melismatic melody the sacred feast or saint commemorated on that day. Following the Doxastikon, a matching Theotokion is appointed with the verse: **"Now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). Doxastika are chanted principally at the conclusion of the Lamplighting Sticheron verses (*Esperia*) and the Aposticha at Vespers, and following the Praises (*Ainoi*) at Matins (*Orthros*).

units.slavonic_text: DOXA (Δόξα) KE NYN (Καὶ νῦν): These are abbreviations each for a line of text beginning with them. These texts usually precede prayers and hymns commonly found in all service books of the church. The first word is the abbreviation in Greek for “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit” («Δόξα πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι» and the second (2 words) are an abbreviation for “And now and ever and unto the ages of ages.” («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). See also DOXASTIKON, below.
units.english_text: In the tradition of medieval Slavic chant, the Doxastika of major feast days were distinguished by being set to solemn, ornate melodies (*demestvenny*, *put’*, or *great znamenny* chant) or to early polyphony.

provenance.verbatim_source: In the tradition of medieval Slavic chant, the Doxastika of major feast days were distinguished by being set to solemn, ornate melodies (*demestvenny*, *put’*, or *great znamenny* chant) or to early polyphony.

units.slavonic_text: *DOXASTIKON, -A (Δοξαστικόν, τό, pl. Δοξαστικά, τά): A hymn (STICHIRON) sung after the short doxology “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit’ (Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ καὶ Ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι) at the end of a cycle of stichira at Vespers or Matins. It sings in an extended and melodically elaborate manner of the sacred event or person celebrated in each occasion. After the Doxastikon, another hymn is sometimes sung with the verse “And now, and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν»). Doxastika are mainly chanted at the end of the Esperia and APOSTICHA in Vespers and after the Praises (Eni) in Matins (Orthros).
units.english_text: **DOXOLOGY** (*Δοξολογία, ἡ*; lit. "a hymn of glorification"; Slav. *Slavoslovie*): A structured series of scriptural and hymnographic verses glorifying God, opening with the angelic proclamation: **"Glory to Thee, Who hast shown us the light"** («Δόξα σοι τῷ δείξαντι τὸ φῶς»), chanted toward the end of Matins (*Orthros*) before the Divine Liturgy.[^606]

units.english_text: This ancient hymn of praise is common to both East and West. In the Byzantine rite, it possesses two forms: the Great Doxology and the Lesser Doxology. The Great Doxology is sung solemnly at Matins on Sundays and Feasts; the Lesser Doxology is read at daily Matins and at Compline. Like the Latin *Te Deum*, the hymn concludes with a series of versicles drawn from the Psalter. The Great Doxology terminates with the singing of the Trisagion (*"Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us"*). The Lesser Doxology concludes with the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day without sin"**, which, at both daily Vespers and non-festal Matins, precedes the prayer of the bowing of heads by the presbyter. The designation *doxology* also applies to shorter ascriptions of glory to the Holy Trinity. See **DOXASTIKON** and **EKPHONISIS**.

units.slavonic_text: This ancient hymn of praise is common to both East and West. In the East it has two forms, the Greater and Lesser Doxology. The former is used at Matins on Sundays and Feasts, the latter at Matins on ordinary days and at Compline. Like the Latin Te Deum, the hymn itself is followed by a series of verses from the Psalter. The Great Doxology ends with the solemn singing of the Trisagion. The Lesser Doxology ends with the prayer “Grant, Lord, this day,” which, at both Vespers and non-festal Matins, precedes the bowing of heads by the priests. The word ‘doxology’ is also used for other short ascriptions of praise to the Holy Trinity. See DOXASTIKON and EKPHONISIS. (AE).

units.english_text: **EFCHOLOGION TO MEGA** (*Εὐχολόγιον τὸ Μέγα* / Great Euchologion; Slav. *Trebnik* and *Sluzhebnik*; lit. "Great Book of Prayers"): The Slavonic term *Trebnik* signifies "Book of Needs" (*Treby*). The comprehensive Euchologion contains the sacerdotal prayers for the priest and deacon, and petitions for the reader at Vespers, Matins (*Orthros*), and the Divine Liturgies (the rites comprising the *Sluzhebnik* or *Liturgikon*), as well as the Holy Mysteries (Sacraments) and sacramental blessings for various pastoral occasions. units.english_text: **EKPHONISIS** (*᾿Εκφώνησις, ἡ*; Slav. *Vozglas*): A liturgical exclamation intoned aloud in a solemn, declamatory chant style. See also **EXCLAMATION**. Applied preeminently to the concluding trinitarian doxology that terminates silent priestly prayers, it is intoned aloud by the priest even when the preceding prayer is directed to be read secretly (*mystikos* / *μυστικῶς*).[^607]

units.english_text: In melodic contour, *ekphonisis* occupies an intermediate position between simple psalmody—wherein inflections from the reciting tone (*ison* or *basis*) occur only at the beginnings and cadences of phrases—and ornate hymnody, which possesses defined melodic and rhythmic forms. units.slavonic_incipit: Traditional patterns of ekphonisis were notated
units.slavonic_text: Traditional patterns of ekphonisis were notated in earlier times by a special ekphonetic notation, and were also preserved as oral tradition. In terms of the character of a melody, ekphonisis stands between Psalmody, in which deviations from the main reciting tone (the ISON or vasis) occur only at the beginnings and endings of phrases, and singing proper, which has a well defined melodic and rhythmic form. In the Liturgy, ekphonisis is used primarily for the rendering of the Epistle, the Gospel, and Old Testament, as well as for the prayers exclaimed by the priest or deacon.

units.english_text: **ENGOLPION** (*᾿Εγκόλπιον, τό*; lit. "that which is worn on the breast"; Slav. *Panagia*): In early Western usage, the designation encompassed pectoral crosses; in the contemporary Eastern Church, it denotes an oval medallion bearing the sacred icon of the Theotokos (hence *Panagia*) or Christ the Savior, suspended around the neck by a decorative chain over the chest. It constitutes part of the pontifical vesture of an Eastern hierarch and is worn over the omophorion. When vesting with the Engolpion, the Bishop prays: **"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me"** («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου»—Psalm 50:12 [LXX 50:12 / MT 51:10]). See also **VESTMENTS**. The term *Engolpion* also designates a handy liturgical manual, such as the Reader's Handbook (*᾿Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*).

units.slavonic_text: ENGOLPION (᾿Εγκόλπιον, τό) Lit. ‘an item worn on the chest’. In the Western Churches, originally the term also included pectoral crosses. In the Orthodox Church today, however, the term is used for a medallion with an icon in its center which is worn, suspended from the neck by a decorative chain where it hangs over the mid-chest. It is part of the vesture of an Orthodox or Eastern Catholic HIERARCH and is worn over his OMOPHORION. As the Bishop vests with the Engolpion, he prays: “Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου.») See also VESTMENTS. The term Engolpion is also used for a liturgical book such as the one used by the READER (᾿Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου).

units.english_text: **EOTHINON** (*῾Εωθινόν, τό*, pl. *῾Εωθινά, τά*; lit. "pertaining to the dawn"): Derived from the Greek *heos* ("dawn"). The term designates either: (a) one of the eleven Resurrectional Matins Gospels (*Eothina Evangelia*) read in cyclical order on Sundays at Matins; or (b) the eleven Idiomela Doxastika composed by Emperor Leo VI the Wise (reigned 866–912), chanted on Sundays at the conclusion of the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Lauds*) at the verse **"Glory to the Father..."**. Each idiomelon corresponds poetically to one of the eleven Matins Gospels, providing a poetic synthesis of the Resurrection appearance. In the ancient Constantinopolitan cathedral ("Asmatic" or "Sung") office described by Saint Symeon of Thessalonika († 1429), these hymns were chanted immediately preceding the reading of the Resurrection Gospel at Matins.

units.slavonic_text: EOTHINON (῾Εωθινόν, τό): Meaning ‘of the dawn’ in Greek. The word is used to refer either to (a) one of the eleven Gospels (Eothina Evangelia), read each Sunday at Matins, or to (b) the eleven Idiomela Doxastika by the Emperor Leo the Wise [866-912] that are sung in the Orthros on Sunday at the end of the Praises or Lauds (Αἶνοι.) There is one such idiomelon to correspond to each of the eleven Gospels, of which they are poetic summaries. In the old ‘Sung’, or ‘Cathedral’ office, as described by St Symeon of Thessaloniki [† 1429], they were sung immediately before the Resurrection Gospel in the ORTHROS. (AE)
units.english_text: **EPIGONATION** (*᾿Επιγονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *Palitsa*; cf. *Nabedrennik*): A liturgical vestment awarded as an ecclesiastical distinction. The term derives from the Greek *epi gonatos* ("upon the knee"). It consists of a stiff, diamond-shaped (rhomboid) fabric suspended from one corner by a ribbon worn over the left shoulder, hanging at the right knee below the waist. In the Greek tradition, it signifies that a presbyter holds advanced theological degrees and possesses the episcopal blessing to serve as a spiritual father (*Pnevmatikos*) and hear confessions. In the Slavic tradition, it is awarded as a liturgical honor for distinguished service; when a presbyter is awarded both the oblong *nabedrennik* (thigh-shield) and the rhomboid *palitsa* (*epigonation*), he wears the *palitsa* on the right hip and shifts the *nabedrennik* to the left. Liturgically, the Epigonation symbolizes the spiritual sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (cf. Ephesians 6:17).

units.slavonic_text: EPIGONATION (᾿Επιγονάτιον, τό) Slav. Nabedrennik: The epigonation (Greek: “upon the knee” or Russian palitsa is a vestment used by clergy in the Orthodox Church as a special honor. It is a stiff, rhomboid-shaped cloth that hangs over the knee on the right side of the body below the waist. It is suspended by one corner from a strap drawn over the left shoulder. In the Greek tradition it is usually a sign that the priest has an advanced academic degree and a blessing to hear confessions. In the Russian tradition it is an award for service. If a Russian priest has been awarded both the nabedrennik and the palitsa, he shifts the former to the left side. It is considered to symbolize the weapon of the Holy Word or a sword of Christ.

units.english_text: **EPIKLISIS** (*᾿Επίκλησις, ἡ*; lit. "invocation" or "calling down from above"): The solemn section of the Anaphora (Eucharistic Prayer) in which the celebrating bishop or priest invokes the Holy Spirit upon the gifts of bread and wine, that He may change them into the precious Body and Blood of Christ. In the Byzantine rite, the Epiklesis follows the Words of Institution and the Anamnesis (*remembrance*) of the Savior’s saving passion, cross, tomb, and resurrection.

units.slavonic_text: EPIKLISIS (᾿Επίκλησις, ἡ): The “invocation” or “calling down from above” is that section of the ANAPHORA or Eucharistic Prayer by which the priest invokes the Holy Spirit (or the power of His blessing) upon the Eucharistic bread and wine. In the Greek Orthodox Church, the Epiklisis comes after the ANAMNISIS or remembrance of Jesus’ words and deeds at the Last Supper.
units.english_text: **EPIMANIKIA** (*᾿Επιμανίκια, τά*; Slav. *Poruchi* or *Narukavnytsi*): Sacerdotal cuffs laced securely around the wrists and forearms of deacons, presbyters, and hierarchs. The deacon wears them over the sleeves of his inner cassock, beneath the wide sleeves of the *sticharion*; priests and bishops wear them over the cuffs of the *sticharion* / *podryasnik*. Mystically, they signify spiritual strength, patience, and divine power, recalling the cords that bound the sacred hands of our Savior Jesus Christ during His holy Passion.

units.english_text: **EPITRACHILION** (*᾿Επιτραχήλιον, τό*; Slav. *Epitrakhil*, *Obvyjnik*): An Eastern liturgical vestment derived from the two Greek words for upon (*epi*) and neck (*trachilos*); functionally equivalent to the Western stole. The principal morphological distinction is that the Epitrachilion is joined together down the front seam, either sewn continuously or fastened by a series of ornamental buttons. It is also broader than the Western stole. It is the indispensable sacerdotal vestment, worn by bishops and priests; a presbyter does not celebrate any divine service or sacred mystery without donning the epitrachilion.

units.slavonic_text: EPITAFIOS (᾿Επιτάφιος, ὁ): A cloth icon enclosed within a large embroidered cloth and depicting the entombed Christ. See also KUVUKLION.
units.english_text: When vesting with the Epitrachilion, the Priest prays: **“Blessed is God Who poureth His grace upon His priests, as ointment upon the head, that runneth down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, running down to the fringe of his garment (Psalm 132:2 [LXX 132:2 / MT 133:2]); always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ ἐκχέων τὴν χάριν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἱερεῖς αὐτοῦ· ὡς μύρον ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ πώγωνα, τὸν πώγωνα τοῦ ᾿Ααρών, τὸ καταβαῖνον ἐπὶ τὴν ᾤαν τοῦ ἐνδύματος αὐτοῦ» [Ψαλμ. 132:2 / MT 133:2]. Πάντοτε νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.)[^611]

units.slavonic_text: EPITRACHILION (᾿Επιτραχήλιον, τό) Slav. Epitraxil, Obvyjnik: An Orthodox liturgical vestment derived from the two Greek words for the neck (trachos) and upon (epi) and in that sense is the equivalent of the Western STOLE, the chief difference being that the Epitrachilion is always joined down the middle, normally by a series of ornamental studs. It is also broader then the Western Stole. It is the characteristic priestly vestment, worn only by bishops and priests. A priest should not celebrate any service unless he is wearing it. (AE)

units.english_text: The Epitrachilion may be understood historically as the deacon's **Orarion** (*᾿Ωράριον*), looped around the neck and adapted for priestly and episcopal ministry. It is draped around the neck with both ends hanging down equally in front to the lower hem of the sticharion, the two adjoining inner edges being sewn or buttoned together down the midline, leaving an aperture at the upper loop through which the head passes. In established liturgical practice it remains permanently joined. It is customarily fashioned of rich brocade or damask and adorned with seven embroidered crosses: one situated behind the neck, and three descending down each side.

units.english_text: The priest wears the epitrachilion whenever performing any sacerdotal function (as distinguished from merely being present in choir). For lesser offices and treby (e.g., Vespers, Matins, or molebens without full vesting), he dons the epitrachilion over his cassock. When fully vested for the Divine Liturgy, he wears the epitrachilion over the **Sticharion** (*Στιχάριον*) and beneath the **Zone** (*Ζώνη*) and **Felonion** (*Φελόνιον*).

units.slavonic_incipit: It could be considered as essentially
units.slavonic_text: It could be considered as essentially the ORARION of the DEACON, adapted for use by priests and bishops. It is worn around the neck with the two ends hanging down equally in front (more or less to the ankle) and with the two adjacent sides sewn or buttoned up together in the center, leaving enough space at the top through which to place the head. In practice it is never unfastened. It is usually made of brocade with seven embroidered or appliquéd crosses, one at the back of the neck and three down each side. (modified from wikipedia free encylopedia http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epitrachelion)
units.english_text: If a priest is present in choir without celebrating, he remains unvested in his cassock, but dons his epitrachilion (and customarily his **Epimanikia** [*᾿Επιμανίκια*]) before approaching to receive the Holy Mysteries.

provenance.verbatim_source: If a priest is present in choir without celebrating, he remains unvested in his cassock, but dons his epitrachilion (and customarily his **Epimanikia** [*᾿Επιμανίκια*]) before approaching to receive the Holy Mysteries.

units.slavonic_text: The priest wears the epitrachilion whenever he is serving as a priest (as opposed to simply attending a service). For some services, e.g. Vespers or Matins, he wears the epitrachilion by itself. When he is fully vested for the Divine Liturgy, he wears the epitrachilion over the STICHARION and under the ZONI and the FELONION.
units.english_text: **EQUAL OF THE APOSTLES** (*᾿Ισαπόστολος, ὁ / ἡ*): A hagiographical title bestowed upon a saint whose missionary labors, martyrdom, or defense of the Orthodox faith elevated them to a stature and dignity comparable to that of the Holy Apostles (e.g., Saint Mary Magdalene, July 22; Saints Constantine and Helen, May 21; Saint Vladimir the Great, July 15).

units.english_text: **EVLOGITOS** (*Εὐλογητός*): An abbreviation designating the initial blessing and sacerdotal exclamation that opens the majority of liturgical services: **“Blessed is our God always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») This exclamation commences Vespers, the Midnight Office (*Mesonyktikon*) on Sundays, and, in the absence of a concurring feast, the services during the seasons of the Triodion and Pentecostarion when coinciding with a Feast of the Mother of God or a ranked Saint. At Small Vespers following the prayer of the Ninth Hour, no dismissal is made, and Vespers at that point begins without the *Evlogitos*. The exclamation is likewise intoned at Sunday Matins (*Orthros*) and at every other divine service, with three principal statutory exceptions: (a) the Divine Liturgy, (b) the Mystery of Holy Baptism, and (c) the Mystery of Holy Crowning (Matrimony). In these three mysteries, the opening exclamation is: **“Blessed is the kingdom of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Εὐλογημένη ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ῾Αγίου Πνεύματος, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») Furthermore, at Vespers and Matins during Bright Week (Renewal Week), as well as on the **Apodosis** (lit. "Leave-taking", *᾿Απόδοσις*) of Pascha (Easter), and likewise prior to each daily recitation of the **Six Psalms** (*῾Εξάψαλμος* / Exapsalmos), the opening exclamation is: **“Glory to the holy, consubstantial, life-giving, and undivided Trinity, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** («Δόξα τῇ ῾Αγίᾳ καὶ ῾Ομοουσίῳ καὶ ζωοποιῷ καὶ ἀδιαιρέτῳ Τριάδι· πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») [See our translation of the *Protheoria*, pp. 4–5, and the *Typikon*, p. 4; also the *Synekdimos*, p. 246.] Note that Morning Prayer or Matins (*Orthros*) commences immediately following the dismissal of the Midnight Office (*Mesonyktikon* / *Μεσονυκτικόν*).

units.slavonic_text: EVLOGITOS (Εὐλογητός): Used as an abbreviation for the complete opening prayer of many services. This prayer text line is as follows: “Blessed is our God always, now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen.” («Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πάντοτε, νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») This prayer is used at the beginning of VESPERS, the MESONYKTIKON of Sunday and, without any concurring feast, during the period of the MOVABLE FEASTS of the Triodion and Pentikostarion if the feast coincides with a Feast of the Mother of God or a celebrated Saint. In small Vespers after the prayer of the 9th Hour a dismissal prayer is not done because at this point the VESPERS begins without the Evlogitos. The prayer is also done at Sunday MATINS and every other service except for a) The Divine Liturgy b) The Service of Holy Baptism and c) The Service of Holy Matrimony. In the latter three cases, the opening prayer is “Blessed is the kingdom of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Εὐλογημένη ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ῾Αγίου Πνεύματος, νῦν καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.») At VESPERS and MATINS during bright or renewal week, as well as the APODOSIS or LEAVE-TAKING (᾿Απόδοσις) of Pascha (Easter) and also prior to each daily read EXAPSALMOS the opening prayer is “Glory to the holy, consubstantial, life-giving and undivided Trinity, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.” («Δόξα τῇ ῾Αγίᾳ καὶ ῾Ομοουσίῳ καὶ ζωοποιῷ καὶ ἀδιαιρέτῳ Τριάδι· πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν») [See our translation of the Protheoria pgs. 4-5 and the Typikon pg. 4; also the Synekdimos pg. 246.] Note that the service of the morning prayer or ORTHROS begins immediately following the dismissal of the MIDNIGHT SERVICE or MESONYKTIKON (Μεσονυκτικόν).

units.english_text: **EXAPOSTILARION, pl. EXAPOSTILARIA** (*᾿Εξαποστειλάριον, τό· ἐξαποστειλάρια, τά*; Slav. lit. *Svetilen*; lit. "Hymn of Light"): In Greek the term signifies "that which is sent forth". These are one or two proper hymns chanted before the **Praises** (*Αἶνοι* / Eni) toward the conclusion of Matins (*Orthros*). On ordinary Sundays, there are eleven Resurrectional Exapostilaria composed by the son of Emperor Leo the Wise, Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (reigned 912–959). Each of these Exapostilaria corresponds poetically to one of the eleven Resurrection Gospels, the overarching theme of which is the radiant Resurrection of Christ and the events surrounding it.

units.slavonic_text: *EXAPOSTILARION, pl. EXAPOSTILARIA (ἐξαποστειλάριον, τό· ἐξαποστειλάρια, τά) Slav. Svetilen. Lit. Hymn of Light: In Greek the word means “to send out”. These are one or two hymns chanted before the ENI (Hymns of Praise) toward the end of the Orthros (Morning Prayer). On regular Sundays, there are eleven Exapostilaria written by the son of Leo the Wise, Constantine Porphyrogenitos [912-959]. Each of these Esapostilaria corresponds to one of the eleven Resurrection Gospels whose general theme is the Resurrection and the events surrounding it. (AE)
units.english_text: In summary, there exist three classes of Exapostilaria: (1) Resurrectional, which follow the elevenfold cycle of Sunday Resurrection Gospels and Gospel stichira; (2) Festal, which pertain to the specific feast being celebrated; and (3) Trinitarian (*Triadika*), which are chanted at certain Lenten services in honor of the Holy Trinity.

provenance.verbatim_source: In summary, there exist three classes of Exapostilaria: (1) Resurrectional, which follow the elevenfold cycle of Sunday Resurrection Gospels and Gospel stichira; (2) Festal, which pertain to the specific feast being celebrated; and (3) Trinitarian (*Triadika*), which are chanted at certain Lenten services in honor of the Holy Trinity.

units.english_text: **EXAPTERYGA** (*῾Εξαπτέρυγα, τά*): The liturgical processional fans representing the celestial choir of Seraphim, derived from the Greek meaning literally "six-winged". These fans are metallic disks embossed with images of the six-winged Seraphim, mounted on shafts and carried by acolytes during solemn liturgical processions. When not carried in procession, these shafts stand in sockets behind the Holy Table on either side of the central processional Cross. In Greek, the fan is also designated a **Ripidion** (*ῥιπίδιον, τό*), and in Latin, a *flabellum*.

units.slavonic_text: EXAPTERYGA (῾Εξαπτέρυγα, τά): The so-called ‘fans’ representing an order of angels and in Greek meaning literally ‘six-winged.’ These ‘fans’ are metallic disks carried on poles by acolytes during liturgical processions. These poles normally stand in a containing box behind the altar table on either side of a central pole holding the cross. The fan in Greek, has also been called a RIPIDION (ριπίδιον, τό) and in Latin, a flabellum.

units.english_text: **EXERETOS** (*᾿Εξαιρέτως*; lit. "especially" or "above all"): The initial word of the great sacerdotal exclamation commemorating the Mother of God during the Anaphora of the Divine Liturgy: **“Especially our most holy, spotless, most blessed and glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary.”** («᾿Εξαιρέτως τῆς παναγίας, ἀχράντου, ὑπερευλογημένης, ἐνδόξου, Δεσποίνης ἡμῶν Θεοτόκου, καὶ ἀειπαρθένου Μαρίας.») In the Divine Liturgy, it is immediately followed by the singing of the hymn designated the **Megalynarion** (*Μεγαλυνάριον* / Slav. *Zadostoinyk*). The customary hymn sung at this point is **“It Is Truly Right”** (*῎Αξιόν ἐστιν ὡς ἀληθῶς...* / *Axion Estin*). This hymn is replaced on Great Feasts by the proper festal Megalynarion (the Heirmos of the Ninth Ode with its refrain) appointed for the feast or Saint of the day, as instructed in the *Protheoria* of the *Typikon*. These festal hymns are also compiled in a collection at the conclusion of the *Handbook of the Church Reader* (*῾Εγκόλπιον τοῦ ᾿Αναγνώστου*) or *Holy Services of Vespers, Matins, and Divine Liturgy* (Thirteenth edition, 1992, Athens, Greece, published by Apostoliki Diakonia of the Church of Greece).

units.slavonic_text: EXERETOS (᾿Εξαιρέτως): ‘Especially’ or ‘above all.’ This is a common abbreviation for a longer prayer in the Divine Liturgy which is as follows: “Especially our most holy, blessed and glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary.” («᾿Εξαιρέτως τῆς παναγίας, ἀχράντου, ὑπερευλογημένης, ἐνδόξου, Δεσποίνης ἡμῶν Θεοτόκου, καὶ ἀειπαρθένου Μαρίας.») In the Divine Liturgy, it is immediately followed by the singing of a hymn type called the Magnificat (Μεγαλυνάριον.) The most commonly used Megalynarion is the “It is truly fitting to call you blessed...” («῎Αξιόν ἐστιν ὡς ἀληθῶς...») This hymn may be replaced by another magnificat proper to the feast or Saint of the day as instructed in the Pretheory of the Typikon. These hymns are also listed in a collection located at the end of the Handbook of the Church Reader or Holy Services of Vespers, Matins and Divine Liturgy, Thirteenth edition, 1992, Athens, Greece published by the Apostoliki Diaconia of the Church of Greece.

units.slavonic_text: FELONION, -A (Φελόνιον, τό· pl. Φελόνια, τά): See also VESTMENTS. Today the Felonion is a liturgical vestment worn by a priest in the Orthodox Church. It is worn over the priest’s other vestments and is similar to the chasuble used in the Roman Catholic Church. The Felonion is an ornate circular garment with a opening in the center for the wearer’s head. When worn, it reaches to the wearer’s wrists in front, so that if the wearer holds both arms straight out, the Felonion forms a semi-circle when viewed from the front or the back. In its present form, the front is largely cut away (from about the waist down) to facilitate the movement of the priest’s hands. The rubrics may direct that the priest is to ‘lower the Felonion’, that is to let it fall over his hands at the moment of the Dismissal, indicating that the service is finished. Russian felonia often have a row of buttons across the chest so that the front of the vestment can be raised or lowered. The Felonion is a descendant of a first-century paenula (a garment worn as a coat by both sexes.) (Modification of AE)

units.english_text: **FELONION, pl. FELONIA** (*Φελόνιον, τό· pl. Φελόνια, τά*; Slav. *Phelon*, *Ryza*): See also **VESTMENTS**. In contemporary practice, the Felonion is the principal sacerdotal vestment worn by a priest in the Eastern Church. It is worn over the priest’s other vestments (*sticharion*, *epitrachilion*, and *zone*) and corresponds functionally to the Western chasuble. The Felonion is an ample, conical or circular vestment with an opening in the center for the celebrant’s head. When donned, it reaches to the wearer’s wrists in front, so that when the celebrant holds both arms extended, the vestment forms a semicircle when viewed from front or back. In its developed Byzantine form, the front is deeply cut away (from approximately the waist downward) to facilitate the unimpeded movement of the priest’s hands during liturgical ministrations. Rubrics occasionally direct the priest to “lower the Felonion”, that is, to let it fall over his hands at the Dismissal (*Apolysis*), indicating that the divine service is completed. Slavic *felonia* frequently feature a stiffened collar rising behind the neck, and occasionally a row of small buttons across the chest so that the front of the vestment can be raised or lowered. The Felonion descends historically from the Greco-Roman *paenula*, an outer protective garment worn as a cloak in the early centuries.

Amen.” («Οἱ ἱερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται (Ψαλμ. 131 (132):9). Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν.»)
units.english_text: **FESTAL PRECEDENCE**: When two feasts coincide on the same day, one takes precedence over the other by reason of its higher liturgical rank (e.g., a Feast of the Lord takes precedence over a Saint’s Feast). This precedence determines the hierarchical order of hymnody: the hymns of the dominant feast precede the hymns of the lesser feast within each liturgical section (e.g., at the **Praises** [*Αἶνοι*] or among the **Dismissal Troparia** [*᾿Απολυτίκια* / lit. *Apolytikia*] chanted at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy).

units.slavonic_text: *FESTAL PRECEDENCE: When two feasts are celebrated together, one takes precedence over the other because of its higher rank (e.g., a Lord’s Feast takes precedence over a Saint’s Feast). units.english_text: (*δισκάριον*, lit. "small tray") and in the chalice—both covered with veils and united under the Great Veil (**Aer**)—from the table of the **Prothesis** (*Πρόθεσις*). They exit the **Sanctuary** through the north door, moving to the center of the **Soleas**, where they pause to recite commemorative prayers. They re-enter the Sanctuary through the central Holy Doors (the Beautiful Gate), and lay the paten and the chalice upon the **Holy Table** (*῾Αγία Τράπεζα*) or **Altar**. This procession takes place during the chanting of the Cherubic Hymn (*Χερουβικόν*) in the Divine Liturgy. When a bishop is officiating, the ritual movements and prayers of the procession expand in length and solemnity.

units.english_text: **HOLY EUCHARIST** (*Θεία Εὐχαριστία, ἡ*): Instituted by Christ Himself at the Mystical Supper, the Holy Eucharist is the central and most exalted sacramental Mystery in the life of the Church. It is celebrated in the Divine Liturgy as its culminating sacrifice and is synonymous with it. During the Holy Eucharist, the bread and wine are changed by the power and descent of the Holy Spirit into the Body and Blood of Christ. The faithful receive the consecrated Holy Gifts in Holy Communion and thereby become one with Christ. As Mystery, the Holy Eucharist accomplishes the most perfect communion between God and man. At the same time, it unites the communicants with one another as members of Christ’s Body, the Church. The faithful offer thanksgiving (*Eucharistia*) to God for His many blessings and for the salvation that He hath wrought for them, especially through His earthly ministry, His death upon the Cross, and His third-day Resurrection.

It is celebrated in the Divine Liturgy as its central event and is synonymous with it. During the Holy Eucharist, the bread and wine are changed by the power of the Holy Spirit into the Body and Blood of Christ. The faithful receive the consecrated elements through communion and thus become one with Christ. As sacrament, the Holy Eucharist effects the most perfect union between God and man. At the same time, it unites the communicants with one another as members of Christ’s Body, the Church. The faithful offer thanks (eucharist or ‘thanksgiving’) to God for His many blessings and for the salvation that He has wrought for them, especially through His ministry on earth, His death and resurrection.

units.english_text: **HOURS** (*῞Ωρα, ἡ, pl. ῏Ωραι, αἱ*; Slav. *Chasy*): Though predominantly celebrated in holy monasteries, the Hours are services regularly celebrated in parish churches in cities and towns. The First, Third, and Sixth Hours are chanted before Matins (*Orthros*), and the Ninth Hour before Vespers. The text of these Hours is found in the liturgical book *The Great Horologion* (*῾Ωρολόγιον τὸ Μέγα* / *Chasoslov*), preceding the Service of Matins (*Orthros*). A distinct solemn cycle called the Great (or Royal) Hours is celebrated on the Eve of the Nativity of Christ, the Eve of Theophany, and on Great and Holy Friday. Their texts are contained in the festal propers of those days.

units.english_text: **HYMN OF KASSIANI** (*Τροπάριον τῆς Κασσιανῆς, τό*): Saint Kassiani is also known by the names Kassia, Casia, Ikasia, Cassia, Cassiane, Kassiana, or Eikasia. She was a Byzantine hymnographer (9th c.) born in Constantinople to a noble family, who later matured as an extraordinarily gifted, beautiful, and learned woman—so much so that she was chosen to participate in a "bridal show" (bride-show), at which the Emperor Theophilos was to select an empress. Struck by Kassiani's radiant beauty, the Emperor approached her and remarked: "Through a woman came forth the baser things," referring to Eve's transgression. Kassiani readily replied: "Through a woman came forth the better things," referring to the redemptive Incarnation of Christ through His Most Pure and Virgin Mother. Stung by her sharp and intelligent reply, the Emperor rejected her and instead chose Theodora as his wife. Following this, Kassiani embraced the monastic life and founded a women's monastery in Constantinople, closely affiliated with the renowned Monastery of the Stoudion. Serving as abbess (hegumenia) of the monastery, she composed numerous liturgical hymns, at least twenty of which are preserved in the liturgical books of the Church. Of these compositions, the most famous is the renowned Doxastikon of Holy Wednesday Matins (customarily chanted on the evening of Great and Holy Tuesday), known universally as the **Hymn of Kassiani** (**"Lord, the woman fallen into many sins"** / *Κύριε, ἡ ἐν πολλαῖς ἁμαρτίαις περιπεσοῦσα γυνή*). Her feast is commemorated on September 7.

units.slavonic_text: HYMN OF KASSIANI (Τροπάριον τῆς Κασσιανῆς, τό): St. Kassiani is also known by the names Kassia, Casia, Ikasia, Cassia, Cassiane, Kassiana,or Eikasia. She was a Hymnographer (9th c.) born in Constantinople to a noble family, who later matured as an unusually beautiful and learned woman— so much so that she was chosen to participate in a 'bridal show', at which the Emperor Theophilos was to choose a wife. Struck by Kassiani's beauty, the Emperor approached her and said 'Through a woman came forth the baser things,' referring to Eve's transgression. Kassiani responded, 'Through a woman came forth the better things', referring to the redemptive Incarnation of Christ through His Most Pure and human Mother. Stung by her too intelligent reply, the Emperor rejected her and instead chose Theodora as his wife. Following this, Kassiani entered monastic life and founded a women's monastery in Constantinople, closely allied with the famous Stoudion Monastery. Serving as abbess of the monastery, she wrote many liturgical hymns, at least twenty of which are included in the services of the Church. Of these hymns, the best-known (or at least most closely associated with her) is the Hymn of Kassiani, sung at the Matins Service of Holy Wednesday, usually sung on Holy Tuesday Evening. Her feast day is celebrated on 7 September.

units.slavonic_text: *IKONOSTASION (εἰκονοστάσιον, τό): Also spelled Iconostasion this is the screen of icons separating the SANCTUARY from the SOLEAS. Also known as the TEMPLON, it has three doors: 1) On the north, depicting the Archangel Michael; 2) On the south, depicting the Archangel Gabriel; and 3) The central door, called the BEAUTIFUL GATE, through which only clergy may pass. While in some jurisdictions, the term 'Royal Door' has been used to describe the Beautiful Gate, it should be used only for the central door leading from the Narthex into the Nave through which Byzantine Royalty entered the church in antiquity.
units.english_text: **IKOS, pl. IKOI** (*Οἶκος, ὁ· pl. Οἶκοι, οἱ*): Stanza or "house" (Slav. *Ikos*). Each of the twenty-four poetic stanzas of the Akathist Hymn to the Most Holy Theotokos is designated an Ikos. Furthermore, in the structure of the liturgical Canon at Matins, the Ikos is the poetic stanza chanted immediately following the Kontakion between the Sixth and Seventh Odes. The Ikos amplifies and unpacks the theological mystery articulated in the Kontakion and, as a rule, terminates with the same refrain as the Kontakion.

units.english_text: Only a bishop possesses the authority to consecrate an Antiminsion. This consecration occurs either during the solemn dedication and consecration of a church, or through an independent episcopal rite. In this rite, the bishop anoints a small sewn relic-pocket within the Antiminsion with Holy Chrism (*Agion Myron*), deposits therein the sacred relics of holy martyrs, and seals them securely with fragrant wax-mastic. He subsequently inscribes the Antiminsion with the dedication of the church for which it is consecrated, subscribes his episcopal signature, and imprints his official diocesan seal upon it.

units.slavonic_incipit: Only a bishop may consecrate an
units.slavonic_text: Only a bishop may consecrate an Antiminsion. This may take place as a part of the consecration of a church, or in a separate rite. In this rite, the bishop will anoint a pocket sewn into the Antiminsion in which to place the Relics of the saints and Chrism sealing them in place with wax mastic. He then inscribes the Antiminsion with the name of the church for which it has been consecrated and signs it. He may also stamp it with his official seal.
units.english_text: **IMEROLOGION** (*῾Ημερολόγιον, τό*): Liturgical calendar or ordo book. In current ecclesiastical practice, this is the annual directorium published under the authority of the Church containing the day-to-day order of services and rubrical assignments for each liturgical year. The volume is compiled annually in strict conformity with the directives of the canonical **Typikon**.

units.english_text: **HEIRMOS** (*Εἱρμός, ὁ*; Slav. *Irmos*; lit. "link" or "drawing together"): The initial thematic stanza or model hymn opening each Ode of a liturgical Canon. The Heirmos fulfills a twofold structural function: it links the Ode thematically to the scriptural Biblical Canticle upon which it is founded, and, by establishing the melodic pattern, rhythm, meter, and acrostic framework for all subsequent troparia in the Ode, it serves as the primary architectural link in the hymnographic chain.

units.slavonic_text: IRMOS (εἱρμός, ὁ): A word meaning “link” in Greek. The Irmos is the first hymn of each ode of a Canon. It has a double function: it “links” the ode thematically with the Biblical canticle which serves as its prototype, and, by establishing the meter and melody for all the other hymns (TROPARIA) of the ode, it is the first “link” in their chain. (From APL)

units.english_text: **KALYMMAFCHION** (*Καλυμμαύχιον, τό*; Slav. *Kamilavka*): The cylindrical black clerical head covering worn by Eastern Christian clergy. In Greek liturgical use, the kamilavka of the secular (married) clergy features a small raised flat rim or peak at the crown, whereas that of monastics remains flat and smooth. Monks and celibate clergy (hieromonks, archimandrites, and bishops) wear the sacred monastic veil or cowl (Greek *koukoulion* / *ἐπανωκαλύμμαυχον*; Slav. *klobuk* / *namitka*) draped over the kamilavka. In the Slavic tradition, the veil is permanently fastened to the stiff cylindrical hat to form the composite vestment known as the *klobuk*, whereas in Greek tradition the epanokalymmafchion remains detachable.

units.slavonic_text: KALYMMAFCHION (καλυμμαύχιον, τό) Slav. kamilavka: The familiar black cylindrical ‘stove pipe’ head covering worn by Orthodox clergy. In Greek use, those of the secular clergy have a small brim on top. Monks, whether priests or not, wear a monastc cowl or veil (Greek koukoulli, or Latin, cucullus) over the top of the hat. When worn by celibate Archimandrites and Bishops this is called an EPANOKALYMMAFCHION (over-kalymmafchion). In Slavic use, the cowl is permanently attached and the whole is called a klobuk, but the Greek cowl can be removed separately, and the rules for when to wear what are quite complicated. (Adapted from AE and FL.)

units.english_text: A monumental hymnographic poetic form comprising most frequently eight or nine Odes (and more rarely, four, three, or two Odes). The Canon commemorates the sacred mystery, feast, or saint of the day and forms the liturgical center of Matins (*Orthros*). Each Ode consists of an opening model hymn (**Heirmos**) followed by a prescribed series of poetic strophes (**Troparia**). Each of the nine Odes corresponds to and is typologically patterned after one of the nine Biblical Canticles of Holy Scripture, establishing an Old Testament event as the prophetic archetype of a New Testament revelation in Christ. Complete Canons encompass nine Odes; however, the Second Ode (patterned upon the severe song of condemnation in Deuteronomy 32) is sung exclusively during the weekdays of Great Lent. The Great Penitential Canon of Saint Andrew of Crete is chanted in sections during the first week of Great Lent and in its entirety on Wednesday evening of the Fifth Week.

units.slavonic_incipit: A hymn form that consists most
units.slavonic_text: A hymn form that consists most often of eight or nine odes, and more rarely, of four, three or two odes. This hymn form pertains to the sacred event or the saint(s) being commemorated and is sung at the service of Matins. Each ode consists of several stanzas or troparia. Each of the nine odes is patterned after a CANTICLE from the Holy Scriptures (i.e. a biblical canticle) which relates to an Old Testament event which prefigures a New Testament event. Complete Canons, as a rule, have nine odes; the Second Ode, however, is most frequently omitted because of its severe divine condemnation of mankind. The special service known as the Great Canon is sung on the evening of Wednesday of the fifth week of Great Lent.

units.slavonic_text: KATANYKTIKON, KATANYKTIKA (Κατανυκτικόν, τό), pl. (Κατανυκτικά, τά): Hymns whose content is penitential, speaking of contrition and repentance.
units.english_text: **KATAVASIA, pl. KATAVASIE** (*Καταβασία, ἡ· pl. Καταβασίαι, αἱ*; Slav. *Katavasiya*): A liturgical classification of festive model hymns chanted at the conclusion of each Ode of the Canon at Matins (*Orthros*). In Greek ecclesiastical usage, the term derives from the verb *katabaino* (*καταβαίνω*, "to descend"), designating the ancient monastic practice whereby the chanters descended from their raised choir stalls (*stacidia*) into the center of the nave to unite in chanting these climactic heirmoi together. On Sundays and major festal celebrations, a Katavasia is chanted after every individual Ode. The term "Katavasiai" likewise denotes the complete set of festal heirmoi assigned across the nine Odes of Matins. Katavasiai are seasonal and anticipate upcoming Great Feasts: thus the Katavasiai of the Nativity of Christ (**"Christ is born, glorify Him!"** / *Χριστὸς γεννᾶται· δοξάσατε*) are chanted from November 21 through December 25. The most frequently chanted ordinary Katavasiai are those of the Canon to the Most Holy Theotokos in Tone 4, **“I shall open my mouth”** (*᾿Ανοίξω τὸ στόμα μου*). On ordinary non-festal days, the Katavasia is chanted only after the Third, Sixth, Eighth, and Ninth Odes.

units.slavonic_text: KATAVASIA, KATAVASIE (Καταβασία, ἡ), pl. Καταβασίαι, αἱ): The title for a classification of hymns which conclude each ODE of a CANON. In Greek, the title suggests the act of descending since these hymns were sung when the chanters descended (Greek καταβαίνω) from their stalls (στασίδια) and gathered together to sing them. On Sundays and major Feasts there is a katavasia after every ode. “Katavasie” refers also to the entire CANON with its 9 Odes which is chanted mostly before the Morning Gospel in the ORTHROS. Katavasie are often ‘seasonal’ and anticipate the next Great Feast. Thus the katavasie of Christmas are sung from the 21 November up to and including 25 December. The Katavasie most frequently chanted are those of the Canon to the Mother of God in Mode IV, “I shall open my mouth”(«᾿Ανοίξω τὸ στόμα μου». On non-festal days katavasie occur after the 3rd, 6th, 8th and 9th Odes only. (Adapted from AE.)

units.english_text: - First, a Kathisma is one of the twenty major divisions or sections into which the Septuagint (LXX) Old Testament Psalter is partitioned for liturgical recitation throughout the weekly cycle in the Byzantine and Slavic traditions. Each Kathisma is subdivided into three states or antiphons (*Staseis* / *Στάσεις*), each comprising a variable group of psalms (e.g., Kathisma 1 = Psalms 1–8; Kathisma 2 = Psalms 9–17, etc.), concluded by the Doxology ("Glory... both now... Alleluia").[^627]

Each Kathisma is divided into three sections (Στάσεις) composed of a variable number of Psalms, e.g., Kathisma #1 = Psalms 1-8; Kathisma #2 = Psalms 9-17; etc.

units.english_text: - Second, Kathismata denote a class of liturgical troparia (**Sessional Hymns**, Slav. *Sedalni*). These short poetic hymns are chanted following the reading of each Kathisma of the Psalter, after the Polyeleos, and after the Third Ode of the Canon at Matins. The designation derives from the Greek verb *kathezomai* (*καθέζομαι*, "to sit"), indicating the rubrical dispensation allowing the clergy and faithful to sit during their recitation, in contrast to the standing posture required during solemn psalms and prayers.

units.english_text: - Third, in monastic administration, a Kathisma denotes a small solitary monastic dwelling or hermitage. On the Holy Mountain of Athos, each subordinate monastic settlement (*skete*, *cell*, *kalyve*, *hesychasterion*, or *kathisma*) exists under the jurisdiction of one of the twenty sovereign ruling monasteries. The Kathisma constitutes one of the smallest establishments, designed as a simple habitation for a single solitary hesychast monk.

units.slavonic_incipit: On Mount Athos, the Autonomous Monastic
units.slavonic_text: On Mount Athos, the Autonomous Monastic State of the Holy Mountain, a monastic republic in northern Greece, each of the monastic establishments (sketae, kellia, kalyvae, hesychasteria or kathismata), large or small, exists under the jurisdiction of one of twenty Sovereign Monasteries. One of the smallest types of these monastic establishments is called a Kathisma, a simple abode for one solitary monk.
units.english_text: **KE NYN** (*Καὶ νῦν*): Lit. "And now"; the standard rubrical abbreviation for the concluding phrase of the liturgical doxology: **“Both now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”** (*Καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ᾿Αμήν*). This cue is employed ubiquitously in the **Typikon** and liturgical books, routinely following the abbreviation **Doxa** (*Δόξα* / "Glory...").

units.english_text: **KEROS** (*Καιρός, ὁ*; Slav. *Vremya*): Lit. "appointed time", "due season", or "opportunity". In liturgical practice, "taking keros" (*Kairon*) designates the preliminary sacerdotal rite of preparation performed by the priest and deacon before vesting for the Divine Liturgy. The sacred ministers stand before the Holy Doors of the icon screen, make three reverences, venerate the holy icons of Christ, the Theotokos, the Forerunner, and the patron saint of the temple, recite the appointed penitential and vesting prayers, turn and bow to the people to ask forgiveness, and enter the Sanctuary to vest.[^628]

units.slavonic_incipit: Traditionally, in cathedrals, monasteries and larger
units.slavonic_text: Traditionally, in cathedrals, monasteries and larger churches such as chapels belonging to seminaries and major parishes there would have been a kliros on both the north and south sides of the soleas at the eastern end of the church. The result is two choirs which may sing antiphonally. This was the practice in the Byzantine Imperial Cathedral of Hagia Sophia, in Constantinople, whose historical liturgical practice became the standard for all churches following the Byzantine liturgical tradition.
units.english_text: In traditional cathedral and monastic architecture, two choirs (*kliri*) are situated on the north (left) and south (right) flanks of the Soleas before the icon screen, enabling the antiphonary execution of hymns between the right and left choirs. This antiphonal choir arrangement was perfected in the Great Imperial Church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, establishing the benchmark for all monuments within the Byzantine liturgical sphere.

units.slavonic_incipit: This arrangement presupposes a number of
units.slavonic_text: This arrangement presupposes a number of singers on each side, adding up to a reasonably large total, and two highly-trained chanters skilled in leading the services. Unfortunately, highly-trained chanters are exceedingly rare today, and most churches have only one kliros, usually on the right of the SOLEA. Nevertheless some patriarchal cathedrals, larger monastic communities, seminaries, and churches with sufficient resources and singers, may continue to have two kliri.
units.english_text: This classical structure presupposes two complete choirs led by two master chanters (*protopsaltes* and *lampadarios*). In contemporary parish practice, where resources are limited, a single kliros is often maintained on the right side of the Soleas, or singing is supported from a choir loft situated at the western end of the nave above the narthex.[^629]

units.english_text: **KONTAKION, pl. KONTAKIA** (*Κοντάκιον, τό· pl. Κοντάκια, τά*; Slav. *Kondak*): The Kontakion was the preeminent poetical and hymnographic genre of early Byzantine hymnology, achieving its classic zenith in the inspired verse of Saint Romanos the Melodist (6th century), many of whose masterpieces remain central to the liturgical life of the Church. Thematically, the classical Kontakion presented an expansive narrative and dramatic homily upon the great feast of the day, notably the Nativity of Christ. Structurally, an ancient Kontakion consisted of 18 to 30 or more stanzas, each designated an **Ikos** (*Οἶκος*), composed in identical meter and rhythm and sung to the same melody. The initial letters of these stanzas formed an acrostic, spelling out the title of the feast, the poet’s name, or the Greek alphabet. These stanzas were preceded by a short independent introductory stanza called the **proimion** (*προοίμιον*) or **kukulion** (*κουκούλιον*), which established the musical Mode and the concluding refrain (**efymnion** / *ἐφύμνιον*) repeated at the end of every subsequent Ikos.

The ordinary daily Kontakion chanted at the Divine Liturgy is the beloved Theotokion: **“The Protection of Christians”** (*Προστασία τῶν Χριστιανῶν*), honoring the Mother of God as an unashamed intercessor before the Creator.[^630]

KONTAKIA (κοντάκια, τά): The Kontakion was a major poetic form in Byzantine hymnology which achieved its most sublime expression in the work of St. Romanos the Melodist (6th cent.), many of whose Kontakia are still in use today. Its narrative and theological topic is one of the great feasts, such as the Nativity of Our Lord (Christmas). A Kontakion is made up of 18-30 or more STROPHES or STANZAS each called an IKOS (οἶκος), which are structurally and metrically alike and thus set to the same melody. The initial letters of these stanzas formed an acrostic, spelling out either the name of the celebrated feast, or the name of the author-poet, or merely the Greek alphabet. Today, only the short introductory hymn, now bearing the name Kontakion, is performed in the Divine Liturgy immediately prior to the Trisagios or Thrice Holy Hymn. units.english_text: Originally, the Kontakion was a poetic "verse sermon" consisting of an introductory preamble or Proimion (*Προοίμιον*) followed by a series of longer stanzas, the Ikoi (*Οἶκοι*), all terminating with an identical recurring phrase or refrain (*ephymnion*). Kontakia were gradually supplanted in the liturgical offices by a subsequent poetic hymnographic cycle, the **Canon** (*Κανών*). In the present ecclesiastical office, only the Proimion (now itself customarily designated simply as the Kontakion) and the first Ikos survive in liturgical recitation. In contemporary Byzantine practice, they are regularly read at Matins (*Orthros*), except on great feasts, and the final phrase is repeated by the choir—a living survival of the ancient practice. The Kontakion is likewise read at the Little Hours and chanted at the Divine Liturgy, where in standard usage the proper kontakia are seasonal, coordinating with the prescribed Katavasiai.

units.english_text: No direct documentary evidence survives to establish the exact date at which the Kontakion was formally incorporated into the Byzantine liturgical system. No reference to this poetic genre is to be found in imperial Byzantine documents or writings during the initial era of its flourishing. Even the technical name *Kontakion* appears for the first time only in ninth-century sources; the monastic hymnographers who originally composed works of this genre designated such a composition variously as a Hymn (*ὕμνος*), Psalm (*ψαλμός*), Poem (*ποίημα* or *ἔπος*), Canticle or Song (*ᾠδή* or *ᾆσμα*), Praise or Laud (*αἶνος*), Prayer (*προσευχή*), or Supplication (*δέησις*).

units.slavonic_text: Originally the Kontakion was a 'verse sermon' consisting of an Introductory preamble or Proimion (Προοίμιον) followed by a series of longer stanzas, the Iki (Οἶκοι), all ending with the same phrase similar to a refrain. Kontakia were gradually displaced by a subsequent poetical form, the CANON (κανών). In the present office only the Proimion or preamble, now called the Kontakion, and the first Ikos survive. In current Greek use they are normally read at Matins (῎Ορθρος), except on great Feasts, and the final phrase is repeated, a survival of the ancient practice. The Kontakion is also read at the Hours and sung at the Liturgy, though in Greek use those at the Liturgy are 'seasonal', like the KATAVASIES. (AE)
units.english_text: A complete historical Kontakion comprised from eighteen to thirty, or even more, structurally and metrically identical stanzas. A single stanza is designated a Troparion (*Τροπάριον*), varying in length from three to thirteen poetic lines. All subsequent Troparia in the work are composed upon the exact metric and rhythmic model of an initial stanza, the **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*). A Kontakion is either constructed upon the pattern of an Heirmos composed expressly for that poem, or adopts the meter of a pre-existing Heirmos previously composed for another Kontakion. units.slavonic_text: No evidence is available to determine the date at which the Kontakion was received into the Byzantine liturgy. No reference to it is to be found in Byzantine documents or writings during the time it was in use. Even the name Kontakion only occurs for the first time in the ninth century; the monk who composed a hymn of that kind called it a Hymn (ὕμνος), Psalm (ψαλμός), Poem (ποίημα or ἔπος), Song (ᾠδή or ᾆσμα), Praise or Laud (αἶνος), Prayer (προσευχή) or Petition (δέησις).

units.slavonic_text: stage, often consists of two or three stanzas. Proimion and Kontakion are linked together by the refrain, the Ephymnion (ἐφύμνιον) with which all the stanzas end, and by the musical mode (ἦχος). The occurrence of the refrain at the end of each stanza indicates that the Kontakia were sung by a soloist, the choir singing the refrain. The stanzas of the Kontakion are connected either alphabetically or by a different acrostic, in the following way: The first letters of each stanzas sequentially are either the letters of the Greek alphabet in its usual order, or form a short sentence containing the name of the hymn-writer and the title of the poem. The acrostic is indicated in the title of the Kontakion. From the title we may learn, therefore, (1) the day of the feast on which the Kontakion is sung, (2) the feast for which it is composed, (3) the acrostic, (4) the musical mode of the melody. Taking for example the Kontakion 'Joseph the Chaste' by Romanos which the Orthodox church sings on Great Monday of Holy Week. This title, in Greek, reads as follows: «Τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ μεγάλῃ δευτέρᾳ. Κοντάκιον εἰς τὸν Ἰωσὴφ φέρον ἀκροστιχίδα τήνδε· ᾿Αλφάβητον ῾Ρωμανοῦ, Πλάγιος δ΄. Πρὸς τὸ ῾Ο υἱός σου παρθένε πανάμωμε.» From this title we learn the following: This Kontakion, sung on Monday in Holy Week, was composed in honor of Joseph; further, that each stanza began with a letter of the Greek alphabet, followed an acrostic consisting of the letters in the two words ᾿Αλφάβητον ῾Ρωμανοῦ; that the melody was written in Mode IV Plagal and was modelled on an already existing hymn beginning with the words ῾Ο υἱός σου παρθένε πανάμωμε. units.slavonic_text: TD-89
units.english_text: In another instance, in an anonymous hymnographer's poem composed in memory of Saint John Chrysostom, this principle of letter doubling is expanded even further. The prescription in the title: *«φέρον ἀκροστιχίδα τήνδε· εἰς τὸν χρυσόστομον»* ("bearing this acrostic: Unto Chrysostom") is executed through extensive gemination: *εις τον χχρρυυσσοοοσσττομον*. At the period when the classic Kontakia were composed, the Greek language had already surrendered the classical distinction between long and short vowels, which constituted the foundation of the quantitative meter of ancient classical poetry. The vowels and diphthongs *η*, *ει*, and *οι* had become phonetically equivalent to *ι* (iota), and *αι* equivalent to *ε* (epsilon). Consequently, a new tonic-rhythmic system of versification arose, founded upon the strict rule that all stanzas must possess the exact same number of syllables as the model **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*) upon which they were modeled, and that the word stress accents must occupy identical positions across all stanzas as in the corresponding verses of the Heirmos. The composition of a Kontakion—or, in later centuries, of a **Canon** (*Κανών*)—was a sophisticated undertaking that could be accomplished only by a poet who was simultaneously a master composer and musician. Melody and verse formed a single entity. In adapting the Troparia to the melody of the Heirmos, it was not merely necessary to equate the syllable count of each line with the model strophe; the dynamic melodic stress accents had to coincide precisely with the accented syllables of the hymnographic text.

At the time when the Kontakia were written the Greek language had already lost the difference between long and short vowels, the basis of the quantitative metre of classical poetry; what had become equal to o, h, ei, and oi were pronounced as a short i, ai as e. A new system of versification had developed based on the principle that all the stanzas had to have the same number of syllables as the Irmos on which they were modelled and that the stress accents had to have the same place in all the stanzas as in the verses of the Irmos.... The composition of a Kontakion, or, at a later date, of a Kanon, was a task which a poet could not achieve who was not also a skilled musician. Music and poetry had to make a single entity. To adapt the Troparia to the melody of the Irmos it was not sufficient to make each line, corresponding to a line of the model strophe, of equal length, i.e. with the same number of syllables, but the stress accents must also fall on the same syllable as in the Irmos, in order to make the accentuated notes of the melody coincide with the accentuated syllables of the text of the stanzas. The Kontakion makes its appearance suddenly, without antecedents. Byzantine hagiography attributes its introduction into Eastern liturgy to Romanos, who is praised by Germanos, the author of a hymn in honor of the saint who gives the Greek hymn and its description and explanation. The association of the name of Romanos with the rise of the Kontakion makes it possible to fix the date of its reception into Byzantine liturgy within the first decades of the sixth century. units.english_text: The Kontakion appeared in Byzantine worship with striking suddenness, without direct literary antecedents in classical Greek forms. Byzantine hagiographical tradition attributes its introduction into Eastern Christian worship to Saint Romanos the Melodist, celebrated by Saint Germanos, who composed a hymn in his honor providing an account of his miraculous divine inspiration. The historical association of Saint Romanos with the rise of the Kontakion allows us to date its formal entry into the Constantinopolitan liturgical tradition to the early decades of the sixth century. Saint Romanos was of Jewish lineage, born in Emesa upon the Orontes River (modern Homs, Syria). He was ordained deacon at Berytus (Beirut) in Phoenicia, and subsequently journeyed to Constantinople during the reign of Emperor Anastasios I (491–518), joining the clergy of the Church of the Most Holy Theotokos in the Kyros district. There, according to sacred tradition, the Mother of God appeared to him on the Feast of the Nativity of Christ, bestowing upon him the miraculous charism of hymnography, whereupon he composed more than one thousand Kontakia. In August 535, a catastrophic earthquake devastated a substantial portion of Constantinople, which was subsequently commemorated each[^633]
