Saint Romanos, who frequently incorporated references to contemporary historical events into his compositions, commemorated this earthquake in a hymn (styled a "Psalm") chanted on Wednesday of the third week of the Great Fast. Because this Kontakion was composed under the vivid and immediate impression of the disaster, and because no historical event occurring after 535 is mentioned anywhere in the corpus of Saint Romanos, it is reasonably concluded that he reposed shortly after that date. Notable antecedents to the literary form of the Kontakion existed in Syriac Christian poetry, with which Saint Romanos, being of Syrian provenance, was intimately familiar. His supreme achievement lay in translating and adapting these Semitic poetic structures into the spirit, elegance, and melody of Byzantine hymnography, thereby establishing an entirely new genre in the liturgical life of Constantinople. Scholars identify three primary genres of classical Syriac poetry: the *Memra*, the *Madrasha*, and the *Sogitha*. The *Memra*, or metrical homily, served as the principal structural prototype for the Kontakion: like the *Memra*, the Kontakion occupied a fixed station in the Morning Office (Matins) immediately following the reading of the Holy Gospel, providing an extensive poetic amplification and paraphrase of the sacred scriptural narrative. Yet an essential distinction remains: while the Syriac *Memra* remained strictly an homiletic discourse in verse, the Kontakion in the masterworks of Saint Romanos transcends mere moral exhortation and, by absorbing the lyricism of the *Madrasha* and the dramatic dialogue of the *Sogitha*, blossoms into a sublime theological contemplation and celebration of the sacred mystery of the feast. (Adapted from *A History of Byzantine Music and Hymnography* by Egon Wellesz).

units.slavonic_text: TD-90
units.english_text: Originally, the Kontakion was an extended liturgical poem comprising eighteen to twenty-four stanzas, whose substantial length necessitated the use of a continuous parchment scroll. Saint Romanos the Melodist (+c. 556) stands as the pre-eminent master of these monumental compositions. Over time, these extended hymnographic cycles fell out of active liturgical performance in the Byzantine Rite. Today, what survives in the printed liturgical books under the designation of **Kontakion** represents only the brief introductory strophe (the ancient Proimion) accompanied by the initial **Ikos** (*Οἶκος*). In the current liturgical ordo, the Kontakion is chanted following Ode 6 of the Canon at Matins (jointly with the Ikos), at the Little Hours, and following the Dismissal Troparia at the Divine Liturgy. The Kontakion is never chanted at Vespers.[^634]

units.slavonic_text: year on the day it had happened by hymns and prayers. Romanos, who in his Kontakia frequently alludes to contemporary events, mentions the earthquake in a 'Psalm', which was sung on Wednesday of the third week of Lent. Since the Kontakion was obviously written under the immediate impression of the disaster, and no event later than the disaster is mentioned in a poem by Romanus, it may be assumed that he died shortly after 535. Antecedents of the Kontakion existed in Syriac ecclesiastical poetry, and it may also be assumed that Romanus, being of Syrian origin, was well acquainted with them. It was his great achievement to have adapted them to the spirit of Byzantine hymnography, and to have introduced the new form of ecclesiastical poetry into the liturgy of Constantinople. Here follows a comparison of the main forms of Syriac poetry the Memra, Madrasha, and Sogitha. The memra, the poetical homily, must be regarded as the most important for the development of the Kontakion. Like the Memra, the Kontakion had its place in the Morning Office after the reading of the Gospel and paraphrased the text of the Scriptures. There is, however, a noticeable difference between Memra and Kontakion. The Memra invariably has the character of a sermon, while the Kontakion in the most perfect hymns of Romanos loses this homiletic character and, by assimilating elements from Madrasha and Sogitha, develops into a poetical description of the object of the feast on which it is sung. (This foregoing description is from A History of Byzantine Music and Hymnography by E. Wellesz). Originally, the Kontakion was a hymn of many stanzas (18-24) whose lengthy text indeed required the use of a scroll. St. Romanos the Melodist (+556) is the most famous composer of such lengthy, free-style hymns. The hymns in their original, lengthy form have fallen into disuse in Orthodox worship. What now remains in the liturgical books as Kontakia are merely the short, preliminary stanzas of the earlier and longer hymns. The Kontakion is sung after Ode 6 (together with the Ikos, (or first strophe of the more ancient, lengthy kontakion) of the Canon at Matins, during the Hours, and after the Troparia at the Divine Liturgy. The Kontakion is not sung at Vespers. (Modified from APL)

units.english_text: **KUVUKLION** (*Κουβούκλιον, τό*): A ceremonial canopy structure, typically carved of wood, representing the Holy Sepulchre and Tomb of Christ. During the solemn Vespers and Matins services of Great and Holy Friday and Holy Saturday, it is erected upon the Soleas (or before the Tetrapod) to enshrine the sacred cloth icon of the entombed Savior, the **Plashchanytsia** (*Epitaphios* / *᾿Επιτάφιος*).

units.english_text: **LAMB** (*᾿Αμνός, ὁ*; Slav. *Agnets* / *Агнецъ*): The square Eucharistic host stamped and extracted from the principal liturgical loaf (**Prosphora** / *Προσφορά*), bearing the sacred cruciform inscription **IC XC NIKA** (Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Νικᾷ, "Jesus Christ Conquers"). This consecrated portion is excised with the holy Lance during the Office of Preparation (**Proskomide** / *Προσκομιδή*) for subsequent Eucharistic consecration at the Divine Liturgy. The Holy Scriptures designate Christ as the "Lamb of God" (John 1:29, 1:36), fulfilling the prophetic vision of Isaiah concerning the suffering Servant: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before its shearer, so He opens not His mouth" (Isaiah 53:7 [LXX 53:7]).

Agnec: Is the raised stamped section of the sacramental bread loaf (PROSPHORA) indicated by the stamp ΙΣ ΧΣ ΝΙ KA, which abbreviate the Greek words Jesus Christ Conquers. This section is removed from the Prosphora during the PROSKOMIDI for later consecration in the Divine Liturgy. The New Testament refers to Christ as the "Lamb of God" (John 1:29 and 1:36). The Prophet Isaiah also refers to the coming Messiah as "the Lamb." (Isaiah 53)

units.english_text: **LITI** (*Λιτή, ἡ*; Slav. *Litiya* / *Литія*): (1) Liturgically, an earnest, prolonged entreaty and supplication. It denotes the solemn liturgical procession of the sacred ministers and choir into the Narthex of the church during Great Vespers on the eve of great feasts, accompanied by the chanting of festive idiomela stichera, lengthy petitions for ecclesiastical and civil well-being, and the solemn blessing of five loaves, wheat, wine, and oil (Artoklasia). During this procession, proper **Stichera at the Liti** are chanted according to the feast. (2) Also designates a brief memorial service for the departed, consisting of the Trisagion Prayers, the funeral Dismissal Troparia, and a memorial litany.

units.english_text: **LITURGICAL COLORS**: Across the Byzantine liturgical tradition, shared by Eastern Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic Churches, no rigid, uniform color canon exists comparable to the post-Tridentine Western rubrical system. In the authoritative Greek Typikon of George Violakis, rubrical directions regarding vesture focus primarily upon specifying "bright" (*λευκά* / light) or "dark" (*σκοτεινά*) vestments. In modern Greek practice, deep red, maroon, or burgundy vestments are customary for solemn feast days, while a broad spectrum of colors is employed on other occasions, with gold and white prevailing as standard festive tones.

units.slavonic_text: LITURGICAL COLORS: In the Orthodox Byzantine Rite, which is used by all the member churches of the Eastern Orthodox Church and by the Greek-Catholic Churches (Eastern Catholic Churches of Byzantine Rite), there is no universal system of colors being used. In the Typikon of today's Greek Orthodox Church little is said about liturgical colors except for specifying “light” or “dark” vestments. In the Greek tradition, maroon or burgundy are common for solemn feast days, and a wide variety of colors are used at other times, the most common of which are gold and white.

units.english_text: example, are associated with the Paschal season (although in certain local traditions red vestments are donned at Pascha), symbolizing the radiant joy of Christ's resurrection and the destruction of death, echoing the apocalyptic vision: "He that overcomes, the same shall be clothed in white raiment" (Rev. 3:5). Green, signifying life, spiritual rebirth, and renewal, is appointed for Pentecost and the feast of the Holy Trinity, symbolizing the descent of the Holy Spirit, as well as for the feasts of venerable monastic saints who dwelt in the wilderness. Red vestments are worn at the Nativity of Christ, the feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and on the commemorations of holy martyrs who shed their blood for Christ. Blue is traditionally appointed for feasts of the Most Holy Theotokos, honoring Her as the Queen of Heaven. Deep purple or dark crimson is worn during the Great Fast as a solemn remembrance of the passion of Christ and the purple robe with which the Roman soldiers mockingly clothed Him before His Crucifixion. Outside of specific festal seasons, gold vestments serve as the universal standard, evoking the heavenly Jerusalem: "and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass" (Rev. 21:18). Liturgical vesture not only elevates the visual beauty of divine worship, but transforms the ministers—from the presiding hierarch to the youngest acolyte—into living icons of the heavenly court.

units.slavonic_text: TD-93
units.english_text: Historically, six principal liturgical colors developed in Byzantine practice: white, green, purple, red, blue, and gold. In later centuries, black vestments were introduced, particularly for weekday services in Great Lent. In various regional customs, amber, saffron, or rust-colored vestments are also utilized. Liturgical commentators have attributed rich theological symbolism to these colors: white represents the uncreated light of the Divine Energies; green represents the life-creating power of the Holy Spirit and the life-giving Cross; purple signifies the suffering and sovereignty of Christ; deep red recalls the Precious Blood shed upon the Cross and the witness of the martyrs; blue honors the virginity and heavenly glory of the Mother of God; and gold represents the splendor of the Kingdom of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit. While in ancient Eastern tradition white was the mourning color of Christian burial—signifying the hope of resurrection—black became widespread in the West and eventually entered Slavic funeral usage. In traditional Ruthenian and Slavic lands, red (*krasny*) is the color of festal majesty, spiritual beauty, and joy. None of these specific color systems is mandated in the statutory text of the Typikon, and diverse local traditions preserve distinctive usages.[^637]

units.slavonic_incipit: example, are associated with the Paschal
units.slavonic_text: example, are associated with the Paschal period (although in some churches the tradition for Paschas is to use red), as the brightest and most radiant celebration of the vanquishing of death. It is a visual reminder that, “He that overcomes, the same shall be clothed in white raiment” (Rev. 3:5). Green, the color of life and spring, is used at Pentecost to symbolize the beginning of the life of the Church. It is also used on feasts of certain saints, particular monk saints, who dwelt in the wilderness. Red is used at the Nativity, on the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and for Martyrs. Blue is the traditional color of the Mother of God, as she is the Queen of Heaven. Deep purple is used during Lent as a reminder of the purple robe which the soldiers put on Christ to mock Him before His Passion. Outside of festal periods gold is used to remind us of the heavenly Jerusalem: “and the city was pure gold” (Rev. 21:18). The use of vestments, then, not only adds to the visual splendor of the church, but this use has a far greater significance in transforming the celebrants, even young acolytes, into representatives of the Kingdom of heaven, reflecting that otherworldliness which is the essence of Orthodoxy. (From a talk given at the St. Herman Winter Pilgrimage, Redding, California, 1983).

units.english_text: **LITURGICAL YEAR** (*Λειτουργικὸν ἔτος, τό*): The annual cycle of ecclesiastical seasons, festal periods, fasts, and commemorations in the Eastern Church governing the celebration of feasts, memorials, daily scriptural lections, and proper hymnography. In the Byzantine Rite, the liturgical year commences on September 1, designated the Feast of the Indiction and the beginning of the Ecclesiastical New Year, and concludes on August 31. Distinct liturgical colors and propers correspond to each liturgical cycle throughout the church year.

units.english_text: The liturgical calendars of the Christian East and West share a common historical foundation and structural logic, though divergent calendar reckonings (Julian and Gregorian) and computational methods for calculating the date of Pascha create variations in festal dates. Feasts that fall upon a fixed calendar date every year (such as the Nativity of Christ on December 25 or the Dormition on August 15) are designated **Immovable Feasts** (*᾿Ακίνητοι ἑορταί*), whereas feasts whose annual celebration depends upon the moveable date of Holy Pascha (such as the Ascension, Pentecost, and all services of the Triodion and Pentecostarion) are designated **Moveable Feasts** (*Κινηταὶ ἑορταί*).

units.slavonic_text: LITURGICAL YEAR (λειτουργικὸν ἔτος, τό): The liturgical year, also known by some as the Christian year or church year, consists of the cycle of liturgical seasons in the Eastern Orthodox Churches which determines when Feasts, Memorials, Commemorations, etc., are to be observed and which portions of Scripture are to be read. This cycle is reckoned as beginning on September 1, the date of Indiction, and ending August 31. Also, various and distinct liturgical colors may be used in connection with the different seasons of the liturgical year as mentioned under LITURGICAL COLORS.

units.slavonic_text: The dates of the festivals or feasts vary somewhat between the Eastern Orthodox churches and the western Church (Roman Catholic, Anglican, and Protestant) though the sequence and logic is the same. In both East and West, the dates of many festivals vary between years, in most cases because of the variation in the always shifting date of Pascha (Easter). In the Greek Orthodox Church those feasts which occur on the same date each year are known as IMMOVABLE FEASTS, while those that depend on the shifting date of Pascha (Easter) are called MOVEABLE FEASTS.

units.slavonic_text: 2) The Divine Liturgy of our Father among the Saints, Basil the Great, was the Bishop of Caesaria in Cappadocia from A.D. 370 to 379. According to the tradition of the Eastern Orthodox Church, this Liturgy is practically the work of St. Basil, due allowance being made for changes and amelioration over the course of time. This liturgy is older than either of the other two Byzantine Liturgies (that of Chrysostom and that of the Presanctified Gifts). It is normally celebrated ten times during the year as follows: On the Feast of St. Basil, 1 January. On the first five Sundays of the Great 40-day Fast (Lent). On Holy Thursday, usually as a Vesperal Liturgy. On Holy Saturday, usually as a Vesperal Liturgy. On the eve (PARAMONI) of the Nativity of Christ (Christmas) On the eve (PARAMONI) of the Feast of Theophany (Epiphany). units.slavonic_text: Of the foregoing liturgies, the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, is traditionally thought to be a shortened form of the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil. Both are related to the earlier Divine Liturgy of St. James of Jerusalem, which is traditionally attributed to St. James or James the Just, the first bishop of Jerusalem (not to be confused with James, the brother of Saint John the Evangelist). Today, the Liturgy of St. James is celebrated once a year on his feast day and traditionally only in Jerusalem. Today, it is occasionally celebrated in other places as well.
units.english_text: Among these liturgical rites, the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom represents an anaphoral abbreviation and condensation of the earlier liturgical tradition exemplified in the Liturgy of Saint Basil, both of which share ancestral roots with the ancient Liturgy of Saint James of Jerusalem.[^639]

units.english_text: **The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts**: Celebrated on Wednesdays and Fridays of the Great Fast, on Thursday of the Great Canon, and on the first three days of Great and Holy Week (Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday). This rite is structurally an Office of Solemn Vespers conjoined to a communion rite, wherein the faithful receive the Holy Mysteries previously consecrated at the Divine Liturgy on the preceding Sunday and reserved upon the Holy Table. Sacerdotal tradition attributes the compilation and ordering of this service to Saint Gregory the Dialogist (Pope of Rome).

units.slavonic_text: TD-96
units.english_text: The Great Fast is fundamentally an "aliturgical" season on weekdays, meaning that the full celebration of the Eucharistic sacrifice with its festal, resurrectal character is precluded on ordinary Lenten days and reserved for Saturdays and Sundays. The celebration of the Presanctified Liturgy was instituted to strengthen the faithful through frequent reception of Holy Communion during their ascetic struggle without interrupting the penitential character of the fast.

units.slavonic_text: The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, served on Wednesdays and Fridays during the Great Fast (Great Lent) and on the first three days of Holy Week is essentially the office of Vespers with an appended communion service, as the Holy Gifts were already consecrated and reserved for later use on the previous Sunday. It is traditionally attributed to St. Gregory the Dialogist.
units.english_text: **LONCHI** (*Λόγχη, ἡ*; Slav. *Kopíye* / *Копіе* / Lance or Spear): A sacred liturgical implement consisting of a small, double-edged steel blade mounted upon a wooden or metal handle terminating in a cross. The priest employs the holy Lance during the Office of Preparation (**Proskomide**) to excise the **Lamb** (*᾿Αμνός*) and particles from the loaves of **Prosphora** (*Προσφορά*). The piercing action of the Lance mystically commemorates the Roman soldier piercing the side of Christ hanging upon the Cross, from which flowed blood and water (John 19:34).

units.slavonic_incipit: Lent is generally a period called
units.slavonic_text: Lent is generally a period called “aliturgical,” which means that the celebration of the Divine Liturgy and the festive manner of its celebration in honor of the Resurrection is limited to Sundays. During the week the celebration of the Liturgy of the Presanctified is prescribed to allow more frequent communion of the faithful.
units.english_text: **MAKARISMOS, MAKARISMOI** (*Μακαρισμός, ὁ· pl. Μακαρισμοί, οἱ*; Slav. *Blazhenni* / *Блаженни*): The Beatitudes; the eight evangelical blessings pronounced by Christ in His Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5:3–12). In the Byzantine Rite, the Beatitudes constitute the standard Third Antiphon at the Divine Liturgy, interspersed with Troparia from the Oktoechos or the feast. The term also designates the formal patriarchal address "Your Beatitude" (*Μακαριώτατε*). Special hymnographic Beatitudes are likewise appointed for specific solemn offices, such as the Twelve Passion Gospels on the evening of Great and Holy Thursday. See **BEATITUDES**.

units.slavonic_text: LONCHI (Λόγχη, ἡ): A small knife or lance with a triangular-shaped, double edged tip at one end and a cross on the handle at the other end, used by the priest to cut out the particles of the altar bread (PROSFORA) used in the service of the Preparation of the Holy Gifts (see PROSKOMIDI). The Lonchi used here commemorates the piercing by a soldier of the side of Christ hanging on the cross.
units.english_text: **MANDYAS** (*Μανδύας, ὁ*; Slav. *Mantiya* / *Мантія*): The monastic mantle or episcopal cloak, worn by bishops as their solemn non-eucharistic and processional vesture. Crafted of rich purple or crimson fabric, the episcopal mandyas features long flowing trains, red and white horizontal stripes representing the streams of divine teaching (*potamoi* / *струи*), and four embroidered square tablets or medallions at the neck and hem depicting the Four Holy Evangelists (or seraphim). It fastens at the neck and lower front. (See also under **VESTMENTS: NON-LITURGICAL ATTIRE OF THE CLERGY**).

In traditional monasteries it is celebrated daily in the early morning so as to conclude at sunrise.

units.slavonic_text: TD-97
units.english_text: Matins is the longest and most complex service of the daily cycle. It is normally celebrated in the early morning, on occasion preceded by the Midnight Office, and regularly followed immediately by the First Hour. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as the principal component of an All-Night Vigil on the preceding evening, conjoined with Great Vespers and the First Hour. In the Greek parish tradition, Matins is normally celebrated in the morning immediately preceding the Divine Liturgy. In the Slavic tradition, an All-Night Vigil is celebrated on every Saturday evening preceding Sunday.

units.slavonic_text: MATINS (ὄρθρος, ὁ). Slav. Utrenya: Matins is a western term which, in Greek Orthodox Churches, is known by the Greek term ORTHROS meaning "early dawn" or "daybreak." A part of the daily cycle of services, it is the last of the four night offices, which include Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office and Matins. In traditional monasteries it is celebrated daily so as to end at sunrise.
units.english_text: The fixed psalmody of the service comprises primarily the Six Psalms, fixed morning psalms, and litanies. The variable hymnography of Matins is drawn principally from the canons and hymns of the **Paraklitiki** (**Oktoechos** / *᾿Οκτώηχος*), the liturgical volume containing the hymnographic cycle for each of the eight Tones across each day of the week, cycling over eight weeks, and from the **Menaion** (*Μηναῖον*, pl. **Menaia** / *Μηναῖα*), the twelve monthly volumes comprising the propers for each calendar day of the ecclesiastical year. During the Great Fast (Lent), portions of the Oktoechos and Menaion are superseded by the proper hymnography of the **Triodion** (*Τριῴδιον*), and during the Paschal Season by the joyful hymnography of the **Pentecostarion** (*Πεντηκοστάριον*). On Sundays, Matins also features Gospel lections and proper hymns from the eleven-part cycle of Resurrectional Gospels (*῾Εωθινὰ Εὐαγγέλια*).

units.slavonic_text: Matins is the longest and most complex of the daily cycle of services. It is normally celebrated in the early morning, sometimes preceded by the Midnight Office, and usually followed by the First Hour. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as part of an All-Night Vigil on the evening before, combined with Vespers and the First Hour. In the Greek parish tradition, Matins is normally served just before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy on Sunday morning. In the Slavic tradition, an All-Night Vigil is served every Sunday (commencing on Saturday evening).

units.slavonic_text: The fixed portion of the service is composed primarily of psalms and litanies. The variable parts of Matins are composed primarily of HYMNS and CANONS from the PARAKLITIKI (OKTOICHOS), a book containing a cycle of hymns for each of eight modes for each day of the week, covering eight weeks), and from the MINEA, i.e., 12 books containing hymns for each of the 12 months of the year. During Great Lent, some of the portions from the Oktoichos and the Minea are replaced by hymns from the book called the TRIODION and during the Paschal Season with material from the book called the PENTIKOSTARION. On Sundays there are also Gospel readings and hymns from the eleven-part cycle of Resurrectional Gospels.

units.english_text: **MEGA SYNODIKON** (*Μέγα Συνοδικόν, τό*): A Synodikon is defined as a formal conciliar decree and synodal proclamation promulgated in churches summarizing the dogmatic definitions and canonical decisions of a council of bishops. With the qualifying epithet *Mega* ("Great"), it designates pre-eminently the solemn liturgical text proclaimed in the Eastern Church on the Sunday of Orthodoxy (the First Sunday of the Great Fast), originally compiled in 843 under Patriarch Methodios I upon the definitive triumph over Iconoclasm.

units.english_text: **MEGALYNARION** (*Μεγαλυνάριον, τό*; Slav. *Velichanie* / *Величаніе*): A hymn of praise and magnification in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos or a sacred feast, chanted following the epiklesis and the hymn **"We praise Thee, we bless Thee"** (*Σὲ ὑμνοῦμεν*) during the Anaphora of the Divine Liturgy. The Megalynarion is frequently the model strophe or **Heirmos** (*Εἱρμός*) of the Ninth Ode of the Canon appointed at Matins for the feast, such as **"Shine, shine, O New Jerusalem"** (*Φωτίζου, φωτίζου*) from the Ninth Ode of the Paschal Canon. On other occasions, the Megalynarion is an independent festive composition, such as **"All of creation rejoices in thee"** (*«᾿Επὶ σοὶ χαίρει»*) chanted at the Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great. The Megalynarion standardly chanted at the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom is **"It is truly meet"** (*«῎Αξιόν ἐστιν»*).[^642]

units.english_text: **MEGALYNARION AT THE DIPTYCHA** (*Μεγαλυνάριον εἰς τὰ Δίπτυχα*): A proper Megalynarion dedicated to a specific saint or sacred commemoration, chanted in addition to the customary Megalynarion of the Divine Liturgy. It is sung by the choir immediately preceding its liturgical response **"And each and all"** (*«Καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»*). For the proper rubrical order, see the *Ieratikon* (ed. Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, 1977 and 1987, p. 182). The *Engolpion tu Anagnostu* (*Manual of the Church Reader*, ed. Apostoliki Diakonia, Athens, c. 1970, p. 83) records a modern variant custom wherein the Megalynarion at the Diptycha is sung immediately preceding the priest's intercessory petition: **"Remember also, Lord, those whom each of us calls to mind and all Your people"** (*«Καὶ ὧν ἕκαστος κατὰ διάνοιαν ἔχει καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»*). The Typikon of George Violakis references only two such Diptych Megalynaria: for Saint Basil the Great on January 1 (pp. 137–138, § 3), and for the Life-Giving Spring (**Zoodochos Pege** / *Ζωοδόχος Πηγή*) on Bright Friday following Pascha (pp. 374–375, § 8). The *Engolpion tu Anagnostu*, by contrast, provides several additional compositions, composed after the publication of the 1888 Typikon.

units.slavonic_text: *MEGALYNARION AT THE DIPTYCHA (Μεγαλυνάριον εἰς τὰ Δίπτυχα): A Megalynarion dedicated to a specific saint or sacred object, sung in addition to the Megalynarion of the Divine Liturgy. It is sung by the choir immediately before its response "Ke panton ke pason" («Καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν»). For the order, see the Ieratikon, ed. Apostoliki Diakonia (Athens, 1977 and 1987), p. 182. The Egkolpion tu Anagnostu (Manual of the Church Reader), ed. Apostoliki Diakonia (Athens, ca. 1970), p. 83, proposes a less common yet recent practice: that the Megalynarion at the Diptycha be sung immediately before the priest's petition "Remember also, Lord, those whom each of us calls to mind and all Your people." («Καὶ ὧν ἕκαστος κατὰ διάνοιαν ἔχει καὶ πάντων καὶ πασῶν.») Violakis' Typikon refers to only two such Megalynaria: for St. Basil, 1 January (pp. 137-138, ¶ 3); and for the Zoodochos Pigi, Friday following Easter Sunday (pp. 374-375, ¶ 8). The Egkolpion tu Anagnostu, on the other hand, contains several of them, possibly written after the publication of the Typikon (1888).

units.english_text: **MEGAS SYNAXARISTIS** (*Μέγας Συναξαριστής, ὁ*): The Great Synaxaristes; a monumental twelve-volume compilation of the lives of the holy saints, arranged sequentially according to their calendar commemorations across each month of the ecclesiastical year. A concise abridgment of these hagiographical biographies is contained in the liturgical book entitled the **Synaxarion** (*Συναξάριον*), and corresponding summaries are likewise printed within the twelve volumes of the **Menaia**.

units.slavonic_text: MEGAS SYNAXARISTIS (Μέγας Συναξαριστής, ὁ): An extensive history of the lives of the saints in 12 volumes, organized into collections arranged by the month in which the saint is celebrated. A brief summary of these biographies is presented in a service book of the church called the SYNAXARION. Similar brief summaries are also included in the 12 books of the MINEA.
units.english_text: **MESOPENTIKOSTI** (*Μεσοπεντηκοστή, ἡ*; Slav. *Prepolovenie Piatidesiatnitsy* / *Преполовеніе Пятидесятницы*): Mid-Pentecost; the feast marking the midpoint of the fifty-day joyful season between Holy Pascha and Pentecost Sunday. The Feast of Mid-Pentecost is celebrated on Wednesday following the Sunday of the Paralytic (the Fourth Week of Pascha).

units.english_text: **METANIA** (*μετάνοια, ἡ*; Slav. *poklon* / *поклонъ*): An external bodily act of penitence and reverence, signifying spiritual repentance. The term designates either a waist bow (lesser metania) wherein the fingers of the right hand touch the ground, or a full prostration (great metania) cast upon the pavement in humble adoration and penitence before the Holy Mysteries or holy icons.

units.english_text: **MINEON, pl. MINEA** (*Μηναῖον, τό· Μηναῖα, τά*; Slav. *Mineya* / *Минея*): The **Menaion**, derived from the Greek noun for "month" (*μήν*). The Menaia comprise the liturgical volumes containing the variable offices for each calendar day of the twelve months of the liturgical year. For smaller parishes lacking the complete twelve-volume set of the Menaia, there exists in both Greek and Slavonic tradition a single-volume compendium containing common offices for each class of saint, designated the **General Menaion** (*᾿Ανθολόγιον* / Slav. *Obshtaya Mineya* / *Общая Минея*). The Greek and Slavonic General Menaia diverge in content: the Slavonic edition provides expanded propers, including complete All-Night Vigil texts for each order of saint, as well as common propers for feasts of the Lord and the Mother of God.

units.slavonic_text: *MINEON, pl. MINEA (Μηναῖον, τὸ· Μηναῖα, τά) Slav. Mineya: From the Greek word for 'month'. The Minea are books containing the services for each day of the month of the calendar year. There are thus twelve volumes of the Mineon. For places without a full set of Minea there exists in both Greek and Slav. a volume containing general offices for each category of saint called the General Menaion. The contents of the Greek and Slavonic General Menaia are not identical, the Slavonic containing more offices, as well as texts for a full Vigil for each category of saint, and also for the Lord and the Mother of God. units.english_text: **MITRA** (*μίτρα, ἡ*; Slav. *Venets* / *Вѣнецъ* or *Mitra* / *Митра*): The Byzantine Miter or Crown; an ornate, domed liturgical head covering worn by bishops (and by archimandrites or mitred archpriests by special award). It is richly embellished with embroidered or enameled icons of Christ and the Four Evangelists and decorated with precious jewels and pearls, surmounted by the Holy Cross. It symbolizes the Crown of Thorns, the imperial majesty of the King of Kings, and the episcopal authority conferred upon the hierarch at his consecration.[^645]

'Apolytikia') chanted at the Small Entrance of the Divine Liturgy.

units.slavonic_text: (1.) Irmologic (εἱρμολογικόν): The melodies are syllabic in character; that is, nearly each syllable of the text is sung to a different interval, lasting one and sometimes two beats. They are chanted in a rapid tempo, allegretto to vivace, often in cut-time. A good example of the Irmologic style is that used for the eight Resurrection Dismissal Hymns (APOLYTIKIA) sung at the SMALL ENTRANCE in the DIVINE LITURGY.
units.english_text: 3. **Papadic** (*παπαδικόν*): The melodies are highly melismatic, expansive, and elaborate. The tempo is stately and slow, though certain ornate passages are executed more rapidly. The Cherubic Hymn (*Χερουβικόν*) and the Communion Hymns (*Κοινωνικά*) serve as classic models of the Papadic genre. The particular melodic style chosen alters and expands the modal characteristics outlined above.

units.slavonic_text: (2.) Sticheraric (στιχηραρικόν): the melodies are more ornate than in the Irmologic style; each syllable is given the average of two intervals and one to three beats. The tempo ranges generally from allegretto to andante. The sticheraric style is found in hymn types such as the Kekragaria in Vespers, Pasapnoaria in Orthros, and some of the Megalynaria in the Divine Liturgy.
units.english_text: This eightfold modal classification system in Byzantine chant and hymnology gave rise to the weekly cycle of the Eight Tones. units.english_text: In Byzantine liturgical music, eight canonical Tones are recognized: Tone 1 (Mode I), Tone 2 (Mode II), Tone 3 (Mode III), Tone 4 (Mode IV), Tone 5 (Mode I Plagal), Tone 6 (Mode II Plagal), Tone 7 (Varys / Grave Tone), and Tone 8 (Mode IV Plagal). All hymnography of the Byzantine liturgical tradition is set within one of these eight Tones. The Eight Tones constitute the foundational architectural framework around which the Church organizes the daily offices and their hymnographic cycles throughout the ecclesiastical year. This structural logic is codified within the principal liturgical book of the daily cycle, the **Paraklitiki** (**Megali Oktoichos** / *Μεγάλη ᾿Οκτώηχος*).

units.english_text: The Paraklitiki contains the appointed services and propers for every day of the week across the year. It is divided into eight modal sections or tone periods (*περίοδοι τῶν ἤχων*), each comprising the complete services of a full week from Sunday through Saturday. Each of the eight modal sections is sung in one of the eight Tones, advancing sequentially from Tone 1 through Tone 8. When the entire eight-week sequence has concluded, the cycle recommences with Tone 1, repeating continuously throughout the church year.

units.slavonic_text: In Byzantine music, there are eight modes: First, Second, Third, Fourth, First Plagal, Second Plagal, Varys (Third Plagal), and Fourth Plagal. All the hymnology of the Byzantine Greek Orthodox Church is sung using one of the eight modes. The eight modes, in fact, serve as an overall structure within which the church has organized its daily services and their extensive hymnology. This structure can be seen in one of the most important liturgical books of the church, the PARAKLITIKI, also called the Megali Oktoichos (the Great Book of the Eight Modes).

units.slavonic_incipit: The PARAKLITIKI contains the appointed services
units.slavonic_text: The PARAKLITIKI contains the appointed services and the hymnology for every day of the year. It is divided into eight sections or modal periods (περίοδοι τῶν ἤχων), each containing the services of one week, subdivided into its individual days from Sunday to Saturday. Each of the eight sections, or modal periods, is sung in one of the eight modes, moving progressively from Mode I to Mode IV Plagal. When the whole sequence of the eight modes has been gone through, a new one begins with Mode I, repeating itself as a cycle throughout the church year. This cycle of modes is initiated on each Sunday of Pascha (Easter) with Mode I, as is evident by the predominant use of Mode I in the Eni (Αἶνοι) or Hymns of Praise of the Easter Service sung in Mode I, before the Doxology in the Orthros. Through similar borrowings from the Paraklitiki in their services, the days in the week following Easter fall into the following modal pattern: Easter Monday—Mode II; Easter Tuesday—Mode III; Easter Wednesday—Mode IV; Easter Thursday—Mode I Plagal; Easter Friday—Mode II Plagal; Mode Varys (the Grave Mode) is omitted; Easter Saturday—Mode IV Plagal. The Second Sunday of Easter (Sunday of Thomas) returns to Mode I. From this point on, the modal pattern becomes weekly, the mode changing at the Vespers Service the night before each successive Sunday. Thus, the Third Sunday of Easter (Sunday of the Myrrh Bearers) moves to Mode II, and so on in the Sundays that follow, until Mode IV Plagal is completed. When Mode I is resumed, a new modal sequence begins, repeating itself cyclically until the Fifth Sunday of Lent of the following year. Palm Sunday,
units.english_text: On the Second Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of Saint Thomas), the weekly cycle returns to Tone 1. From that day forward, the modal pattern shifts weekly, changing at Great Vespers on Saturday evening before each Sunday. Thus, the Third Sunday of Pascha (Sunday of the Myrrh-Bearing Women) is appointed in Tone 2, and so forth in unbroken progression through the subsequent Sundays until Tone 8 is completed. Upon reaching Tone 1 again, a new modal cycle begins, repeating cyclically until the Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast of the following year. Palm Sunday,[^647]

units.english_text: **MOVEABLE FEAST** (*κινητὴ ἑορτή, ἡ*): A liturgical feast whose celebration is not tied to a fixed calendar date of the civil or ecclesiastical year. Moveable feasts are governed by the liturgical cycles of the **Triodion** and **Pentecostarion**, which together establish the liturgical framework of the Paschal cycle. This framework commences on the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and concludes on the Sunday of All Saints (the First Sunday after Pentecost). Every moveable feast stands in a fixed temporal relationship to the Sunday of Holy Pascha, which may occur between March 22 and April 25 on the Julian Reckoning (corresponding to April 4 and May 8 on the revised calendar). The precise calendar date for any moveable feast depends directly upon the date of Pascha in that particular year. (For the earliest and latest possible calendar limits of all moveable feasts, see scholarly liturgical tables and typikon guides).

units.slavonic_text: *MOVABLE FEAST (κινητὴ ἑορτή, ἡ): A feast that is not fixed to any particular calendar date of the LITURGICAL YEAR. Movable feasts occur within the periods of the TRIODION and PENTIKOSTARION, which constitute the whole framework of movable feasts. This framework begins with the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee and ends with the Sunday of All Saints. Each movable feast has a fixed relationship to the Sunday of Pascha (Easter), which in the Gregorian Calendar may occur as early as April 4 and as late as May 8. The day on which a particular movable feast may be celebrated depends, therefore, on the date on which the Sunday of Pascha (Easter) falls each year. (For the earliest and latest possible dates of all the movable feasts, see p. 284 of Bogdanos' The Byzantine Liturgy: Hymnology and Order. For the dates of both the movable and imovable feasts falling on Sundays in a particular year, see Schedule of Sunday Modes and Movable Feasts (A.D. 1992-2099), in Appendix D of the above Bogdanos book.

units.english_text: A third profound mystery is the divine action of the Holy Mysteries in uniting man unto God. In the Holy Eucharist, humble earthly gifts of bread and wine are transformed by the Holy Spirit into the true Body and the true Blood of Christ. Pronouncing over the bread and the chalice at the Mystical Supper: **"This is My Body... This is My Blood"**, Christ Himself instituted the Sacrament of Holy Communion for all generations. By receiving the Holy Mysteries, the Christian is united unto Christ, becoming a partaker of the Divine Nature through grace. The Church recognizes seven principal Holy Mysteries: Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist (Holy Communion), Holy Orders (Priesthood), Repentance (Confession), Holy Unction (Anointing of the Sick), and Holy Matrimony (Crowning). Through these Holy Mysteries, man is consecrated in faith and united unto God from birth until the conclusion of his earthly life.

units.slavonic_text: teries—Ἅγια Μυστήρια) refers to dogmas or tenets as well as sacramental rites (or Sacraments) of the Christian faith that are beyond full human comprehension, embraced through faith rather than through pure reason and objective knowledge. A central Christian mystery is the Incarnation and its "process," wherein God takes on the nature of His creature, man, uniting divine and human nature in the person of Jesus Christ. Another key mystery is that of the Resurrection: God, the creator of existence, being beyond the limits of non-existence, transcends death and rises above it. Another profound mystery is the nature and the function of the sacraments in their binding of man to God. For instance, man cannot understand how two humble, earthbound elements, bread and wine, are transubstantiated by the Holy Spirit into Christ's very body and blood. Pointing to the bread and the wine at the Last Supper, Christ said "this is my body...this is my blood," thus Himself instituting for posterity the Sacrament of Holy Communion. Today, by taking Holy Communion, the believer becomes one with God, partaking of His divine essence. The Orthodox Church celebrates seven Sacraments: Baptism, Chrismation, Communion (the Eucharist), Ordination (holy orders), Confession (Penance), Holy Unction, and Marriage. These sacraments sanctify and consecrate man in his faith and unite him with God, from birth to the end of his days on this earth.

units.slavonic_text: the dead as they light candles and reverence icons. In early Christianity, the Narthex provided the Church many a service. On Sundays, it was filled with catechumens (candidates for baptism) and penitents who would follow the Liturgy; the poor and the lame also might be present asking for alms. Church history also recounts many priests and hierarchs who would stand in the Narthex and block the entrance of the impious who had strayed from the Orthodox way.
units.english_text: **NAVE** (*ναός, ὁ*): The central hall of the church building situated between the Narthex (vestibule) and the Sanctuary. In Eastern Christian theology, the tripartite structure of the church building (Sanctuary, Nave, and Narthex) mirrors the tripartite structure of the ancient Tabernacle and Solomon's Temple (Holy of Holies, Holy Place, and Outer Court). While the Holy of Holies was entered exclusively by the High Priest once a year on the Day of Atonement, the Christian Sanctuary enshrines the Holy Table where the Eucharistic Sacrifice is continually offered, while the faithful assemble within the Nave to participate in the sacred mysteries.

units.slavonic_incipit: During the years of Turkish occupation
units.slavonic_text: During the years of Turkish occupation in Greece and the years of Communist rule throughout Eastern Europe, the Narthex was often used for another purpose. Christian children would gather at nightfall to learn of the faith from the priest and, in some cases, to even learn to read and write. These secret schools, for years, took place in the sanctity of the Narthex. Today, as we offer material gifts for the work of the Church, light candles, and reverence icons, catechumens are no longer found in their traditional place. We may however find catechetical resources for those wish to learn more about their faith (i.e. books, tapes, icons, prayer ropes, prosforo seals, all in a kiosk). The poor and the lame who, following services, would, with out-stretched hand, ask for alms no longer are present. Instead, a container or tray is provided for the collection of donations that are then offered to an outreach ministry.

The Holy of Holies was not used for daily worship and only the high priest could enter and then only once a year. The worship was held in the main part of the temple.

units.english_text: The distinguishing liturgical vestment of a bishop, worn over the shoulders, and the supreme emblem of his spiritual and pastoral authority. Originally fashioned from unbleached white sheep's wool, in modern usage it is tailored from rich liturgical brocade embroidered with crosses, worn encircling the neck and draped across the shoulders. Symbolizing the lost sheep that the Good Shepherd sought out and carried home upon His sacred shoulders, it signifies the bishop's pastoral vocation as a living icon of Christ.

units.slavonic_text: Sometimes spelled Omophorion Slav. Omofor, omoforij, nadramenia: A form of STOLE worn over the shoulders of a bishop. In the Orthodox tradition, the Omoforion is the distinguishing vestment of a bishop and the symbol of his spiritual and ecclesiastical authority. Originally of wool, today it is a band of brocade decorated with crosses and worn about the neck and shoulders. By symbolizing the lost sheep that is found and carried on the Good Shepherd's shoulders, it signifies the bishop's pastoral role as the icon of Christ.
units.english_text: While every Eastern bishop vests in the Omophorion, a corresponding vestment in Western Christianity is the archiepiscopal *pallium*, whose liturgical employment is governed by distinct canonical rubrics and limitations.

units.slavonic_text: Clergy and ecclesiastical institutions subject to a bishop's authority are often said to be "under his Omoforion".
units.english_text: The Omophorion exists in two distinct forms: the ancient **Great Omophorion** (*μέγα ὠμοφόριον*), which passes around the neck, folds across the breast, and descends past the knees in both front and back; and the **Small Omophorion** (*μικρὸν ὠμοφόριον*), which is simpler in form, passing around the neck and descending in front similar to an **Epitrachilion** (stole), yet broader and shorter, reaching just past the waist. Owing to the intricate arrangement of the Great Omophorion and the liturgical dignity of the episcopal rank, whenever the bishop vests in this Omophorion or removes it, he is assisted by two subdeacons.[^651]

units.english_text: During the Divine Liturgy, the rubrics prescribe that the bishop vest in and remove the Omophorion repeatedly. When first vested before the Liturgy, the subdeacons place the Great Omophorion upon him; subsequently, when the rubric calls for him to resume the Omophorion, it is replaced, for practical convenience, with the Small Omophorion. In local traditions where multiple hierarchs concelebrate, customary usage assigns the Great Omophorion exclusively to the principal presiding celebrant at appointed rubrical moments, while the other concelebrating bishops wear the Small Omophorion throughout the celebration.

units.slavonic_incipit: During the Divine Liturgy, the rubrics
units.slavonic_text: During the Divine Liturgy, the rubrics call for the bishop to put on and take off the Omoforion several times. When he is first vested, the subdeacons place the great Omoforion on him, but afterwards, when the rubric calls for him to wear the Omoforion, it is replaced, for the sake of convenience, with the small Omoforion. In some places, when several bishops celebrate together, it is now the custom for the chief celebrant to use the great Omoforion when called for, and the other bishops to wear the small Omoforion throughout.
units.english_text: In the early Church, the Omophorion consisted of a broad band of white wool embroidered with crosses and draped loosely around the neck, over the shoulders, and across the breast. The modern Roman pallium developed from this primitive Omophorion; however, in the West it evolved over the centuries into a narrow circular woolen band resting upon the shoulders, with short, weighted pendants hanging before and behind. In contemporary times, the papal pallium adopted by Pope Benedict XVI returned closer to the original form of the ancient Omophorion.

units.slavonic_incipit: Development: In the early church, the
units.slavonic_text: Development: In the early church, the Omoforion was a broad band of white wool ornamented with crosses and draped loosely over the neck, shoulders, and breast. The modern Roman pallium developed from this early Omoforion; however, in the West it has changed over the centuries into a circular, thin woolen garment for the shoulders, with short, weighted pendants before and behind. Today, the papal pallium adopted by Pope Benedict XVI is closer to the original Omoforion.
units.english_text: In the Christian East, the only structural alteration in the Omophorion has been an increase in its width and the adoption of embroidered silk and gold brocade in place of wool. Distinct historical testimony confirming the Omophorion as the liturgical vestment of the bishop is preserved in the epistles of Saint Isidore of Pelusium (c. 400). At that early date, it was already woven of wool and viewed as an explicit symbol of the pastoral duty of bishops shepherding their spiritual flocks. In the miniature illuminations of an Alexandrian World Chronicle, written probably during the fifth century, pictorial representations of the Omophorion already appear. In later centuries, the same depiction is found upon the celebrated ivory relief of Trier, depicting the solemn translation of holy relics. Among the sacred images dating from the seventh and eighth centuries in which the Omophorion appears are the frescoes uncovered in the church of Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum. The representation in these frescoes is essentially identical to its modern form.[^652]

units.slavonic_incipit: The only change in the Omoforion
units.slavonic_text: The only change in the Omoforion in the East has been the augmentation of its width, and the material from which it is made. We find distinct testimony to the existence of the Omoforion as a liturgical vestment of the bishop in Isidore of Pelusium about the year 400. It was made of wool and was already seen as symbolic of the duties of bishops as shepherds of their flocks. In the miniatures of an Alexandrian Chronicle of the World, written probably during the fifth century we already find pictorial representation of the Omoforion. In later times we meet the same representation on the renowned ivory tablet of Trier, depicting the solemn translation of relics. Among the pictures dating from the seventh and eighth centuries, in which we find the Omoforion, are the lately discovered frescoes in S. Maria, Antiqua in the Roman Forum. The representation in these frescoes is essentially the same as its present form.

units.english_text: The Omophorion probably evolved from the civil omophorion, a shoulder mantle or dignitary scarf in common civic use in late antiquity. Either the bishops introduced it directly by positive canonical enactment as a liturgical pontifical badge—a humeral cloth resembling the secular omophorion and bearing its name—or the civil omophorion was initially adopted by hierarchs as a simple dignitary ornament without special mystical signification, and in the course of time developed into an exclusively episcopal vestment, ultimately acquiring the canonical character of an episcopal badge of office.

units.slavonic_text: The Omoforion probably developed from the civil Omoforion, a shoulder garment or shawl in general use. Probably either the bishops introduced directly by a positive precept as a liturgical pontifical badge a humeral cloth resembling the ordinary Omoforion and called by that name, or the civil Omoforion was at first used by the bishops as a mere ornament without any special significance, but in the course of time gradually developed into a distinctively episcopal ornament, and finally assumed the character of an episcopal badge of office.

units.english_text: "Lord, bless those who praise Thee and sanctify those who trust in Thee. Save Thy people and bless Thine inheritance. Preserve the fullness of Thy Church; sanctify those who love the beauty of Thy house. Glorify them in return by Thy divine power, and forsake us not who place our hope in Thee. Grant peace unto Thy world, unto Thy churches, unto the priests, unto our civil authorities, unto the armed forces, and unto all Thy people. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from Thee, the Father of lights. And unto Thee we send up glory, thanksgiving, and worship, to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."

units.slavonic_text: *ORDER OF SERVICE (τάξις, ἡ): See TYPIKON. The sequence of hymns, prayers, and ritual actions in each service of the church as ordained by the Holy Synod of the Patriarchate of Constantinople and stipulated in the Typikon by George Violakis, published in 1888. Orders of service may be found also in the key service books of the church such as the Mineon, the Triodion, the Pentikostarion, the Paraklitiki, the Efchologion and the Ieratikon. Since its publication, the Typikon has been modified from time to time by the Ecumenical Patriarchate—a continuous practice of the church.

units.english_text: the word signifies "early Morning Prayer" or "daybreak." Orthros precedes the Divine Liturgy and constitutes the longest and most complex office of the daily cycle of services. In monasteries, Orthros is celebrated in the early morning and is regularly followed immediately by the First Hour. On Great Feasts, it is celebrated as an integral part of an All-Night Vigil commencing on the preceding evening, conjoined with Great Vespers and the First Hour. In Eastern parish tradition on Sunday mornings, Orthros is standardly served immediately preceding the Divine Liturgy. The office concludes with the Great Doxology and the festal **Dismissal Troparion** (lit. 'Apolytikion') of the day.

units.slavonic_text: the word means the 'early Morning Prayer'. Orthros precedes the Divine Liturgy and is the longest and most complex service of the daily cycle of services. In monasteries, Orthros is normally celebrated in the early morning and is usually followed by the First HOUR. On Great Feasts it is celebrated as part of an All-Night Vigil beginning the evening before, and is combined with Vespers and First Hour. In Greek parishes on Sunday morning, Orthros is normally served just before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy. The service concludes with the Doxology and the DISMISSAL HYMN (APOLYTIKION) of the then occurring feast.

units.english_text: **PARAKLITIKI** or **OKTOICHOS I MEGALI** (*Παρακλητικὴ* ἢ *᾿Οκτώηχος ἡ Μεγάλη*; Slav. *Oktoikh* / *Октоихъ*, *Paraklitik* / *Параклитикъ*): Both Greek titles designate the **GREAT OKTOECHOS**, one of the most foundational and ubiquitous liturgical volumes of the Church. units.english_text: **PATEN** (*Δισκάριον, τό*; Slav. *Diskos* / *Дискосъ*): The Diskos; a sacred shallow plate set upon a permanent base or foot, which holds the bread prepared at the Table of **Prothesis** during the rite of the **Proskomide** (Office of Oblation). It represents the cave of Bethlehem in which Christ was born and the tomb wherein He was laid. In its circular shape, it likewise symbolizes the heavens that encompass God.

units.english_text: The name Polyeleos is likewise given to the great chandelier suspended directly beneath the central dome of an Eastern church. It symbolizes Christ, the All-Merciful Light. When this chandelier was furnished with oil lamps, it was so designated because it employed "many oil lamps" (*poly-elaion* / *πολυέλαιον*). On the Holy Mountain of Athos, during solemn all-night vigils, the Polyeleos is illuminated and swung in a wide arc to spectacular effect at Vespers during the singing of **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Κύριε ἐκέκραξα*) and during the chanting of the Polyeleos at Matins. It is also illuminated at the Great Entrance on major feasts and at funeral services. Encircling the Polyeleos there often hangs a great brass or metal corona decorated with icons, normally depicting the Twelve Apostles, and surmounted by tapers. This circular chandelier is known as a **Choros** (*χορός*).

units.slavonic_text: reduced to one or two, accompanied by a MEGALYNARION. The name Polyeleos is also given to the great chandelier which hangs directly from the central dome of an Orthodox church. It symbolizes Christ, the 'all-merciful'. When this chandelier was furnished with oil lamps, it used 'many oil lamps' (Greek poly-eleos.) On the Holy Mountain of Athos, the monastic state in Greece, the Polyeleos is lighted and swung to spectacular effect in VESPERS at 'Lord, I have cried' and during the Polyeleos at great Vigils. It is also lighted at the Great Entrance on major Feasts, and also at funerals. Around the polyeleos there often hangs a great metal circle, decorated with icons, normally including the twelve Apostles, and surmounted by candles. This is known as a choros. (AE)

units.english_text: **PROFITOLOGION** (**PROPHETOLOGION** / *Προφητολόγιον, τό*; Slav. *Paremiynik* / *Паремійникъ*): The Old Testament Lectionary containing the scriptural readings (**Paroimiai** / *Παροιμίαι*, *Paremias*) assigned to Vespers, the Royal Hours, and other divine services throughout the ecclesiastical year. When a separate edition of this lectionary is unavailable, the appointed Old Testament readings are extracted from the **Menaia**, the **Triodion**, or the **Pentecostarion**. In English, classic collections containing these appointed lections include the *Divine Prayers and Services of the Catholic Orthodox Church of Christ* by Father Seraphim Nassar.

units.slavonic_text: PROFITOLOGION (Προφητολόγιον, τό) Slav. Paremijnik: Spelled by some as Prophetologion. This is a liturgical book that contains the Old Testament Lectionary readings assigned to Vespers and to other services during the Church year. Unfortunately, there has not been an edition of this book published in English. Old Testament readings are typically taken from the Mineon or other texts that contain these readings. There have also been texts containing the Lenten Lectionary which have been published in English. One classic text that contains the most commonly used portions of the entire Lectionary is the "Divine Prayers and Services of the Catholic Orthodox Church of Christ" by Fr. Seraphim Nassar. (From Orthodox Wiki)

units.english_text: **PROSFORA** (**PROSPHORA** / *Προσφορά, ἡ*; Slav. *Prosvira* / *Просвира*, *Proskura* / *Проскура*; lit. 'offering' or 'oblation'): A round loaf of leavened Eucharistic bread of pure wheat used in the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Upon its upper surface it bears a round relief seal, in the center of which is a square stamp inscribed with the sign of the Cross and the Greek letters **IC XC NIKA** (**ΙΣΧΣ ΝΙΚΑ**) at the four corners, representing *Jesus Christ Conquers* (**IC** being the abbreviation for Jesus, **XC** for Christ, and **NIKA** for Victor).

units.slavonic_text: PROSFORA (Προσφορά, ἡ): Lit. ‘offering’ or ‘oblation’. Slav. prosvira: A round loaf of leavened eucharistic bread used in the Consecration of the Holy Gifts. On its upper surface it bears a round stamp in the center of which is a square with the sign of the Cross and the Greek letters ΙΣΧΣ ΝΙΚΑ at the 4 corners; ΙΣ is the abbreviation for Jesus Christ, while NIKA is the abbreviation for Victor.
units.english_text: **PROS KYRION, TA** (*Τὰ Πρὸς Κύριον*): Lit. "Unto the Lord." A standard abbreviation commonly used in the **Typikon** for the entire Eighteenth Kathisma of the Septuagint (LXX) Psalter. This Kathisma encompasses a total of fifteen Psalms, from Psalm 119 to Psalm 133 inclusive (the Songs of Ascents). See also **PSALM 119**.

units.english_text: **PROSKOMIDI** (**PROSKOMIDE** / *Προσκομιδή, ἡ*; Slav. *Proskomidiya* / *Проскомидія*): Often rendered *Proskomide* or *Office of Oblation* (lit. 'the offering or bringing of gifts to God'). This is the Service of Preparation performed before the Divine Liturgy. In this service, the priest prepares the bread and the wine for the Holy Eucharist at the Table of **Prothesis** (**Table of Oblation**). This table or alcove is situated on the north side of the Sanctuary. The service standardly takes place while **Orthros** (Matins) is being chanted.

units.slavonic_text: *PROTHEORIA (προθεωρία, ἡ): Lit. Pre-theory. In his Typikon, George Violakis devotes the introduction—which he calls the Protheoria—to defining the general principles that he uses to order the services of the church. In the main body of his Typikon, he applies these principles in a detailed fashion to the order of service of each specific feast day in the church calendar for both immovable and movable feasts.
units.english_text: If one were to gaze through the central Holy Doors (the **Beautiful Gate** / *῾Ωραῖα Πύλη*) of the icon screen (**Iconostasis** / *Εἰκονοστάσιον*), one would observe small alcoves, marble shelves, or tables on either side of the eastern sanctuary wall. The alcove upon the left (north) is designated the **Prothesis**, while the corresponding area upon the right (south) is known as the **Diakonikon** (*Διακονικόν*). The distinct liturgical function of each within the Sanctuary is realized by the sacred vessels and implements that rest upon them and the sacred icons mounted upon the wall immediately behind them.

units.slavonic_text: *PROTHESIS (Πρόθεσις, ἡ): The small alcove or the table where the service of PROSKOMIDI takes place. This area is located inside the SANCTUARY on its north side.
units.english_text: Situated in the Sanctuary, the Prothesis is the appointed place where the Eucharistic Gifts of bread and wine are prepared during the morning office of **Orthros** (Matins), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. In addition, the Prothesis serves as the repository where the sacred Eucharistic vessels and implements—namely, the Holy Chalice (*Ποτήριον*), the Holy Paten (*Δισκάριον*), the Asterisk (*᾿Αστερίσκος*), the liturgical spear (*Λόγχη*), the communion cloths, the communion spoon (*Λαβίς*), and the veils—are preserved. Upon the wall behind the Table of Prothesis is traditionally depicted the icon of the Nativity of Christ or the Extreme Humility (*Ἄκρα Ταπείνωσις*).

units.slavonic_text: If one were to peer through the central BEAUTIFUL GATE of the IKONOSTASION, one would likely see small alcoves, marble shelves or tables on either side of the back wall of the Sanctuary. This area on the left is known as the PROTHESIS while the area on the right is known as the DIAKONIKON. The unique purpose of each in the Sanctuary is realized by the various items that rest upon them and the various icons that are found on the wall immediately behind them.

units.slavonic_text: Located in the SANCTUARY, the Prothesis is the place where the Eucharistic Gifts are prepared during the Morning MATINS Service (ORTHROS), prior to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy. Additionally, the Prothesis is the place where the Eucharistic items i.e., the Holy Chalice, the Holy Paten, the communion cloths, the spoon used to distribute the Holy Gifts, etc., are stored. On the back wall of the Prothesis is traditionally found the icon of the Nativity.

units.english_text: **PSALM** (*ψαλμός, ὁ*; Slav. *Psalom* / *Псаломъ*; lit. "a psalm, song of praise"): According to ancient monastic discipline, monks recited all 150 Psalms of the Psalter on a continual, recurring cycle. In early Christian antiquity, desert hermits recited the entire Psalter daily. With the historical emergence and spread of cenobitic (communal) monasticism, the practice was instituted of chanting the Canonical Hours in common, and the Psalter thus became the foundational bedrock of the Daily Office, augmented by liturgical hymnography, prayers, and scriptural lessons. The universal monastic custom of chanting through all 150 Psalms every week during the course of the divine offices was established in due course.

units.slavonic_text: PSALM (ψαλμός, ὁ): Lit. A Psalm. According to ancient practice, monastics would recite all 150 Psalms on a recurring basis. Originally, the hermits in the desert would recite the entire Psalter every day. With the spread of coenobitic (communal) monasticism, the practice began of chanting the Canonical Hours in common, and the Psalter thus became the foundation of the Daily Office, augmented by numerous hymns, prayers and scriptural readings. The custom of reciting all 150 Psalms each week during the course of the servies developed over time.

units.english_text: **PSALM 50** (*Ψαλμὸς Ν΄, ὁ*; Slav. *Psalom 50* / *Псаломъ 50*): This psalm is frequently abbreviated as *«ὁ Ν΄»* in the rubrics of the *Typikon*. It is the preeminent penitential psalm of King David, opening with the incipit: **"Have mercy on me, O God, according to Thy great mercy, and according to the multitude of Thy compassions blot out my transgression"** (*«Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου, καὶ κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν σου ἐξάλειψον τὸ ἀνόμημά μου...»*). Its complete text is contained in the liturgical Psalter (*Ψαλτήριον*).

units.english_text: **PSALM 119** (*Ψαλμὸς ΡΙΘ΄*): This psalm, which begins the **Eighteenth Kathisma** (*Δέκατον Ὄγδοον Κάθισμα, τό*) of the Septuagint Psalter, opens with the Greek incipit *Pros Kyrion* (*Πρὸς Κύριον*, "Unto the Lord"). The title **Ta Pros Kyrion** (*Τὰ Πρὸς Κύριον*) is the standard rubric abbreviation in the Violakis *Typikon* designating the entire Eighteenth Kathisma, which encompasses Psalms 119 through 133 inclusive (the fifteen Songs of Ascents / Gradual Psalms).

units.english_text: **PULPIT** or **AMBO** (*Ἄμβων, ὁ*; Slav. *Amvon* / *Амвонъ*; lit. "an elevated place, podium"): See also **AMVON**. The pulpit is an elevated platform or elaborate architectural podium situated forward of the icon screen (**Iconostasis**) upon the north (left) side of the **Soleas** (*Σολέα*). Embellished with iconographic representations of the Four Evangelists, it is the designated station from which the deacon or priest proclaims the Holy Gospel or delivers the homily.

units.slavonic_text: PULPIT (Ἄμβων, ὁ) Slav. Amvon, “an elevated place, a podium”. See also AMVON. The pulpit is a raised platform or elaborate podium in front of the icon screen (IKONOSTASION) at the left (north) side of the SOLEAS. Decorated with representations of the four Evangelists, it is the place from which the deacon or priest reads the Gospel or delivers his sermon. (From FL)

Such an individual is formally consecrated to these sacred duties by the bishop through the imposition of hands and appointed prayers in the rite of clerical tonsure.

units.slavonic_text: READER (Ἀναγνώστης, ὁ) Slav. Anagnost, Pricetnik, Chtets: The individual assigned to read, chant, and give responses in church services. Usually such a person will be blessed for these functions by the bishop with special prayers in a special ceremony called a “tonsure.”
units.english_text: **REFECTORY** (*Τράπεζα, ἡ*; Slav. *Trapeza* / *Трапеза*): The communal dining hall of a monastery. In Byzantine and Eastern monasticism, the Refectory is revered as a sacred liturgical extension of the church; in many monastic establishments, it is architecturally fashioned with an altar and icon screen. An icon of Christ or the Mother of God, before which a vigil lamp (*lambada*) burns perpetually, is always present. Specific liturgical offices are appointed to be celebrated in the Trapeza, such as the Rite of Mutual Forgiveness at the opening of Great Compline in monastic communities.[^666]

units.english_text: **RELICS** (*λείψανα, τά*; Slav. *Moshchi* / *Мощи*): The physical bodily remains of a canonized Saint, or sacred personal possessions such as garments or vestments hallowed by a saint's life. Holy relics are venerated with religious devotion throughout the Church. When a new church is consecrated, the consecrating bishop permanently encloses and seals holy relics within the Holy Altar Table (**Holy Table** / *Ἁγία Τράπεζα*), perpetuating the primitive Christian tradition wherein the Holy Eucharist was celebrated upon the tombs of the holy Martyrs.

units.english_text: **RIGHTEOUS SAINT**: In Eastern Christian hagiology, **Righteous** (*Δίκαιος, ὁ*; fem. *Δικαία, ἡ*; Slav. *Pravednyy* / *Праведный*) designates a lay or married saint of the Old or New Covenant who lived in holy obedience to God in the world (such as Righteous Joseph, or the Holy and Righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna). This title is distinct from that of a monastic ascetic, who is designated **Osios** (*Ὅσιος, ὁ*; Slav. *Prepodobnyy* / *Преподобный*, Venerable Monastic). See **OSIOS, OSIA**.

units.english_text: **RIPIDION** (*ῥιπίδιον, τό*; pl. **RIPIDIA** / *ῥιπίδια, τά*; Slav. *Ripida* / *Рипида*; lit. "a fan"): Derived from the Greek verb *ripizo* (*ῥιπίζω*, "to fan"). In liturgical practice, this motion of fanning is witnessed in the Eucharistic Anaphora when the priest fans or gently waves the **Aer** (*ἀήρ*) over the Holy Gifts prior to the consecratory epiclesis, reciting the prayer: *"So that they may be to those who partake of them for vigilance of soul, forgiveness of sins, communion of Thy Holy Spirit, fulfillment of the kingdom of heaven, confidence before Thee, and not in judgment or condemnation..."* (*«Ὥστε γενέσθαι τοῖς μεταλαμβάνουσιν εἰς νῆψιν ψυχῆς, εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν, εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ Ἁγίου σου Πνεύματος, εἰς βασιλείας οὐρανῶν πλήρωμα, εἰς παῤῥησίαν τὴν πρὸς σέ, μὴ εἰς κρῖμα ἢ εἰς κατάκριμα...»*). See also **AER** and **EXAPTERYGA**.

units.english_text: **SAKKOS** (*σάκκος, ὁ*; pl. *σάκκοι, οἱ*; Slav. *Sakkos* / *Саккосъ*; from Hebrew *saq*, sackcloth): The episcopal vestment (corresponding in form to the Western dalmatic) originally signifying a garment of humble sackcloth or tunic of mockery worn by Christ during His Passion. In modern liturgical usage, the Sakkos is a magnificent tunic tailored from rich brocade, modeled upon the imperial tunic bestowed by Byzantine emperors upon the Ecumenical Patriarch. Formerly reserved as an exclusive Patriarchal vestment, it is now worn by all bishops as the primary hierarchical vestment replacing the priestly **Phelonion** (**Felonion** / *φαιλόνιον*).

units.slavonic_text: SAKKOS (σάκκος, ὁ pl. σάκκοι, οἱ): The Sakkos (or in Western Christianity, the Dalmatic) was originally a ‘sackcloth’ garment symbolizing the garment of humility or tunic of disgrace worn by Christ during his trial and mockery. units.english_text: The Sanctuary of the Church is the Holy of Holies, the earthly reflection of the heavenly court wherein the sacred ministers, by the grace of God, unite with the angelic hosts in offering thanksgiving, adoration, and ceaseless praise unto our Heavenly Father. While possessing an exalted mystical dignity, it serves as the functional presbytery designed to facilitate the ceremonial actions of the clergy who officiate at the divine offices.

units.slavonic_incipit: the rising sun which is considered
units.slavonic_text: the rising sun which is considered to be a symbol or icon of the spiritual Son of God, Who will likewise rise from the East and illumine the world. However, because of local architectural circumstances, some churches may not be situated with the sanctuary exactly facing the east. In the center of the Sanctuary stands the ALTAR TABLE, at which the sacrament of the HOLY EUCHARIST takes place. The table of the PROTHESIS is situated on the north side of the Sanctuary while the area of the DIAKONIKON is situated on the south side.
units.english_text: No person may enter the sacred precincts of the Sanctuary unworthily or without the explicit blessing of the presiding priest. Clergy alone are appointed to minister within the altar, entering only after devout spiritual preparation to serve among the angels in the presence of God. Within the ecclesial body, clergy, laity, catechumens, and penitents occupy their designated stations, participating in the divine praises according to their ordained charisms within the royal priesthood of all believers. In these sacred spaces we fulfill our stewardship unto Christ, and "glorify God in every place of His dominion" (Ps. 102:22 LXX).

units.slavonic_incipit: The sanctuary of the Orthodox Church
units.slavonic_text: The sanctuary of the Orthodox Church is a holy place, a place where man, by the Grace of God, joins the angels in offering thanksgiving and all glory to our Heavenly Father. Even with its divine character, it remains a very functional place in the church. In other words, the Sanctuary like the NARTHEX and the NAVE is structured in such a manner to best facilitate the needs of those who utilize this sacred space, in this case, the clergy who officiate at Divine Services.

units.slavonic_incipit: No one should enter the sanctuary
units.slavonic_text: No one should enter the sanctuary unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for a specific task. Clergy alone are intended to enter into the altar, and then only after they have spiritually prepared to serve among the angels and glorify God as they are ever present in the Sanctuary or Holy of Holies. As clergy, as laity, as catechumens, and as penitents, we find our respective places within the structure of the Church. As we each participate in the services from our specific place we are distinguished according to our roles within the priesthood of all believers. It is in these places that we both realize our stewardship to Christ, and “glorify God in every place of His dominion.” (Modified from the Church of the Holy Cross, Belmont, CA: http://www.goholycross.org.

units.english_text: **SCALE** (*κλῖμαξ, ἡ*; *μουσικὴ κλῖμαξ, ἡ*): In music theory and acoustics, a scale is a structured sequence of musical tones arranged in ascending or descending pitch order. Scales are determined by the fundamental frequencies of their constituent pitches, providing a calibrated measure of musical intervals. The interval between two successive pitches is designated a scale step.

units.slavonic_incipit: SCALE: Generally, in music, a scale
units.slavonic_text: SCALE: Generally, in music, a scale is a sequence of musical tones in ascending or descending order. Scales are ordered by the pitch of the tone which is the position of a tone in the scale with the sound being determined precisely by the frequency of vibration of the source of the tone. Such ordering of tones provides a measure of musical distance. The distance between two successive notes in a scale is called an interval or scale step.
units.english_text: Diverse modal scales have developed across sacred musical cultures. In the sixth century B.C., Pythagoras formulated the mathematical ratios of the fundamental intervals: the octave (2:1), fourth (4:3), and fifth (3:2). In Christian antiquity, the ancient Greek tonal system was adapted into the eight ecclesiastical modes—the Byzantine **Oktoechos** (*᾿Οκτώηχος*, Tones 1 through 8) and Western church modes.

units.slavonic_text: In the science of acoustics, tones are measured by the frequency of their vibration numbers. Such frequencies are measured in cycles per second (CPS) or, in German, Hertz.
units.english_text: In Western ecclesiastical practice, the modal framework was gradually transformed by polyphony into the diatonic major and minor scales. The diatonic major scale comprises five whole tones (t) and two semitones (s) in the pattern: t–t–s–t–t–t–s (exemplified by the white keys of the keyboard from C to C′), which served as the foundation of classical Western musical architecture.[^670]

units.slavonic_incipit: In music, a tone is distinguished
units.slavonic_text: In music, a tone is distinguished from noise by having a definite frequency or pitch, caused by the regularity of the vibrations which produce it. Further, in addition to frequency, any tone will also possess the physical attributes of intensity (loudness), and quality (timbre or color); the latter helps identify the source of the tone (such as the voice or an instrument.)

units.english_text: cal tonality; tonality, in music, is the quality by which all tones of a composition are heard in relation to a central tone designated the keynote or tonic. The diatonic minor scale is based upon the interval sequence: tone–semitone–tone–tone–semitone–tone–tone (t–s–t–t–s–t–t). This arrangement produces the lower third, sixth, and seventh degrees characteristic of the minor mode; the higher seventh degree, situated a semitone rather than a whole tone below the primary note or "tonic," is frequently borrowed from the major mode for use at cadential resolutions. Until the close of the nineteenth century, the use and influence of the diatonic scale in Western music remained predominant.

units.english_text: Related to musical scales is the fundamental concept of key. In musical theory, the term "key" is employed to designate the scale from which the tonal material of a given composition is derived. To state, for example, that a composition is set in the key of C major signifies that it utilizes as its primary tonal material the intervals proper to that scale.

units.slavonic_text: cal tonality; tonality, in music, is the quality by which all tones of a composition are heard in relation to a central tone called the keynote or tonic. The diatonic minor scale is based on t-s-t-t-s-t-t. This arrangement produces the lower third, sixth, and seventh degrees that are characteristic of the minor mode; the higher seventh degree, a semitone rather than a whole tone below the main note, or “tonic,” is often borrowed from the major mode for use at cadences. Until the end of the 19th century, the use and influence of the diatonic scale in Western music was therefore predominant.
units.english_text: The conception of key developed wherein a home tone, or tonic, serves as the principal focus of a musical composition, while the remaining tones assume structural importance according to their harmonic relationship to the tonic. The increasing complexity of musical instruments necessitated more refined tuning systems for assigning specific pitches to the twelve Western pitch classes that constitute the octave. In standard usage, this procedure designates the method employed in the tuning of keyboard instruments.

units.slavonic_incipit: Related to musical scales is the
units.slavonic_text: Related to musical scales is the concept of key. In music, the term “key” is used to indicate the scale from which the tonal material of a given composition is derived. To say, for example, that a composition is in the key of C major means that it uses as its basic tonal material the intervals of that scale.
units.english_text: By the era of J. S. Bach, equal temperament—the calibrated adjustment of specific intervals from their mathematically pure acoustical ratios in order to establish a tuning system wherein music may modulate freely from key to key without unacceptable dissonance—had become firmly established. The resulting chromatic scale comprises twelve semitone intervals within the octave (represented by the white and black keys of the keyboard). Although the diatonic scale is fundamentally heptatonic (seven-toned), compositions set in standard major or minor tonality employ the remaining five tones of the chromatic scale as auxiliary or ornamental pitches. Music that employs them freely is characterized as highly chromatic, whereas music that employs them sparingly is designated diatonic.
