units.slavonic_text: Priest (Ἱερεύς, ὁ): (Note that his vestments are listed in the order in which they are vested.)
units.english_text: When vesting in the Sticharion, the priest takes it in his left hand, bows toward the East, and blesses the cross upon the back, proclaiming: **"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*). He continues: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον»*). He then recites the vesting prayer: **"My soul shall rejoice in the Lord, for He hath clothed me with the garment of salvation, and with the tunic of gladness hath He encompassed me; as a bridegroom He hath set a crown upon me, and as a bride hath He adorned me with ornament; always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Ἀγαλλιάσεται ἡ ψυχή μου ἐπὶ τῷ Κυρίῳ· ἐνέδυσε γάρ με ἱμάτιον σωτηρίου, καὶ χιτῶνα εὐφροσύνης περιέβαλέ με· ὡς νυμφίῳ περιέθηκέ μοι μίτραν, καὶ ὡς νύμφην κατεκόσμησέ με κόσμῳ [Isaiah 61:10]. Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.english_text: (2) The **Epitrachelion** (**Priestly Stole** / *ἐπιτραχήλιον, τό*; Slav. *epitrakhil* / *єпитрахиль*; from *epi*, upon, and *trachelos*, neck): The epitrachelion consists of a broad band of brocade worn about the neck and hanging straight down in front, permanently joined along its entire length. It signifies the outpouring of sacerdotal consecrating grace upon the priesthood (Psalm 132:2 [MT 133:2]). The priest, like the deacon, cannot celebrate any divine office without his stole. Vested in the Epitrachelion alone, without the **Phelonion** (*φαιλόνιον*), he celebrates the less solemn offices: Small Vespers, ordinary Compline, the Midnight Office (Greek *Mesonyktikon* / Slav. *Polunoshchnitsa*), and the Hours (when no Gospel is appointed to be read). At diverse prayer services (*treby*) in private dwellings, such as the prayer at the birth of a child or the blessing of homes, the priest likewise wears the Epitrachelion.[^700]

units.english_text: The **ZONE** (**Girdle** or **Belt** / *ζώνη, ἡ*; Slav. *poyas* / *поясъ*): A textile belt wherewith the priest girds himself over his Epitrachelion and Sticharion to secure them in place for convenience during divine service. It symbolizes the gift of spiritual strength wherewith God assists him in his sacerdotal ministry, and admonishes him unto purity and blamelessness of life. It likewise denotes the priest's readiness to serve the Lord and that he is bound unto Christ. In putting on this girdle, he blesses the cross embroidered upon it and prays: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Blessed is God Who girdeth me with strength, and hath made my way blameless"** (Psalm 17:33 [MT 18:32]); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεός, ὁ περιζωννύων με δύναμιν, καὶ ἔθετο ἄμωμον τὴν ὁδόν μου· Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.english_text: The **EPIGONATION** (*ἐπιγονάτιον, τό*, or *ὑπογονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *palitsa* / *палица*; from *epi*, upon, and *gonu*, knee): A stiffened, lozenge- or diamond-shaped piece of brocade suspended by a ribbon from the belt (Zone) over the right hip as an ecclesiastical award of distinction for a deserving priest (protoiereus, archpriest, or economos). Its historical origin is traced to the Byzantine imperial practice whereby emperors awarded ceremonial swords to military commanders in recognition of valor in defense of the empire. Such swords were accompanied by an elaborate thigh-shield suspended beneath the hilt to shield the warrior's leg from bruising caused by the motion of the scabbard. Spiritually, the Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:17). It is likewise interpreted mystically as symbolizing the linen towel wherewith the Lord girded Himself to wash the feet of the disciples at the Mystical Supper (John 13:4–5). In Slavic traditions, a priest awarded the Epigonation (*palitsa*) may previously have received the rectangular thigh-shield (Slav. *nabedrennik* / *набедренникъ*). The *nabedrennik* is likewise a stiffened brocade vestment, rectangular in shape, worn suspended over the right hip by a strap passed over the left shoulder. The *nabedrennik* is not utilized in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slavic usage, if a priest possesses only the *palitsa*, it is worn upon the right hip; if he has also been awarded the *nabedrennik*, the *palitsa* is transferred to the left hip, while the *nabedrennik* occupies the right hip.

units.slavonic_text: The EPIGONATION (Ἐπιγονάτιον, τό or Ὑπογονάτιον, τό), Slav. Palitsa) is a stiffened diamond shaped piece of brocade, which is suspended from the ZONI as an award of distinction for a priest. Its origin is traced to the practice of Byzantine Emperors awarding ceremonial swords to their military commanders in recognition of their valor in defending the empire. Such swords were often used with an elaborate thigh-shield which was suspended from the belt under the sword and protected the leg from bruising caused by the constant bumping of the sword against the thigh. The Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. It has also been explained as being symbolic of the towel with which the Lord girded himself to wash the disciples’ feet. In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored to wear the Epigonation or Palitsa may also be honored to wear the Thigh-shield (Slav. Nabedrennik). The Nabedrennik is also a stiffened brocaded fabric, rectangular in shape and worn over the right hip, suspended by a strap drawn over the left shoulder and attached to the two upper corners. It is not worn in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slav use, the Palitsa is worn over the right hip; however, if the Priest has also been awarded the use of a Nabedrennik, the Palitsa is worn over the left hip.

units.english_text: The **PHELONION** (**Felonion** / *φελόνιον* or *φαιλόνιον, τό*; Slav. *felon* / *фелонь* or *riza* / *риза*): The distinctive outer vestment of the priest. It is a long, sleeveless conical vestment resembling a cape, shortened in the front to facilitate the unhindered movement of his hands, with an opening for the head. The Phelonion is donned over all the other sacerdotal vestments.

units.english_text: It symbolizes the seamless robe and the purple mantle wherewith Christ was clothed during His Passion. It stands as a reminder that the priest is clothed with righteousness (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]) and thereby shielded from all iniquities. For many centuries, the phelonion (specifically the polystavrion) was likewise worn by bishops until it was replaced among hierarchs by the **Sakkos** (*σάκκος*). The Eastern phelonion corresponds historically and functionally to the Western chasuble.

units.slavonic_text: The FELONION (Φελόνιον, τό) is the distinguishing vestment of the Priest. It is a long, sleveless conical vestment similar to a cape, shortened in front to facilitate the movement of his hands and with an opening for his head. The Felonion is worn over all the other vestments.
units.english_text: When vesting with the Phelonion, the priest reverences the cross upon the back of the vestment as he prays: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thy priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and Thy holy ones shall rejoice with joy"** (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]); **"always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἱερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται· Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.english_text: The **SAKKOS** (*σάκκος, ὁ*; Slav. *sakkos* / *саккосъ*; lit. "sackcloth" or garment of penitential humility): In divine services, with the sole exception of the Phelonion, the bishop wears all the vestments of a priest. Originally, bishops likewise wore the phelonion (embellished as the polystavrion), but it was subsequently replaced by the Sakkos, a tunic-like garment with short half-sleeves, modeled after the imperial dalmatic of Byzantine emperors; as such, it constitutes a mark of high ecclesiastical honor and episcopal dignity. Symbolically, while recalling the mockery of the purple robe placed upon the Savior, it admonishes the bishop to ascend unto eminent holiness of life. As the Bishop vests with the Sakkos, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thy high priests, O Lord, shall be clothed with righteousness, and Thy holy ones shall rejoice with joy"** (Psalm 131:9 [MT 132:9]) (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς Σου, Κύριε, ἐνδύσονται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ οἱ ὅσιοί Σου ἀγαλλιάσει ἀγαλλιάσονται»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).[^705]

units.english_text: The **EPIGONATION** (*ἐπιγονάτιον, τό*, or *ὑπογονάτιον, τό*; Slav. *palitsa* / *палица*): A stiffened diamond-shaped piece of brocade suspended from the Zone (Belt) over the right hip, worn universally by all bishops as a mandatory pontifical vestment, whereas for priests it is granted only as an ecclesiastical award of distinction. Its origin is traced to the custom of Byzantine emperors presenting ceremonial swords to military generals for valor in defending the empire. These swords were accompanied by a padded thigh-shield suspended beneath the weapon to protect the thigh against friction while marching. Mystically, the Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Ephesians 6:17). It is likewise explained as symbolizing the towel wherewith the Lord girded Himself to wash the feet of the disciples (John 13:4–5). In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored with the Epigonation (*palitsa*) may also have been awarded the rectangular thigh-shield (Slav. *nabedrennik* / *набедренникъ*), which is worn over the right hip suspended from a strap over the left shoulder. The *nabedrennik* is not utilized in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slavic usage, if a priest possesses only the *palitsa*, it is worn upon the right hip; if he has also been awarded the *nabedrennik*, the *palitsa* is transferred to the left hip, while the *nabedrennik* is worn upon the right.

units.slavonic_text: The EPIGONATION (Ἐπιγονάτιον, τό or Ὑπογονάτιον, τό), Slav. Palitsa is a stiffened diamond shaped piece of brocade, which is suspended from the ZONI by all Bishops. It is an award of distinction for a priest. Its origin is traced to the practice of Byzantine Emperors awarding ceremonial swords to their military commanders in recognition of their valor in defending the empire. Such swords were often used with an elaborate thigh-shield which was suspended from the belt under the sword and protected the leg from bruising caused by the constant bumping of the sword against the thigh. The Epigonation represents the Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God. It has also been explained as being symbolic of the towel with which the Lord girded himself to wash the disciples’ feet. In the Slavic traditions, those priests honored to wear the Epigonation or Palitsa may also be honored to wear the Thigh-shield (Slav. Nabedrennik). It is also a stiffened brocaded fabric, rectangular in shape and worn over the right hip, suspended by a strap drawn over the left shoulder and attached to the two upper corners. It is not worn in the Byzantine Greek tradition. In Slav use, the Palitsa is worn over the right hip; however, if the Priest has also been awarded a Nabedrennik, the Palitsa is worn over the left hip.

units.english_text: worn when the bishop is vested for the Divine Liturgy from the beginning until the reading of the Holy Gospel. Thereafter, he is revested with the Small Omophorion, which is worn draped about the neck with both ends hanging down over the chest. The word *Omophorion*, signifying a "shoulder-covering," originally denoted a strip of woolen sheepskin worn over the shoulders by the aged and infirm for warmth. In later centuries, it was fashioned from the same rich fabric as the sacerdotal vestments; its spiritual origin, however, perpetually evokes the parable of the lost sheep which the Good Shepherd found and laid upon His own shoulders (Luke 15:4–6). Thus the bishop is reminded that he is entrusted to shepherd his flock safely and to seek untiringly the conversion and restoration of the erring. The Omophorion is the principal symbol of the bishop's apostolic, spiritual, and canonical jurisdiction; clergy and ecclesiastical communities subject to a hierarch's jurisdiction are said to be "under his Omophorion."

units.slavonic_text: worn when the Bishop is vested for the liturgy up to the the time of the reading of the Gospel. Thereafter he is revested with the short version. The word Omoforion meaning “shoulder covering” originally referred to a piece of sheepskin worn over the shoulders by the aged and infirmed for warmth. Later it was made out of the same material as the rest of the vestments, but its origin still recalls the parable of the lost sheep which the good shepherd found and laid on his shoulders. So too, the bishop is entrusted to safely guide his flock and be mindful of the conversion of the erring. The Omoforion is the symbol of the Bishop’s spiritual and ecclesiastical authority and clergy and ecclesiastical institutions subject to a bishop’s authority are said to be “under his Omoforion.”
units.english_text: The flourishing of the Byzantine Empire and the symphonia between Church and State exerted a profound influence upon the development of Eastern pontifical vestments, which have preserved their majestic form essentially intact unto the present day.

units.slavonic_incipit: The equivalent vestment for the Omoforion
units.slavonic_text: The equivalent vestment for the Omoforion in the usage of Western (Roman) Christianity is the archiepiscopal pallium or pal, the use of which is subject to different rubrics and restrictions, while all Orthodox bishops wear the Omoforion.
units.english_text: As the Bishop vests with the Omophorion, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. When Thou didst take upon Thy shoulders our human nature which had gone astray, O Christ, Thou didst ascend and offer it unto God Thy Father"** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. Ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων, Χριστέ, τὴν πλανηθεῖσαν ἄρας φύσιν, ἀναληφθεὶς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρὶ προσήγαγες»*). The Second Deacon then completes the prayer, saying: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.english_text: The **ENGOLPION** (*ἐγκόλπιον, τό*; from *en*, in/upon, and *kolpos*, chest or bosom; Slav. *nagrudnik* / *нагрудникъ*): The sacred badge worn upon the breast by both archpriests (formerly) and bishops, admonishing them that they must not only carry Christ within their hearts, but boldly confess Him before all mankind. Historically, the term *engolpion* included pectoral crosses and reliquary medallions; in modern usage, however, the designation applies primarily to an oval or circular medallion bearing an icon in enamel or relief, worn suspended by a chain over the chest by Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic hierarchs. Certain engolpia are hollowed to serve as reliquaries (*enkolpia-reliquaries*). All bishops wear a specific form of engolpion depicting the Mother of God, designated the **Panagia** (*Παναγία*).

units.english_text: When the Bishop vests with the **First Medallion** (**First Engolpion** / *Ἐγκόλπιον α΄*) or the **Panagia** (*Παναγία, ἡ*; lit. "All-Holy Lady")—a circular icon of our Savior and the Most Holy Theotokos hanging from a golden chain over the breast—it reminds the hierarch that he must perpetually bear in his heart the Lord and His all-pure Mother, the supreme Intercessor before God; and to this end, his heart must remain undefiled and his spirit upright. When the bishop vests with this first engolpion, the Second Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord."** (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν»*). The First Deacon then responds: **"Lord, have mercy."** (*«Κύριε, ἐλέησον»*), and continues: **"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me"** (Psalm 50:12 [MT 51:10]) (*«Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου»*). units.slavonic_text: The Engolpion (In Greek, something ‘worn on the chest’) is worn by both priests and bishops as a reminder that they should not merely carry Christ in their hearts, but also confess Him in the face of all men. Engolpion formerly also included pectoral crosses; however, today, the word Engolpion is used for a medallion with an icon in the center, worn as a vestment by Orthodox and Eastern Catholic bishops. Some Engolpia are hollow, for use as a reliquary. All bishops wear a particular kind of Engolpion called the Panagia (see below).

units.slavonic_incipit: When the Bishop is vested with
units.slavonic_text: When the Bishop is vested with the First Medallion (Ἐγκόλπιον α΄) or the Panagia (Παναγία, ἡ) or All-holy one—a small, circular Holy Image (Icon) of our Savior and the Birth-giver of God which hangs by a gold chain from the neck over the chest by a Bishop and reminds the Bishop that he must always bear in his heart the Lord and His holy Mother (the Theotokos or Panagia), the Intercessor before God; and, to that end, the Bishop’s heart must be pure and his spirit upright. When a bishop vests with the engolpion, the 2nd Deacon prays: “Let us pray to the Lord.” («Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν.») The 1st Deacon then prays “Lord, have mercy” («Κύριε, ἐλέησον.») and continues “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. (Psalm 50:10) («Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός, καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου.») The 2nd Deacon then completes the prayer saying “Always, now and ever and from all ages to all ages. Amen.” («Πάντοτε· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.»)

units.english_text: The **MITER** (*μίτρα*), also spelled *mitre*, is a richly embroidered and adorned domed crown or diadem representing the crown of thorns worn by Christ during His holy Passion, and serving as an insignia of the pastoral authority bestowed upon the bishop as an apostle and shepherd of the Church. It is worn by all hierarchs in episcopal orders and is patterned architecturally upon the imperial crown (*kamelaukion*) of the Byzantine emperors.

provenance.verbatim_source: The **MITER** (*μίτρα*), also spelled *mitre*, is a richly embroidered and adorned domed crown or diadem representing the crown of thorns worn by Christ during His holy Passion, and serving as an insignia of the pastoral authority bestowed upon the bishop as an apostle and shepherd of the Church. It is worn by all hierarchs in episcopal orders and is patterned architecturally upon the imperial crown (*kamelaukion*) of the Byzantine emperors.

units.slavonic_text: The Bishop’s liturgical head covering is the Episcopal Crown or Miter (MITRA).
units.english_text: It is historically improbable that the Christian episcopal miter was derived from the Old Testament high-priestly headdress (*miznephet*), since crown-like miters were not adopted by Eastern bishops until after the fall of Constantinople in the fifteenth century. While in Byzantine Greek usage the miter is reserved exclusively to hierarchs (bishops, metropolitans, and patriarchs), in Slavic praxis the privilege of wearing a miter has in recent centuries been granted to certain distinguished archimandrites and protopresbyters as an ecclesiastical decoration.

units.slavonic_text: The MITER (Μίτρα, ἡ), spelled by some as Mitre, is a richly embroidered crown or diadem representing the crown of thorns worn by Christ at His passion and serving as an emblem of the power bestowed upon the Bishop as minister of the Church. units.english_text: As the Bishop puts on the Miter, the First Deacon proclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. Lord, have mercy. Thou hast set upon his head a crown of precious stones; he asked life of Thee, and Thou gavest him length of days"** (Psalm 20:4–5 [MT 21:3–4]) (*«Τοῦ Κυρίου δεηθῶμεν. Κύριε, ἐλέησον. The Second Deacon then completes the prayer: **"Always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen."** (*«Πάντοτε, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν»*).

units.english_text: The **EAGLE** (**Aetos** / *ἀετός, ὁ*; Slav. *orlets* / *орлецъ*): A small circular or oval liturgical rug depicting an eagle with outspread wings soaring over a fortified city. The bishop stands upon this rug during divine services, and its use is reserved strictly and exclusively unto him. A larger Eagle-rug is placed beneath the bishop-elect during the rite of episcopal consecration, as prescribed in the Pontifical Archieratikon. The representation of the city denotes the bishop's pastoral oversight and canonical governance over his diocese, while the soaring eagle signifies the celestial loftiness and purity of orthodox theological doctrine. Thus the eagle-rug spread beneath the bishop symbolizes that in his life, virtue, and sacred teaching, he must emulate the eagle, which with keen vision soareth above all earthly and corruptible things, fixing its gaze upon heavenly realities.[^710]

units.english_text: The **MANDYAS** (*Μανδύας, ὁ*; mantle / Slav. *mantiya* / *мантія*): The mantle of the bishop is also a monastic garment, which, like a cloak, covers the whole body with the exception of the head. All monks, when present at divine services, must be robed in their mantles. The mantle is not technically speaking a liturgical vestment, but at Vespers and Matins (*Orthros*) it is worn when a bishop first arrives for the divine service and presides from the episcopal throne; it is later removed with assistance by the priests or deacons before he is vested for the Divine Liturgy. In Byzantine Greek practice, the bishop descends from the throne after the chanting of the Katavasiai, enters the sanctuary through the Holy Doors (*Royal Doors* / *Beautiful Gate*) where, after reverencing the Book of the Gospels lying upon the Holy Table, he proceeds to the Diakonikon where the mantle is removed, and if he is to celebrate the Divine Liturgy, he begins vesting with full episcopal vestments. In Slavic practice, after the bishop descends from the throne as described above, he proceeds to the center of the soleas where the mantle is removed and, if he is to celebrate, he is publicly vested for the Divine Liturgy with the assistance of the deacon or priest.

units.english_text: One peculiarity of a bishop's mantle is that it is not black, like the monastic mantle, but usually purple or of some other color. Upon it are sewn the so-called "Tables of the Law" (*Slav. Skrizhali* / *скрижали*), and, in particular, the "Fountains" (*Slav. Istotchniki* / *источники*). The *Tables* (square plaques of fabric sewn at the neck and feet) typify the Old and the New Covenants, from which the ministers of God must draw their doctrine. The *Fountains* are ribbons or stripes of textile, usually red and white in hue, sewn horizontally round about the mantle, representing the streams of divine teaching that flow from the mouth of the bishop. Small bells are attached to the mantle of a bishop, and to his Sakkos, as they were upon the hem of the robe of Aaron, the High Priest of the Old Testament.

units.slavonic_text: The MANDYAS (Μανδύας, ὁ) or mantle of the Bishop is also a monastic garment, which, like a cloak, covers the whole body with the exception of the head. All monks, when present at divine services, must be robed in their mantles. The Mantle is not technically speaking a liturgical vestment but in Vespers and Matins (Orthros) it is worn when a bishop first arrives for the service and is presiding from the episcopal throne; it is later removed with assistance by the priests or deacons before he is vested for the liturgy. In Greek Orthodox practice, the bishop descends from the Throne after the chanting of the KATAVASIE, enters the sanctuary through the BEAUTIFUL GATE where, after reverencing the book of the gospels lying on the altar table, he proceeds to the DIAKONIKON where the mantle is removed, and if he is to be the celebrant of the liturgy, he begins vesting with full episcopal vestments for the liturgy. In Slav. practice, after the bishop descends from the Throne as described above, he proceeds to the center of the soleas where the mantle is removed and, if he is to be the celebrant, he is publicly vested for the liturgy with the assistance of the deacon or priest.

The **ANTIRI** (*Ἀντίρι, τό*; Inner Cassock / *ὑπορράσον*, more often simply designated the *Rason*; Slav. *Podriasnik* / *подрясникъ* or *Zostiko*): A usually black garment, gathered at the waist with a narrow cloth belt or sash and tailored with a high collar buttoned in front. Unlike the Roman Catholic soutane or cassock, the Antiri does not have a long row of buttons extending down the front. It is usually worn beneath the liturgical vestments of all sacred clergy. The Antiri symbolizes the death of the clergyman to this world, his mystical burial, and his subsequent dedication unto God and His heavenly kingdom. It should be noted that the wearing of the inner and outer cassock is common to bishops, priests, deacons, monks, and nuns, and that the privilege of wearing a cassock is sometimes granted by a bishop unto seminarians, monastic novices, subdeacons, and readers. As for liturgical vestment colors, when the *Typikon* specifies anything concerning them, it distinguishes only "light" (*bright*) or "dark" vestments, so that local canonical tradition remains the governing standard.

units.english_text: The **VESTRY** (*Σκευοφυλάκιον, τό* or *Ἱεροφυλάκιον, τό*; sacristy / Slav. *sosudokhranilishche* / *сосудохранилище*): These Greek designations signify the sacred depository where the sacred vestments, holy vessels, and liturgical implements are securely preserved. In early Christian antiquity, the *Skevophylakion* was a separate architectural annex erected adjacent to the sanctuary wherein these holy items were kept when not in use. When required for the Divine Liturgy, they were solemnly carried into the temple in public procession. The Great Entrance of the Divine Liturgy today mystically recalls that ancient transfer.

units.english_text: The **VIGIL** (*Ἀγρυπνία, ἡ*; Slav. *Vsenoshchnoe Bdenie* / *Всенощное бдѣніе* / All-Night Vigil): Watchfulness, alertness, or vigilance; derived from the Greek verb *ἀγρυπνέω* (*agrypneo*), signifying to remain wakeful, watchful, or intently attentive upon a sacred duty. Hence, *agrypnia* denotes literally "without sleep" or "sleepless devotion" (Latin *invigilare*). In Byzantine practice, the All-Night Vigil comprises Great Vespers with the Liti and Artoklasia, Matins (*Orthros*), the First Hour, Third Hour, and Sixth Hour, culminating in the Divine Liturgy. If the Divine Liturgy is celebrated immediately following these offices, the First through the Sixth Hours may be omitted or recited separately. The All-Night Vigil, on account of its great length, is not customarily celebrated in ordinary parochial churches, though it is sometimes observed on major solemnities. In monasteries, it is regularly celebrated on Great Feasts of the Lord and the Mother of God, and on the patronal feast of the monastic community.

units.slavonic_text: VESTRY (Σκευοφυλάκιον, τὸ or Ἱεροφυλάκιον, τό): The titles in Greek mean an area where the Vestments or Holy things may be kept protected. In the earliest history of the church, the SKEVOFILAKION was a separate building adjacent to the SANCTUARY in which these items were stored when not in use. When they were needed for the Liturgy, they were carried into the Church in procession. The Great Entrance of the Divine Liturgy of today recalls this procession.

units.slavonic_text: VIGIL (Ἀγρυπνία, ἡ) Slav. Vsenoshnoe Bdenie: Watchfulness or vigilance; from the verb Ἀγρυπνῶ meaning to be ‘wakeful,’ ‘watchful’ or ‘awake,’ or ‘to be intent upon something.’ Hence, Ἀγρυπνία may be interpreted as ‘without sleep’ or ‘sleeplessness’ (Latin, invigilare). In Byzantine Orthodox practice, the All-Night Vigil follows Great Vespers including Liti and Artoklasia, Orthros, the First Hour, Third Hour, and Sixth Hour, and culminating with the Divine Liturgy. If the Divine Liturgy is celebrated immediately after any of the above offices, the First through the Sixth Hours may be omitted. The All-Night Vigil, because of its length, is not usually celebrated in the parishes; however, on major feast days, it is sometimes done. In monasteries, the service is commonly celebrated on Great Feasts and the patronal feast of the monastic community.

units.english_text: The Vima is separated from the Nave by the **Iconostasion** (*Eikonostasion* / icon screen). Up until the fourteenth century, a low waist-high marble chancel railing, designated the **Templon** (*τέμπλον*), separated these areas. Although the iconostasis physically partitions the sacred space within the temple, its mystical purpose is to unite humanity with the Divine: through the holy icons of Christ, the Mother of God, the angelic orders, and the saints, the earthly congregation joins in offering perpetual adoration unto the Holy Trinity.

units.slavonic_incipit: the sanctuary and is the third
units.slavonic_text: the sanctuary and is the third section in the Orthodox house of worship. As the NARTHEX was historically the place of the penitent and the catechumens and the NAVE was the place of the faithful, the SANCTUARY is the place of the clergy. Although the penitent and the catechumens today find themselves integrated with the faithful in the nave, the sanctuary continues to be the place of the presbyters of the CHURCH.
units.english_text: Regardless of the physical orientation of a local church building, the sanctuary remains an awe-inspiring, holy place. None may enter the Vima unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for an assigned ministry. Sacred clergy and blessed servers alone may enter within the sanctuary, and only after preparing themselves with prayer to stand before the Holy Table and minister alongside the unseen angelic hosts who perpetually surround the Holy of Holies. While all the baptized participate in the royal priesthood of believers according to their respective orders, the sacred ministers execute their stewardship before Christ that all may "glorify God in every place of His dominion" (Psalm 102:22 [MT 103:22]).

units.slavonic_incipit: Regardless of the direction the local
units.slavonic_text: Regardless of the direction the local church faces, the sacred space remains an awesome place. No one should enter the Vima unworthily or without the blessing of the priest for a specific task. Clergy alone are meant to enter into the altar, and then only after the clergy have spiritually prepared to glorify God and serve among the angels who are ever present in this the ‘Holy of Holies’. As clergy, as laity, as catechumens, and as the penitent, we find our respective places within the structure of the Church. As we celebrate the Divine Liturgy from our place we are distinguished according to our roles within the priesthood of all believers and It is in these places that we both realize our stewardship to Christ, and “glorify God in every place of His dominion.”

units.english_text: In contemporary liturgical usage, the **Ypakoe** is the title of the proper Resurrectional troparion chanted during Sunday Matins (*Orthros*). It changes according to the appointed Tone of the week from the Octoechos, occurring immediately after the Evlogitaria (*Resurrectional Troparia with the refrain from Psalm 118:12 [MT 119:12]*: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord, teach me Thy statutes"** / *«Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά Σου»*). The Ypakoe of Pascha is the most renowned instance of this genre, chanted after the Third Ode of the Paschal Canon, during the Paschal Hours, and following the Little Entrance at the Paschal Divine Liturgy.

units.english_text: In the Greek language, *ypakoe* signifies "obedient hearing" or attentive listening (from *hypo*, under, and *akouo*, to hear). The designation indicates a musical and theological response, taking the form of a proper Troparion. Historically and rubrically, the Ypakoe is appointed: (1) at Sunday Compline; (2) at the Sunday Midnight Office; (3) at Sunday Matins before the Antiphons of the Tones and the Matins Gospel; and (4) after the Third Ode of the Matins Canon, taking the place of the Kathisma Hymn (*modified from APL*).

units.slavonic_incipit: Today, the Ypakoi is the title
units.slavonic_text: Today, the Ypakoi is the title of a hymn sung during Resurrectional Matins. It varies according to the Mode of the week from the Oktoichos and comes after the Resurrectional hymns which are sung together with the refrain from Ps. 119: “Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your statutes” («Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε, δίδαξόν με τὰ δικαιώματά Σου.») The Ypakoi of Pascha is the one most commonly known. It is sung after the third ode of the Paschal Canon, during the Paschal Hours, and again after the Small Entrance in the Paschal Divine Liturgy.
units.english_text: Furthermore, the Ypakoe serves as a short poetic strophe that replaces the third Kathisma hymn at Sunday Matins and upon certain Great Feasts of the Lord. In common parish praxis it is read rather than chanted. In Byzantine Greek usage it is also read during the Sunday Hours in place of the Kontakion. In strict Athonite monastic practice, it is chanted at the Divine Liturgy after the Dismissal Troparia (lit. "Apolytikia", *ἀπολυτίκια*) and before the Kontakia (*AE*).

units.slavonic_text: Furthermore, the Ypakoi is a short hymn that takes the place of the third poetic Kathisma at Matins on Sundays and some great Feasts. It is normally read and not sung. units.english_text: The **ZONE** (*Ζώνη, ἡ*; belt, girdle / Slav. *Poyas* / *поясъ*): The liturgical belt surrounding the Sticharion and securing the Epitrachelion in place. The Zone corresponds historically and functionally to the cincture of the Western Church. Symbolically, the Zone denotes the divine power and fortitude wherewith the sacred priest is girded for holy service (*modified from Byzantines.net*).

units.english_text: The **ZOODOCHOS PEGE** (*Ζωοδόχος Πηγή, ἡ*; Life-Giving Spring): Literally, "Life-Receiving or Life-Giving Spring." This is the feast and title bestowed upon the miraculous shrine and spring dedicated to the Most Holy Theotokos situated at Baloukli (*Eptapyrgos*) outside the walls of Constantinople. The sanctuary was originally founded in the mid-fifth century during the reign of Emperor Leo I the Great (*Makelles*). The Orthodox Church commemorates the consecration of this sacred shrine annually on Bright Friday (the Friday of Renewal Week following Pascha).

units.slavonic_text: *ZOODOCHOS PIGI (Ζωοδόχος Πηγή, ἡ) Lit. “life-containing fountain or spring.” This is the name given to a miraculous spring in the church dedicated to the Theotokos. The spring was erected in Eptapyrgos, near Constantinople, in the middle of the 5th century, during the reign of the emperor Leo the Great (called Makelis). The Orthodox Church commemorates the consecration of this sacred edifice every year on the First Friday of Easter.

units.english_text: 42. The Typikon of the Laura of St. Savvas (Sabbas) the Sanctified (439–532), situated in the wilderness of Judea, was derived from the ancient Typikon of Jerusalem consisting of liturgical ordinances handed down unto St. Savvas by St. Euthymius the Great (377–473) and St. Theoktistos († 467), which derived in turn from the ascetic rules established by St. Chariton the Confessor († 350). The monastic Typikon of St. Savvas, damaged and scattered during ancient devastations of the Palestinian monasteries, was collected and reconstituted by St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem (550–638), and subsequently reedited by St. John of Damascus († 749). These historical notices are preserved in ancient Melkite Christian Arabic sources (*see the Melkite Typikon portal at <http://www.typicon.com/>*).

units.slavonic_text: 42. The Typikon of the St. Savvas (Sabbas) (439-532) Monastery, situated in the desert of Judea, was derived from the Typikon of Jerusalem consisting of rules and regulations handed down to St. Savvas by St. Efthimios (Euthymius) the Great (377-473) and by St. Theoktistos (+467), derived, in turn, from rules started and compiled originally by St. Chariton the Confessor (+350). The St. Savvas Typikon, destroyed during the destruction and desecration of the monasteries of Palestine, was assembled and reconstituted by St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem (550-638) and further reconstituted by St. John Damascene (+749). All of this information originates in Melkite Arabic sources. See the Melkite cybertyptypikon athttp://www.typicon.com/.
